Obtaining a transit feed is a common method for accessing public transportation data, but accessing these feeds requires knowledge of their data model, the Transport Maximum File (TMX) specification. Consequently, many developers struggle to acquire these feeds because they lack understanding of the TMX data model. This paper introduces a machine learning approach that enables machines to learn the TMX specification by analyzing examples of transit feeds. Our work addresses three key challenges: first, we define the problem of making the TMX specification available and explore data-driven learning as a solution; second, we develop a neural architecture to solve this issue, demonstrating superior performance over baseline models through experimental validation; and third, we evaluate the generalizability of our solution by testing the trained model against feeds from cities beyond its training data. We validate this generalization experimentally, proposing a new metric to assess schema learning capabilities. Our results indicate that the trained model excels at identifying attributes that are consistent across all feeds. The code for this project is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2001/tmx-spec-learning. Furthermore, this work serves as a foundational step toward enabling machines to link transit feeds to high-level data models, a task we show is feasible by validating connections between feed attributes and higher-level models using our learned recurrent neural network. Future research will focus on developing methods to validate these links and applying them to specific use cases. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant no. 1908874. Few-shot learning seeks to identify new categories based on a minimal number of labeled examples. This study investigates few-shot classification at the class level, where multiple instances of several classes are provided during training, and only a single instance per novel class is presented during testing. Existing approaches typically rely on prototypes derived from all available training instances of a class. However, in class-level settings, a single instance can be highly representative of the class. Consequently, we propose a straightforward yet effective method for class-level few-shot classification by leveraging prototypes from selected few instances. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods on this task. The code and experimental results can be accessed at https://github.com/soheilshahabi/few-shot-classification. Furthermore, this repository has been utilized to evaluate several novel proposals at NEURLC 2021 for few-shot image classification. Finally, our findings indicate that few-shot class-ification represents a distinct and challenging problem that warrants further research.

We investigate systems featuring an infrared non-invertible symmetry, demonstrating that a non-compact version of the Goldstone theorem applies. When a continuous non-invertible symmetry is spontaneously broken, the theorem yields two key results: the emergence of a gapless mode and a specific constraint on the symmetry group of the effective action for that mode. This last condition is distinctive and could potentially signal the presence of the non-invertible symmetry itself. Furthermore, we examine examples illustrating that the non-invertible symmetry constraint is more than just a restatement of an invertible symmetry constraint, and we analyze the implications this has for systems with boundary conditions. Finally, we outline how to extend this argument to higher-dimensional systems possessing non-invertible higher-form symmetries. A directed graph is semi-transitive if and only if it is acyclic and satisfies the condition that for any directed path $u_1 \rightarrow u_2 \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow u_t$ where $t \geq 2$, either the edges $u_1 \rightarrow u_2, u_2 \rightarrow u_3, \ldots, u_{t-1} \rightarrow u_t$ do not form a directed $k$-cycle for any $k \geq 3$, or the edge $u_1 \rightarrow u_t$ exists. It has been established that every split graph possesses a semi-transitive orientation. In this study, we examine two specific classes of semi-transitive graphs: those with a minimum degree of at least $n-1$ and comparability graphs. Additionally, we present a semi-transitive closure operation that transforms an arbitrary graph into a semi-transitive one. Finally, we demonstrate that for any graph $G$, there exists a split graph $H$ such that $G$ is a minor of $H$, provided that the maximum degree of $H$ does not exceed $n(G) + \Delta(G) - 1$. This bound is proven to be tight. Our work generalizes findings by Bouchet, which were subsequently applied by Bouchet, Le Saout, and Maurel to establish the existence of semi-transitive orientations for every graph. We further present applications of this existence theorem. Specifically, we determine that every graph $G$ admits a semi-transitive orientation with an out-degree of at most $\lceil\frac{3n(G)}{2}\rceil - 2$, improving upon the previous bound of $\lceil\frac{4n(N)}{3}\rceil - 2$. This letter introduces the application of a deep neural network (DNN) for distinguishing hadronic tau decays from hadronic jets produced by quarks and gluons within proton-proton collisions. The network architecture features five hidden layers, each containing 128 nodes, followed by a single output node. Performance metrics indicate an efficiency of 53% with an average jet DNN response of 0.425, compared to 52% at a mean b-tagged jet DNN response of 0.425 for rejecting hadronically decaying tau leptons. This approach represents a significant enhancement over the prior best method, which offered 55% efficiency with a mean b-tagged jet response of 0.5. These results demonstrate that hadronic tau decays can be identified with substantially improved signal-to-background ratios, a capability that is critical for the LHCb experiment's physics objectives. Furthermore, the success of this technique for hadronic tau decays suggests that similar DNN approaches could be adapted for identifying leptonic tau decays and detecting taus in environments with large backgrounds from bottom and charm quark jets. Future surveys like the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will generate vast amounts of data, including billions of images and petabytes of time-series information, requiring advanced machine learning techniques for analysis. This work introduces a Bayesian approach to Neural Networks designed for such large-scale tasks. Utilizing a new implementation of Bayesian back-propagation for Multi-Layer Perceptrons, we demonstrate that this method can identify binary classes within massive datasets while quantifying the uncertainty associated with each classification. We validate the efficacy of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) through two simulated cases: single-classification and multi-classification, demonstrating their performance in the limit of big data. Furthermore, we show that these approaches are highly effective for large-scale data analysis, offering superior accuracy and uncertainty quantification compared to other methods. Additionally, we confirm that Bayesian layers can be integrated into Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), a fact we illustrate within the context of image classification for astronomical time series data. Finally, we provide the code for all Bayesian back-propagation layers at our GitHub repository. This tool is easily adaptable to other network architectures, including ResNets, and supports a wide range of functions beyond the ReLU used in our examples. The software is freely accessible at https://github.com/fernandoalvarez/PyBNN. The code was developed and tested on a cluster featuring 128 nodes, each equipped with 2.4 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2650 processors and 64 GB of RAM. Our PyBNN implementation leverages the PyTorch library, which offers the same computational efficiency and scalability as standard PyTorch back-propagation layers. Consequently, the PyBNN code is well-suited for the "big data" era of the Rubin survey. This paper was prepared using the Springer Nature Latex macro package. By leveraging a perturbation method, we created a scalable model for intermodal coupling in PCFs, utilizing a simplified geometry based on the effective index of core air holes. This approach facilitates a rapid and intuitive estimation of the intermodal Brillouin gain coefficient, identifying a suitable fiber design for intermodal coupling. Furthermore, we demonstrated a double-peaked intermodal Brillouin gain spectrum, resulting from the interaction between these two optical modes, which shows promise for applications in intermodal sensing and multiplexing. Additionally, we analyzed the impact of air holes situated away from the core on the coupling strength and identified an optimal configuration that maximizes it. These findings offer a beneficial pathway for achieving high nonlinearity in PCFs, particularly for solid-core designs intended for wavelength division multiplexing. Finally, we provide a comprehensive design framework for optimizing intermodal Brillouin gain in solid-core PCFs. This strategy is applicable to various other phenomena, such as intermodal dispersion management, multiplexing, and mode division multiplexing. Finally, we outline a practical approach for fabricating this optimized fiber design. By strategically arranging air holes around the core, we successfully transformed a single-mode fiber into one supporting two modes with strong intermodal coupling. The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP) are both NP-hard combinatorial optimization challenges. In these scenarios, one must select a subset of items with associated costs from a given collection to fit within a specific budget, thereby maximizing coverage. Coverage is determined by a family of sets where each item belongs to one or more sets, and the union of selected items defines the total covered area. While both problems can be modeled identically, they differ in that BMCP assumes a uniform cost of 1 for all items, whereas SUKP allows varying costs. This study introduces a novel local search approach utilizing a new neighborhood structure designed for efficiency and effectiveness. We employ the A* algorithm to identify improved solutions from any starting point, regardless of whether they are initial or local optima. Additionally, we implement a new strategy to eliminate redundant neighborhood moves and propose a hybrid method that integrates our approach with an existing local search technique. Extensive numerical experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art in both performance and runtime. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/SUKP. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence comparing our results against existing solutions for the BMCP. Finally, we outline several practical applications of these problems. SUKP is highly relevant for real-world tasks such as sensor network deployment, where sensors have varying costs and cover regions defined by their locations. BMCP serves as a powerful tool for resource allocation, exemplified by selecting an optimal subset of news outlets to purchase for maximizing audience reach within a fixed budget. These outcomes are supported by extensive empirical testing. Our results indicate that SUKP is generally harder to solve than BMCP, with the difficulty increasing as the number of available items grows. Consequently, our proposed approach is particularly effective for handling large-scale instances. Our findings suggest that the new approach offers superior performance compared to existing methods, achieving up to a 1000-fold improvement in solution quality. Furthermore, the novel mechanism for removing redundant neighborhoods can substantially reduce computation time. The current state-of-the-art for SUKP relies on simulated annealing, which is computationally expensive and lacks the ability to explore the solution space as thoroughly as our proposed method. In contrast, our approach offers the dual advantage of delivering high-quality solutions from any initial state while maintaining computational efficiency. Churn prediction in online gambling is a business-critical challenge, yet it remains underexplored in both theoretical and practical research. This study investigates two distinct datasets from online gambling operators to evaluate the predictive performance of various machine learning models. Through a comprehensive analysis of model performance and feature importance using statistical methods, the work aims to provide statistically supported insights for data scientists and analysts to enhance model performance. The results indicate that XGBoost and Logistic Regression are the most effective models for predicting churn in online gambling. Additionally, the study offers a detailed examination of feature selection and their impact on churn prediction. Finally, the authors propose several avenues for future research. We establish that gluon transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions (TMDs) can be derived from Euclidean formulations via large-momentum effective theory (LaMET). Specifically, we demonstrate that multi-gluon TMDs can be reconstructed from light-front-averaged gluon correlators, which are Euclidean quantities computable through lattice QCD. Furthermore, we examine how certain gluon TMDs exhibit connections to physical observables in semi-inclusive and inclusive deep-inelastic scattering. Finally, utilizing this framework, we calculate the gluon PDF for the proton at zero transverse momentum, $\textrm{PDF}(x,0)$, for the first time. This result is derived from the gluon correlator $\Phi_{gg}(0,b_\perp)$, which is computed in lattice QCD using quark-meson and staggered quark actions on $6^3\times 12$ lattices at a pion mass of $m_\pi=450$ MeV. Our findings indicate that $\Phi_{gg}(0,b_\perp)$ is non-zero and that ${\rm Re}\left[\Phi_{gg}(0,b_\perp)\right]$ maintains a positive sign, aligning with expectations for the proton PDF at zero transverse momentum. These outcomes provide a foundational approach for determining the gluon PDF from first principles. Additionally, our work offers valuable insights for future lattice calculations aiming to extract gluon TMDs, including the necessary renormalization factors and the potential impact of topological smearing on these extractions. Finally, we present preliminary results regarding the extraction of the gluon PDF on a $9^3\times 32$ lattice, alongside the anticipated effects of finite lattice spacing. These results underscore the efficacy of the large-momentum framework and suggest that zero-transverse-momentum gluon PDFs can be accurately obtained via lattice QCD. This achievement is expected to yield significant insights into the gluon PDF, including its non-perturbative structure and small-$x$ behavior. Furthermore, the methodology established here may facilitate future efforts to extract gluon TMDs directly from first principles. To achieve this, the methodology must be rigorously validated through extensive calculations on larger lattices with finer spacings. We conclude by outlining the steps required to validate the large-momentum framework for gluon TMDs and by discussing the current status of these efforts. Ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions (URHC) offer a unique platform for investigating photon-physics, particularly through ultra-peripheral collisions (UPC) where the primary interaction mode involves photon-photon or photon-nucleus processes. A critical factor in these interactions is the electromagnetic form factor, which describes the photon-nucleus coupling. This study examines the accuracy of the commonly used point-like form factor across various scenarios. By calculating photon-nucleus cross-sections and their correlations with secondary electron-positron pairs, we find that the point-like approximation is valid only for high-transverse-momentum particles. For low transverse-momentum electron-positron pairs, the form factor exhibits significant dependence on the photon energy, making the long-range (exponential) model more appropriate than the short-range (power-law) model. Furthermore, the low transverse momentum of electron-positron pairs is highly sensitive to the precise form factor. These findings suggest that UPC data can be utilized to constrain the exact nature of the form factor. Additionally, we explore the potential of these measurements to address the recently observed anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. Finally, we propose that the transverse momentum spectrum of electron-positron pairs, especially those within the inner shell, could serve as a valuable tool for calibrating the URHC photon flux. These conclusions are based on theoretical calculations utilizing the two-source impact-parameter dependent photon flux and the Weizsäcker-Williams approximation. Our analysis covers a broad energy range, from LHC energies to those of existing and upcoming heavy-ion accelerators. Furthermore, the methodology employed is general and applicable to photon-photon collisions in general-purpose colliders. This work is intended to serve as a reference for photon flux calculations in URHC. All findings are supported by comprehensive theoretical reasoning. Our results indicate that the point-like approximation is insufficient for accurately modeling the entire photon flux spectrum, especially at low photon energies. The ultimate goal of this research is to establish a more precise and reliable model for the URHC photon flux. To achieve this, we have developed a new code, `epu`, which incorporates the most recent theoretical advancements in photon flux calculations. This new code is publicly available for the scientific community. We hope that our work will contribute to a more accurate and reliable understanding of the URC photon flux. Our findings suggest that the exponential form factor provides a better description of the data than the power-law form factor. For cyclists, traffic accidents often result in fatalities or severe injuries, yet the rapid increase in cycling has prompted many cities to promote it as a sustainable mode of transport. To mitigate these risks, this study introduces a dynamic accident probability estimator for shared two-wheeler traffic, utilizing machine learning and computer vision on video footage. The method first detects cyclists and vehicles, then extracts behavioral features from the motion data. Subsequently, a regression model predicts accident probability based on these behavioral characteristics. Finally, the system integrates dynamic behaviors with environmental factors, such as traffic volume, to generate accident risk descriptors. Experimental results indicate that the proposed dynamic accident probability estimator achieves a mean absolute error of 0.039, outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, the generated risk descriptors are displayed to cyclists via an augmented reality interface, enabling them to navigate routes with lower accident probabilities. This approach is designed to be adaptable to various cities by learning from local accident and environmental data. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of accident probability estimation within shared two-wheeler traffic. The source code is available at https://github.com/Deepak-Pradhan/Deepak-Pradhan-Dynamic-Accident-Estimator. The paper is expected to be released via Springer in 2022. This work was conducted as a final year project at the University of the West of England, Bristol, UK. The authors welcome any feedback. Please contact: deepak.pradhan@uwe.ac.uk.

Control Barrier Functions (CBF) are extensively employed to guarantee barrier certificate validity, thereby ensuring forward invariance within state spaces defined by a barrier function. This paper introduces a method for motion planning that utilizes a CBF-based cost function and the associated barrier certificates to ensure safety for both linear and nonlinear dynamical systems featuring uncertain parameters. The proposed approach is robust against control input perturbations and maintains the ability to reach the target state despite such uncertainties. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the optimization problem remains a convex program for both linear and affine systems. For nonlinear systems, the analysis identifies a sufficient condition under which the barrier certificate's validity can be approximated by the solution to the resulting optimization problem. Additionally, numerical simulations are presented to illustrate the application of these CBF-based motion planning costs across various motion planning scenarios. The results indicate that the proposed CBF-based cost effectively balances safety and reachability, successfully navigating obstacles in both static and time-varying forms while reaching the target state. These findings are particularly relevant for uncertain nonlinear systems, such as mobile robots, where the CBF-based cost offers a means to achieve safe target reachability. The paper concludes with an overview of the authors' ongoing research in this area. Specifically, a CBF-based cost incorporating time is developed for uncertain systems to achieve safe motion planning with guaranteed target reachability. This formulation ensures the system arrives at the target state within a specified time window, thereby enhancing efficiency. Initial results for this approach are presented for a mobile robot featuring a differential drive kinematic model. Finally, the paper addresses future work, which includes developing CBF-based motion planning methods for systems subject to uncertain dynamics constraints. In this scenario, CBFs are utilized to enforce velocity constraints that respect uncertain dynamic limits, such as unknown traction capabilities of mobile robots. The outcome of this research is a CBF-based motion planning algorithm that simultaneously ensures safe trajectory tracking and adherence to uncertain dynamic constraints. This represents a significant advancement in CBF-based motion planning, as it enables the safe navigation of uncertain systems through unknown dynamic environments. Initial results for this application are demonstrated using a mobile robot with a simplified dynamics model. The study also highlights another future research direction: extending CBF-based motion planning to uncertain systems operating in uncertain time. Current CBF-based costs rely on time as a parameter, whereas the proposed approach treats time as a random variable. This article investigates the covering numbers of various ring types. A key result establishes that $\operatorname{cov}(R) = 1 + \frac{|R|}{|R - \{0\}|}$. We further examine rings possessing a unique element with additive inverse, obtaining the inequality $\operatorname{cov}(R) \ge \left\lceil \frac{|R|}{\left\lceil \frac{|R|}{2}\right\rceil} \right\rceil$. Nonlocal conservation laws, distinguished by flux functions that depend on a weighted history of the conserved quantity rather than solely on its current state, offer a framework for analyzing traffic dynamics. This study examines the singular behavior of a specific class of these models, where the kernel is not necessarily symmetric or Gaussian. By analyzing the associated formal hyperbolic conservation law derived from rescaling, we establish the admissibility criteria for discontinuous solutions and investigate the convergence of the nonlinear problem to its singular limit. Our approach relies on the relative entropy method, where the explicit form of the kernel is substituted with an appropriate inequality. This allows us to demonstrate the logarithmic integrability of the rescaled density, a key requirement for defining admissibility shock speeds and proving $L^1$-convergence. Furthermore, for a broad category of kernels, we derive an explicit error estimate regarding the convergence rate of the nonlinear problem to its singular limit, demonstrating that this rate scales with the separation between the nonlocal and local problems. These findings are substantiated by numerical experiments. Dilation surfaces extend the concept of translation surfaces by allowing atlas transitions to include local dilation factors. These surfaces possess a singular flat metric characterized by a Euclidean isometry group that acts freely and properly discontinuously away from a set of measure zero. Unlike translation surfaces, orbifolds with a Euclidean quotient are permitted within dilation surfaces. This paper investigates geometric and topological features of dilation surfaces, with a specific focus on interval exchange systems and polygonal billiards. We demonstrate that a generic dilation surface lacks a horizontal horizon saddle connection, meaning no horizontal leaf of the horizontal foliation connects two singularities. This result serves as an analogue to Masur's interval exchange ergodicity conjecture. Furthermore, we establish that if a dilation surface exhibits hyperbolic dynamics, it is generic in the sense that its stable manifold under the renormalization map has a Hausdorff dimension of zero. This finding parallels recent work by Avila, Kucherenko, and Kuchment regarding interval exchange systems. Additionally, we provide a sufficient condition for interval exchange surfaces to be Masur-type: if all horizon saddle connections are non-generic, then all cone angles are non-multiples of $\pi/2$. Finally, for translation surfaces supporting a Morse-Smale dilation vector field with a finite number of singularities, we prove that the set of directions containing horizon saddle connections is finite, offering an affirmative answer to a question posed by Schmiedendahl. These findings are supported by computational evidence, theoretical insights, and illustrative examples. Our approach to horizon saddle connections draws inspiration from recent research on translation surfaces, interval exchange systems, and polygonal billiards. Furthermore, our work contributes to the broader objective of generalizing concepts from translation surfaces to dilation surfaces. This work introduces a conditional Gaussian process model designed to approximate the joint distribution of two stochastic processes while conditioning on an observation of one. By applying Hahn-Banach extension theory, we derive the mean and covariance functions for the unobserved process. Our findings reveal that conditional sampling occurs via an integral operator featuring a degenerate kernel, effectively projecting the process onto a finite-dimensional subspace. We support this theoretical framework with numerical simulations and a case study demonstrating a forecast model enhanced by an economic indicator. Additionally, we propose a Bayesian variant incorporating a Dirichlet prior over subspace dimension selection. To address the resulting high-dimensionality, we employ random feature techniques alongside a novel dimensionality reduction method based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence. This approach facilitates efficient inference and rapid sampling from the posterior. Empirical results indicate that integrating Bayesian techniques with the proposed model can outperform standard Gaussian process regression for both simulation datasets and real-world applications. Furthermore, we illustrate how this framework can be adapted to estimate posterior distributions of dynamical systems by conditioning on observed data. Finally, we present an application to an agent-based model of a double auction market, where our model successfully infers the unobserved dynamics of the price process from transaction time series. This enables the construction of a confidence band for price evolution and a forecast for future prices. Our results suggest that the confidence bands for future prices are significantly narrower than those of traditional Gaussian process models, and the forecast errors are reduced by 10% to 20%. We also demonstrate how to generate price paths consistent with historical observations using our framework. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of Gaussian process regression to non-equilibrium economic time series. We provide a comprehensive R package to ensure the reproducibility of all code and experiments. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. Top tagging is a technique designed to distinguish between signal and background events in top quark studies. Since the discriminative power of top-tagged jets relies on subtle differences between signal and background, we propose a novel machine learning interpretation approach that quantifies how well specific features separate these two classes. By integrating advanced gradient-based methods with Shapley value theory, we can efficiently calculate the impact of individual features to optimally interpret results from graph neural networks. We applied this methodology to analyze the performance of a top tagger based on a graph neural network, which operates on jet constituents within the tracker and calorimeter systems. This tagger is integrated into an enhanced version of the METoNel graph neural network framework, which incorporates a metanetwork to refine the metadata used for training. Our findings indicate that the tagger excels at reconstructing the top quark's hadronically decaying W boson, with reconstructed $b$-jets playing a secondary role. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the performance of METoNel and the advanced top tagger can be interpreted through the lens of their constituent features. These results offer valuable insights for the design and optimization of future top taggers. In coadded image deconvolution, the most prevalent method involves convolving the point spread functions (PSFs) of individual images prior to the deconvolution process. However, this approach is strictly accurate only if all images in the stack share identical PSFs. When all PSFs are known, a practical approximation for cosmological applications can be achieved by calculating a weighted average PSF, where the weights correspond to the integration time for each specific image. This paper examines the mathematical basis of this approximation and investigates the resulting errors. The analysis is applied to a weak lensing cosmological study, with the primary conclusion being that the relative errors in the effective PSF are typically negligible, though they can become significant in specific cases. A Python library is provided to facilitate this approximation, with a usage example available as a Jupyter notebook. This study examines the fracture toughness of brittle, brittle-ductile, and ductile materials through the lens of a stress field near a crack tip. The analysis begins with linear elastic fracture mechanics for brittle solids, followed by inelastic fracture mechanics for ductile ones. The fundamental stress field equations in both scenarios are demonstrated to converge when specific material properties are met. The paper concludes that the notion of fracture toughness is ambiguous unless a distinct failure criterion is established. Consequently, the collapse of the stress field—whether elastic or the elastic-plastic zone—is identified as the critical event defining the failure of crack tips in brittle and ductile materials, respectively. The energy release rate is recognized as the primary driving force for fracture. For brittle solids, the conjugate stress state in fracture toughness testing is shown to be the mode I opening state. In the case of ductile materials, however, the stress state in fracture toughness tests must be selected based on the specific failure criterion employed. Finally, it is proposed that the fracture toughness of ductile materials should be quantified using a three-element parameter instead of a single-value parameter. These findings represent new insights into the field of fracture mechanics. The proposed concepts are illustrated through examples using brittle silicon and ductile aluminum. Furthermore, the study examines a recent controversy regarding the stress state and failure criteria for ductile materials, specifically the assertions made by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) that the opening state is the sole applicable stress state for ductile fracture toughness tests. It is argued that the opening state is appropriate only for brittle fracture and that tests utilizing a bending state can yield more accurate and reliable measurements for ductile materials. The ultimate goal of this work is to advance the understanding and practical application of fracture toughness testing across both brittle and ductile materials. A stochastic log-gas on the upper half-plane, driven by a system of multiple SLEs on boundary, yields a Gaussian free field coupled with a non-Gaussian free field. We demonstrate that this construction remains consistent even when the log-gas is a free fermion model, in which case the coupled Gaussian free field is characterized by a specific boundary condition. The challenge of classical verification for quantum computations stems from two main factors: the complexity of classical circuits required to implement large quantum circuits, and the intricate structure of quantum circuits that complicates identifying efficient classical verification strategies. Prior research established that a random circuit of $O(n^2)$ bits necessitates $O(n^2)$ classical bits for verification, implying that any efficient verification method must function effectively even for randomly generated quantum circuits. In this work, we introduce a new classical verification strategy for free quantum choices within quantum circuits that operates in linear time relative to the number of gates. This approach enables the efficient classical verification of random quantum circuits. Consequently, we demonstrate that a random circuit comprising $O(n)$ quantum gates can be verified using $O(n)$ classical gates and $O(n)$ classical memory. Furthermore, this methodology extends to the efficient classical simulation of large quantum circuits containing solely single-qubit gates. Specifically, such circuits can be implemented via $O(n)$ classical gates and $O(n)$ classical memory. These findings also yield the first explicit example of a large quantum circuit that can be classically simulated in $O(n)$ time using $O(n)$ classical space. Notably, the circuit structures we examine are substantial enough that their classical simulation demands $n$ qubits, rendering these the first explicit examples of large quantum circuits capable of $O(n)$-time, $O(n)$-space simulation. Additionally, the techniques employed hold significant potential for the classical simulation of circuits involving few-qubit gates. Our work also advances the understanding of the relationship between classical and quantum computational complexity. We construct a family of large quantum circuits that can be simulated by $O(n)$-size circuits utilizing $O(n)$ space, thereby illustrating the existence of a non-trivial gap between the classical resources (time and space) required for simulation. Finally, we explore the application of our verification technique to the classical simulation of circuits containing two-qubit gates. By applying our technique to sub-circuits involving two-qubit gates, we develop an algorithm for the classical simulation of large quantum circuits that features low-depth components with an arbitrary number of qubits. This enables the classical simulation of recently proposed algorithms for the many-body Hamiltonian simulation problem, which are implemented using large, low-depth quantum circuits with an arbitrary number of qubits. Our technique also facilitates the construction of a family of large quantum circuits that can be simulated in low depth using $O(n)$ classical space. Blockchain serves as a distributed technology designed to foster trust and collaboration. By leveraging its inherent features—such as immutability, transparency, and traceability—blockchain solutions can enhance security and efficiency in various food supply chains. This paper details our implementation of a blockchain architecture for food supply chains within the Internet of Things (IoT) era. Utilizing the Ethereum blockchain, we developed smart contracts to automate key architecture functions, including device registration, data validation, and the management of data and information sharing. To validate the efficacy of this proposed architecture, we conducted experimental tests that measured latency, data storage costs, and the computational requirements for architecture management. The results demonstrate that the proposed solution is efficient and feasible for real-world deployment. Consequently, this approach offers a robust architecture for enhancing food supply chains, ensuring security, and fostering trust. Generative modeling for cell shape analysis is crucial in fields like cancer research and drug discovery, where it supports applications ranging from virtual clinical trials to high-content screening. This study introduces a novel generative model for cell shapes utilizing explicit representations and implicit models based on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). By employing an implicit model, we can leverage deep learning for shape generation, offering greater flexibility for automated pipelines compared to explicit methods. To our knowledge, we are the first to apply deep learning for cell shape analysis by utilizing neural geometry representations. We evaluate and compare these generative models for both yeast and mammalian cells. Our results indicate that the implicit model surpasses the explicit model by producing more diverse shapes and yielding a higher count of realistic cells. Furthermore, we show that the implicit model can learn to replicate experimental perturbations, such as those caused by chemical treatments or genetic modifications. Finally, we establish a new benchmark for cell shape analysis by releasing a comprehensive benchmark suite for these implicit models. This framework includes over 10,000 annotated and augmented 2D yeast and mammalian cell shapes, which can be accessed to train and assess emerging implicit models for shape generation. The benchmark suite is available at https://github.com/DeepBioGroup/nerf-cells. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepBioGroup/nerf-cells. The source code for all experiments can be found at https://github.com/DeepBioGroup/nerf-cells. Additional details are available at https://github.com/DeepBioGroup/implicit-cells. We anticipate that this work will foster a new research area dedicated to deep learning for virtual perturbation screens involving cell shape analysis. By enabling the creation of synthetic data for cellular perturbations, such virtual screens could significantly reduce the time and costs associated with physical experiments. This capability is particularly valuable for high-throughput screens, such as those used in virtual clinical trials for cancer research or drug discovery. Specifically, it could facilitate large-scale efforts like the one conducted by the Broad Institute, which has released over 100,000 images of perturbed yeast cells for public use. Our work demonstrates the ability to generate realistic images of yeast cells with perturbations matching experimental conditions, including genetic and chemical perturbations. This paves the way for a virtual perturbation screen using deep learning for cell shape analysis, thereby reducing the time and expenses of physical perturbations. A significant portion of text documents, including books, reports, and publications, utilizes an implicit hierarchical structure to enhance readability and facilitate navigation. This study investigates whether machine learning models can learn this implicit structure to aid users in navigating document sections. We demonstrate that various supervised learning models can effectively predict this implicit structure, which is represented as a sequence of set-of-set dependencies. Our analysis of the learning process reveals that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) perform superior to other models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), when provided with local contextual information. Additionally, we show that an RNN-based classifier can enhance human performance in a interactive, game-based navigation task. Finally, we explore the potential application of this capability in aiding users with print impairments. A detailed description of the dataset and a preliminary version of the game are accessible at https://drive.google.

Denoising autoencoder-based pretraining has established a new standard in natural language processing. This paper introduces XLNet, a generalization of the GAE autoencoder, which utilizes an autoregressive model to predict the masked token using the entire context. XLNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on many language understanding tasks without relying on any task-specific architectural changes or training adjustments. Additionally, when applied to smaller models, XLNet consistently and significantly surpasses BERT. We examine several design choices, including the motivation behind employing an autoregressive framework and the concept of pairwise GAE, both of which are crucial to XLNet's success. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed analysis of the GAE's effectiveness across a range of model types and examine its effectiveness and efficiency from a data perspective. This work aims to offer insights into understanding GAE and guiding future research. The code and data are available at https://github.com/facebook/XLNet. Exoplanet transit spectroscopy offers a powerful method for analyzing planetary atmospheres, yet stellar activity introduces significant challenges, particularly for low-resolution observations. This study investigates how such activity impacts the detection and characterization of exoplanetary atmospheres across both low and high-resolution regimes. We developed a simulation framework to generate synthetic transit light curves for a model active star, producing secondary eclipse observations at low, high, and super-high resolutions. These simulated datasets were subsequently analyzed to determine the precision of low-resolution measurements and the information content at higher resolutions. Our results indicate that under typical conditions, activity limits low-resolution studies to detecting only highly abundant species in hot Jupiters. However, we demonstrate that increased spectral resolution effectively suppresses most activity-induced noise, substantially enhancing the sensitivity of transmission spectroscopy for a broad range of exoplanetary atmospheres. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for current and upcoming space-based missions. Research into the swimming mechanics of aquatic centipedes has largely focused on force measurements using high-speed force sensors, often neglecting the detailed dynamics of their movement. This study introduces a novel force-free measurement framework that integrates high-speed video tracking with a custom model of the centipedes' water surface interactions. The model demonstrates that centipedes maintain a near-horizontal orientation while swimming, a finding that aligns with prior force data but offers deeper insights into centipedeelegancekinematics. Furthermore, high-speed tracking reveals that even during straight-line locomotion, these creatures exhibit complex undulatory patterns, indicating that previously observed dynamic swimming behaviors are more widespread than earlier force measurements suggested. Finally, the study indicates that centipedes rely on their legs for propulsion, while their antennae serve to dampen undulations and enhance swimming stability. These findings provide valuable references for bio-inspired, water-surface swimming robots, demonstrating that robots with superior hydrodynamic properties can achieve faster speeds and greater stability than central-species performance would predict. The proposed framework is also applicable to other aquatic species, such as fish, for detailed dynamic analysis. The tracking and modeling code will be made publicly available. This study investigates the fluid dynamics of a tsunami generated by an asteroid impact, evaluating the benefits of recent numerical methods and algorithms. The primary objective is to develop a precise numerical model for disperse wave propagation, capable of handling the extreme conditions of an asteroid striking a deep ocean. To achieve this, we examine a range of algorithms and numerical approaches designed to create a logically seamless transition from an impact zone featuring a highly complex free surface to the far-field disperse wave propagation. We analyze several techniques, including free-surface remeshing, level set methods, and the VOF method, alongside a range of numerical schemes. Furthermore, we implement an approach utilizing multiple domains with distinct mesh resolutions and an adaptive strategy to manage the shift from highly non-linear, near-field flow to weakly non-linear disperse wave propagation. Finally, we explore the application of parallel computing to enhance the efficiency of these simulations. The research concludes with a detailed presentation of tsunami propagation resulting from an asteroid impact into a deep ocean. This simulation, conducted on a high-performance computing system, effectively demonstrates a multi-scale modeling approach that integrates near-field, intermediate, and far-field tsunami modeling. Additionally, we highlight a parallel adaptive strategy that facilitates seamless transitions between different mesh resolutions. The simulation outcomes align well with existing literature, and we provide a comprehensive discussion of the advantages and limitations associated with the various algorithms and numerical schemes employed. Ultimately, this work offers a robust foundation for future research into tsunami modeling across multiple scales. Specifically, the use of adaptive mesh refinement in conjunction with high-resolution numerical schemes holds significant promise for enhancing the accuracy of near-field tsunami simulations. Furthermore, the parallel adaptive strategy developed herein can be readily applied to other problems involving multi-scale flows. Overall, this research represents a vital step toward achieving more accurate and efficient tsunami modeling through adaptive simulation and high-performance computing. We present the first early JWST Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) survey of the optically dark, infrared-luminous galaxy population at $z\sim 2-4$. Utilizing deep NIRCam imaging of the Northern Ecliptic Pole (Nep) field, we identified 1,000 optically dark galaxies (ODGs) spanning $14.5\lesssim$AB$M_{4.44}\lesssim$10.5 mag and $z\gtrsim 2$. These ODGs are predominantly dust-obscured star-forming systems with stellar masses ($M_*$) ranging from $10^8$ to $10^{10} M_{\odot}$ and star formation rates (SFRs) of 0.1 to 100 $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. Leveraging JWST's exceptional imaging capabilities, we conducted a detailed analysis of their stellar populations, dust characteristics, and morphological structures. Our findings reveal that ODGs are primarily compact, star-forming galaxies, with approximately 60% classified as starbursts. Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between stellar mass and dust extinction within this population, indicating that ODGs represent the most obscured yet most numerous sources in the $z\sim 2-4$ dust-selected galaxy population. Finally, by analyzing the morphologies of these compact star-forming systems, we determined that ODGs are not merely star-forming dwarf galaxies but include a significant fraction of massive galaxies. This study establishes a robust framework for investigating the nature of ODGs, a population that will be further explored using future JWST data. For specific values of these coefficients, the topological terms reproduce key aspects of the geometry of 7-superblack holes and 7-dimensional Anti-de Sitter space, thereby generalizing the Einstein action. Additionally, we examine the theory's equations of motion, on-shell actions, and the characteristics of its perturbations. This study examines two-dimensional granular packings of disks with varying sizes and weights into a vertical channel under gravity. While prior research established that channels feeders favor packings with an increasing sequence of increasingly heavy disks, this work investigates packings formed by alternating disk sizes and weights. We demonstrate that such packings can be constructed from a fully packed channel using a specific repacking protocol. The resulting jammed states are characterized by block sequences, where identical disks of a single size and weight are arranged in ascending order. Furthermore, we establish that fully packed jammed states exist only when the sum of the height and weight for any three consecutive disk types does not exceed 1. Finally, we reveal that these packings exhibit a complex distribution of packing fractions that contradicts a naive application of the random close packing model. This anomalous distribution of packing fractions arises because size and weight constraints prevent the system from reaching its most dense configuration. Consequently, we conclude that these packings are governed by a distinct set of principles compared to channels feeders. Specifically, the transition from one packing fraction to another is abrupt, a phenomenon attributed to a first-order phase transition. This behavior contrasts sharply with channels feeders, which display a gradual transition between packing fractions. Overall, this research expands our understanding of jammed granular packings and their underlying organization principles. It underscores the critical role of packing protocols in granular physics and highlights the need for continued investigation into channels feeders to fully understand their unique behavior. Finally, the findings have significant implications for engineering and industrial processes involving granular materials. For instance, the complex distribution of packing fractions observed in these packings may have significant consequences for the design and operation of industrial equipment that utilize channels feeders. By gaining a deeper understanding of the factors influencing packing efficiency, engineers can develop more effective strategies for optimizing material handling and transportation. Additionally, the complex distribution of packing fractions may impact the design of new materials and products that rely on granular packings, as different packing fractions can result in significantly different mechanical properties. By considering the potential effects of varying packing fractions, engineers can make more informed decisions about the selection of appropriate packing protocols to achieve the desired material properties. This study investigates how distinct flavors of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) leave differential marks on global seasonal precipitation extremes. By analyzing 35-year (1982–2016) observational data, we identified the two most distinct western-central Pacific temperature anomalies, termed W-ENSO and E-ENSO. We then assessed the 35-year seasonal precipitation record to determine the most statistically divergent wet and dry seasons. Our results reveal that W-ENSO exhibits a significantly greater correlation with very low precipitation levels than with very high ones. In contrast, E-ENSO shows a stronger connection to very high precipitation levels, though this effect is only detectable in the Northern Hemisphere. Furthermore, the spatial patterns associated with very low precipitation under W-ENSO conditions are more extensive than those linked to very high precipitation. These findings suggest that W-ENSO and E-ENSO influence precipitation extremes in divergent ways, a distinction that could enhance the accuracy of future climate predictions. Additionally, we propose a new framework for characterizing the dual nature of W-ENSO based on these dual responses to precipitation extremes. Finally, we examine the limitations of this approach regarding the selection of the most distinct seasonal precipitation extremes. Overall, these results provide a foundation for understanding the dual nature of W-ENSO and its unique impact on global precipitation extremes. **Keywords:** W-ENSO, E-ENSO, very low precipitation, very high precipitation, seasonal precipitation extremes. **Abbreviation:** ENSO, El Niño–Southern Oscillation. **Acknowledgments:** This research was conducted during YS's visit to the University of Maryland, funded by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) under grant 2017R1A2A1A01006737. The concept of non-affine expansion, which describes the local increase in volume during plastic deformation in amorphous solids, is examined through the lens of non-affine disorder. This analysis reveals that although the non-affine matrix is symmetric, its contribution to non-affine expansion is negligible because the effect of the non-affine stress on the plastic rearrangement vector is minimal. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that measuring the non-affine disorder tensor via dynamic light scattering is feasible, provided that multiple measurements are performed with illumination from various directions. The calculated correlation between non-affine expansion and the mean square of the non-affine disorder tensor is found to be strong, underscoring the value of dynamic light scattering in investigating non-affine expansion. Finally, the correlation between the increase in internal energy and the mean square of the non-affine disorder is estimated, yielding a correlation coefficient close to 1. These findings suggest that dynamic light scattering can effectively monitor both internal energy and non-affine expansion. The study focuses on plastic deformation in a glassy solid, but the methodology is applicable to other athermal materials, including metallic glasses and granular materials. Consequently, the proposed experimental techniques are anticipated to advance the investigation of non-affine expansion and related phenomena in a broad range of athermal materials. This paper introduces a series of non-associative (hypersequent) logics derived from substructural sequent systems via structural rules, specifically focusing on the absence of exchange and incorporating hypersext (the generalization of multisets to sets) instead of multisets. We demonstrate that these logics retain the key property of decidability under linear complexity bounds even with this set-based restriction. Furthermore, we investigate how contraction and weakening influence logical associativity. By employing labeled hypersequents, we define substructural sublogics of $S5$ that achieve linear decision complexity, even in cases where contraction is entirely absent. In contrast, we find that contracting $S5$ results in undecidable logics, whereas weakening leads to systems with polynomial complexity. These findings are complemented by additional observations regarding modal logics operating over non-associative hypersequents. Notably, our results reveal that weakening is insufficient to restore associativity, thereby refuting a conjecture by Reggiani and Uustalu. Finally, we situate our contributions within the broader landscape of existing research. This line of inquiry originated from the investigation into non-monotonic substructural logics, which were formulated using sequents rather than multisets or hypersequents. This foundational approach yielded negative outcomes: the resulting logics exhibited exponential complexity bounds and remained nondeterministic. Our work builds upon these preliminary findings by utilizing labeled hypersequents to establish polynomial complexity bounds. Additionally, we observed that exchange is unnecessary for achieving PTIME complexity, although it remains essential for NP complexity. This insight prompted an exploration of the impact of restricting exchange, leading to the present study. Our findings indicate that this restriction results in only minor modifications to the complexity bounds, thereby rendering the exchange axiom redundant for PTIME analysis. This conclusion extends the scope of our results to encompass PTIME bounds for a broader class of substructural logics. Finally, we establish the robustness of these findings by demonstrating that similar complexity bounds apply to other weakening-based substructural logics, such as those based on $LPK$. Collectively, these results underscore the significance of our contribution in advancing the understanding of substructural logics and their computational limits. Although taxonomies are highly effective for knowledge representation and task enhancement, manually building them is both costly and time-intensive. This paper introduces HyperExpan, a taxonomy expansion framework that experiences taxonomic structures. By leveraging a hyperbolic representation learning framework, HyperExpan L extracts semantic features from text to refine taxonomic edges and generate taxonomic words. Furthermore, we detail a taxonomy completion algorithm that employs taxonomic words to infer missing taxonomic edges. Experimental results across three datasets indicate that HyperExpan L improves original taxonomy-based representations and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in taxonomy expansion. Additionally, ablation studies confirm that contributions from each component are substantial. In summary, HyperExpan demonstrates that taxonomic structures can be learned from text to significantly boost performance in classification and related natural language processing tasks. All code is publicly available at https://github.com/1191162005/HyperExpan.

This study investigates the impact of external electric fields on non-covalent interactions within small molecular clusters, specifically focusing on hydrogen and $\pi$-interactions in a representative set of S66 molecular dimers. The research employs a variety of quantum chemical methods, including HF, MP2, CCSD(T), B3LYP, and a newly developed M06-2X-D3 variant. These calculations serve to validate the unique characteristics of M06-D3 and M06-2X-D3, which are constructed by extending the M06 and M06-2X functionals with the D3 dispersion correction. The study further examines how different components of non-covalent forces respond to variations in electric field strength and orientation. Additionally, it explores potential applications for DFT-MD simulations involving larger systems under external fields. The findings indicate that DFT-D3 methods are exceptionally efficient and accurate for modeling small dimers, while DFT-MD approaches show promise for simulating larger systems. Consequently, this work demonstrates the utility of DFT-D3 as a practical tool for assessing the effects of external electric fields on non-covalent interactions in both small and large molecular systems. This has significant implications for applications such as molecular switches, sensors, and electrostatic tuning of materials. The study also provides new recommendations for handling the components of non-covalent forces when simulating systems subjected to external electric fields. Finally, a comprehensive database of electric field effects on intermolecular interactions for S66 dimers is established and made accessible to facilitate future research. Non-deterministic uncertainty, which arises from unknown future events, is a fundamental element of scheduling in industries exposed to external factors. To address this, various modelling approaches have been developed, notably stochastic programming and robust scheduling. However, these methods are ineffective for unknown future uncertainty because they depend on statistical data from known sources. In the context of unknown future uncertainty, robust scheduling is preferable due to its reactive nature, which allows for re-optimization and the creation of flexible schedules; this flexibility is quantified through robustness metrics. This study introduces a method to enhance robust scheduling by integrating the concepts of schedule robustness and efficiency. The methodology involves: (1) defining a novel probability distribution to represent non-deterministic uncertainty; (2) developing a two-phase heuristic that creates a flexible schedule and adjusts it to minimize robustness measures; and (3) validating the approach using a case study where uncertainty is represented by a normal distribution with a zero mean. The findings demonstrate that robust schedules can be significantly improved by adjusting the uncertainty's standard deviation. Consequently, this research offers a practical framework for formulating non-deterministic uncertainty and a new strategy to improve robust schedules. Both contributions are highly relevant for managing unknown future uncertainty in industries susceptible to external influences. The proposed solution is implemented in the R4.0 software, which is available for download. R4.0 is an integrated package that implements a robust schedule, calculates its robustness, and performs a sensitivity analysis to refine the schedule. Additionally, it provides a method to quantify the degree of flexibility. This tool is valuable for researchers and industry professionals engaged in non-deterministic uncertainty management. R4.0 is freely accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1234567890/R4.0. The repository includes user-friendly documentation, a ready-to-run example, and an R4.0.wix website for easy download. Furthermore, the repository features a new paper titled "Improving non-deterministic uncertainty modelling in Industry 4.0 scheduling," which details the R4.0 implementation. Resilience is a crucial concept for numerous cyber-physical systems, yet its theoretical foundations remain underdeveloped. This paper introduces an STL-based framework for defining resilience in CPS, which integrates signal temporal logic with a new formulae designed to capture transitions between specifications. This approach leverages the flexibility of STL's syntax and semantics to handle diverse tasks, inputs, and outputs, while employing a distance-based metric to quantify resilience. The study provides an algorithm for calculating this distance and utilizes it to formulate resilience for the system. The validity and efficiency of the proposed method are demonstrated through a case study involving a two-link robot arm subjected to cyber attacks. Additionally, the paper extends the definition of resilience to account for both satisfaction and safety, and finally, it presents a resolution method for the STL-based resilience formulae that relies on the distance computation and adapts existing algorithms for STL satisfaction. Dark matter remains one of physics' most significant unresolved mysteries. Although indirect evidence strongly suggests its existence, its fundamental nature remains unclear. If dark matter consists of sub-microscopic particles, they should interact with standard matter through non-gravitational forces, generating signals detectable by modern sensor technology. This study examines the potential of global networks of high-sensitivity accelerometers to detect such signals. We outline the non-gravitational forces relevant to these searches, their relationship with force carrier properties, and the methodologies for constraining them. We present constraints on light and semi-light forces derived from existing data and explore how future extended networks could further expand the accessible parameter space. Additionally, we address technical challenges and propose a path forward to achieve the necessary experimental sensitivity. Our analysis indicates that large-scale deployments of high-precision inertial sensors could reveal new fundamental forces interacting with dark matter candidates. This approach complements other indirect searches for sub-micro forces, offering a promising avenue for future investigations into the dark sector. Consequently, we recommend that the broader physics community consider investing in accelerometer networks to explore these novel search channels. To facilitate this, we have made our code and associated data publicly available. This work was conducted by researchers from diverse disciplines, including particle physics, astrophysics, cosmology, nuclear physics, nuclear engineering, nuclear medicine, and mechanical engineering. We conclude that strong interdisciplinary collaboration is essential to fully realize the potential of accelerometers for detecting dark matter. A primary obstacle to launching new experiments is the lack of a dedicated collaboration; therefore, we have initiated a call for interest in developing an accelerator-based experiment to search for dark matter. We believe that coordinated efforts across the physics community are crucial to investigate this promising new possibility. Our findings are summarized at https://www.discover-accelerators.eu/. We hope this will inspire a new generation of experiments and accelerate the development of accelerometers suitable for dark matter research. We extend our sincere gratitude to all who have shown interest in this field and are working to make this a reality. We are deeply honored to have contributed to this endeavor. We are confident that the future of accelerometers in dark matter searches is bright. We are deeply committed to this cause. We are deeply moved by the possibility of uncovering new fundamental forces. We are deeply touched by the potential to advance our understanding of the dark sector. The source of "compact, faint" radio sources remains a significant but unresolved issue in source counts. This study examines a sample of 100 radio sources with a mean flux density of 1 mJy, selected from the 1.4 GHz FIRST survey, using Stacking Analysis. We investigate how the source population shifts with flux density and angular size. Our findings indicate that low flux density and small angular size do not necessarily imply extreme redshifts or weak star formation. The typical source population at $S_{1.4GHz} \sim 1$ mJy is characterized by moderate star formation rates and sub-Eddington accretion. Furthermore, we observed a flux-deficit stacking result at 8.4 GHz for the source population, which may be attributed to a change in the radio spectrum. Finally, we conclude that the source population at $S_{1.4GHz} \sim 1$ mJy is more complex than previously thought and requires a more comprehensive investigation. This paper introduces abstract hidden Markov models (HMVMs), which extend both probabilistic automata and hidden Markov models by incorporating a probabilistic observation model. In this framework, observations are generated from a hidden state according to a specified distribution, a mechanism that supports non-interference proofs for quantitative information flow scenarios involving probabilistic non-interference. We demonstrate that HMVMs possess a natural monadic structure, enabling the use of guards and the construction of HMVMs through algebraic operations. Leveraging this structure, we outline a general methodology for defining non-interference properties and illustrate its application with several quantitative information flow examples. Finally, we outline a strategy for analyzing HMVMs via abstract interpretation, showing how this monadic structure facilitates the automatic creation of useful HMVM instances. Additionally, we provide Ptime complexity upper bounds for deciding various HMVM properties using automata-theoretic methods. These findings establish HMVMs as a robust framework for non-interference in probabilistic and quantitative information flow contexts, offering a practical method for analyzing such systems.

**Keywords:** Information Flow, Probabilistic Automata, Probabilistic Non-Interference, Quantitative Information Flow, Probabilistic Guarded Commands, Abstract Interpretation, Probabilistic Computation Tree Logic.

We present a category of stochastic advection problems featuring time-dependent drift velocities and diffusivities. These systems generate statistically nonlocal transport of passive scalars, resulting in anomalous diffusion and the emergence of dynamical coherent structures. The passive particle distribution is described by a two-point correlation function that remains scale and time dependent even at infinite separation. We establish a framework comprising existence theorems, upper and lower bounds, and a spectral asymptotic formula for the autocorrelation decay of coherent structures across all times. This statistical nonlocality is demonstrated through a specific model that produces exponential decay in the two-point correlation function at large time lags, despite power-law dependence on one time variable for each lag. Additionally, we examine a family of algebraic models exhibiting self-similar dynamics and deriving the exact two-point correlation function. These findings have significant implications for understanding the large-time behavior of stochastic advection models with passive scalars. Finally, our methodology is applied to three representative cases: anomalous diffusion, an active scalar model displaying both large-scale coherent structures and small-scale intermittency, and a passive scalar advection model characterized by self-similar cascades. In each instance, the two-point correlation function retains its functional form regardless of the time lag. Furthermore, we identify a link between the active scalar model and a recently proposed class of non-equivalent time crystals. Our results suggest that the observed symmetry breaking in these non-equilibrium time crystals may stem from the underlying statistical nonlocality of the advection model. These outcomes are supported by numerical simulations. Our approach offers a unified framework for analyzing both passive and active scalar advection models driven by non-Gaussian, self-similar random forces. This work advances the understanding of large-scale coherent structures, anomalous diffusion, and non-equilibrium time crystals in driven passive scalar and active matter systems. Additionally, it provides a new perspective on the statistical mechanics of non-equilibrium driven scalar fields. These advances are essential for developing a comprehensive theory of large-scale coherent structures, anomalous diffusion, and non-equilibrium time crystals within driven passive scalar and active matter systems. Our findings also hold value for the broader field of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics. Specifically, the passive scalar advection model employed in this study serves as a prototype for studying non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, with our findings offering new insights into the field's fundamental challenges. This approach unifies existing models, including the optical potential method, the impact parameter model, and the wounding model, while offering improved alignment with experimental data. Furthermore, we propose that an analogous theory is necessary for inelastic scattering. Finally, we explore the parallel theory applicable to inelastic scattering. The system is modeled as an infinite set of independent harmonic oscillators, where the oscillation frequencies are determined by the cavity's dimensions and its electromagnetic boundary conditions. By applying statistical mechanics, we derive statistical properties for a system of $N$ weakly coupled, weakly distinguishable harmonic oscillators. We analyze the thermodynamic behavior of this system, specifically accounting for van der waals-type interactions, and compute key thermodynamic quantities such as internal energy, heat capacity, and entropy. Furthermore, we observe that the canonical partition function yields an entropy expression comparable to that of the microcanonical ensemble, adhering to the Nernst heat theorem. Finally, we explore how electromagnetic boundary conditions influence the various calculated thermodynamic quantities. These findings are relevant to scenarios involving electromagnetic radiation in confined spaces, such as cavities or channels, where boundaries induce shifts in the radiation's thermodynamic characteristics. Additionally, we explore the potential of this system to serve as an effective physical model for complex interacting many-body systems, including atoms, molecules, and condensed matter. The study also addresses boundary conditions at the cavity wall, which influence the derived heat capacity values. Finally, we demonstrate that the thermodynamic specific heat of the cavity radiation system varies depending on the specific configuration of the cavity walls. Specifically, when the walls are perpendicular to one of the spatial axes, the specific heat exhibits the characteristic behavior of a simple phase. Conversely, if the walls are oriented parallel to a diagonal plane, the specific heat displays the complex behavior typical of a phase change. This latter scenario arises when the thermal de Broglie wavelength is comparable to the cavity's dimensions, resulting in a blackbody heat capacity that is approximately 10% lower than that of unrestricted radiation. We also note that the thermal energy of the radiation is inversely proportional to the cavity's dimensions. Finally, we show that the total entropy of the system is directly proportional to the cavity's surface area. These results provide a quantitative framework for understanding the complex interactions between electromagnetic radiation and the boundaries of the cavity. Furthermore, our findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the complex thermodynamic behavior of electromagnetic radiation confined within a cavity, thereby advancing our knowledge of this fundamental physical phenomenon. These findings have significant implications for various fields, including quantum electrodynamics, astrophysics, and nanotechnology. Ensuring that users understand how a system interprets their data is a fundamental aspect of transparency, which we examine through the lens of probabilistic models equipped with provable guarantees. Specifically, this paper investigates whether a location-based system, utilizing a hidden Markov model, maintains transparency by explicitly defining how a specific observation is interpreted. To achieve this, we introduce a new metric for interpreting an observation under a prior, which we demonstrate is separable when the underlying hidden Markov model is Gaussian. This explicit formula for the prior enables users to assess their level of understanding when their data is processed. However, we also demonstrate that transparency cannot be ensured when a system's behavior is interpreted through multiple distinct models. To address this challenge, we propose a method for deriving a conditional prior that ensures an observation's interpretation remains consistent across various system behaviors. Our approach is validated through a case study involving interpretable location models. Ultimately, this work advances the field of probabilistic modeling by providing tools to foster greater trust between data processors and users. Additionally, our methodology for generating conditional priors holds broader significance, finding applications in multi-objective optimization, multi-armed bandits, and the design of multi-agent reinforcement learning reward functions. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity serves as a robust biomarker for brain disorders, offering high sensitivity and specificity while maintaining a cost-effective, non-invasive, and accessible profile. Although recent advancements in rs-fMRI-based machine learning have yielded statistically significant findings, the lack of sufficient statistical power often results in limited prediction accuracy and poor generalizability across independent samples. This study evaluates the influence of data volume, subject demographics, and data preprocessing techniques on both statistical power and prediction performance. We conducted a General Linear Model (GLM) analysis on a large, multisite dataset comprising 1,000 healthy individuals to identify neurophysiological markers of age and sex. Subsequently, we applied a Support Vector Machine (SVM) to determine the optimal features for predicting these demographic variables. Our multisite analysis revealed that while increasing the number of runs per subject enhances prediction accuracy, the number of subjects exerts a more profound effect. Furthermore, we identified a robust set of functional connectivity features that predict age and sex with high accuracy (r = 0.75 and r = 0.80, respectively) using only 500 subjects. These findings underscore the necessity of recruiting a substantial number of subjects for rs-fMRI connectivity research. Additionally, we demonstrated that the choice of preprocessing pipeline can significantly alter feature selection outcomes. Finally, our analysis confirms that despite variations in preprocessing methods, the underlying neurophysiological markers for age and sex remain consistent. Our results indicate that functional connectivity can accurately predict age and sex in healthy humans, a capability that holds promise for developing diagnostic tools for brain diseases. Ultimately, we advocate for the establishment of a comprehensive, open-access rs-fMRI connectivity database to advance the field. This resource would enable researchers to validate their discoveries, optimize the design of new studies, and accelerate progress toward diagnosing and treating brain conditions.
