We investigate the distribution of complex eigenvalues $z_1,\ldots, z_N$ associated with random Hermitian $N\times N$ block band matrices that possess a finite-rank complex deformation. Under the assumption that the band width $W$ increases faster than $\sqrt{N}$, we demonstrate that these eigenvalues follow a two-parameter family of Haar measures within an $N_0\times N_0$ Siegel upper half space, where $N_0=2(WW_\mathrm{min})^2$ (with $W_\mathrm{min}$ denoting the minimum band width). This result effectively extends the circular law to scenarios involving localized deformations and narrow bands. Furthermore, we show that the sigma-model approximation accurately describes the distribution of these eigenvalues. This methodology utilizes a nonlinear sigma model defined on a two-dimensional curved manifold, where the model's parameters are determined by the spectrum's mean density and its deviation from circular symmetry. The sigma-model approximation holds significant utility for analyzing eigenvalue distributions in narrow random band matrices and cases where $N_0>2N$. Additionally, we examine the necessary conditions for the sigma-model validity, revealing that its domain of applicability is more constrained than that of the broader nonlinear $\sigma$-approximation. Finally, the methodology is applied to two matrices arising in the theory of disordered media: the discrete Laplacian on a two-dimensional lattice featuring finite-range complex self-energy and a discrete Laplacian on an infinite square lattice incorporating a Gaussian two-dimensional Gaussian deformation. In both instances, the approach yields a comprehensive description of the eigenvalue distribution. These methodologies are implemented within the framework of quasiclassical techniques, which rely on the sigma-model approximation of the eigenspectrum. The efficacy of this framework is underscored by the recent successful analysis of the circular law for a specific class of random band matrices, where the sigma-model approximation was instrumental in deriving a sharp large $N$ limit for the eigenvalue distribution. This limit is characterized by the convergence of empirical eigenvalue distributions to a family of nonlinear sigma measures on Siegel upper half spaces, thereby providing a rigorous foundation for the sigma-model approximation. The study of eigenvalue distributions for random band matrices has been a prominent area of research for over half a century, with a notable resurgence in the 1980s driven by the discovery of delocalized eigenvalues in random band matrices. We introduce semantic-based pre-training for dialogue understanding, which leverages external knowledge to model dialogues as natural language inference tasks. This approach frames general dialogue semantics inference to capture semantic features without task-specific dependencies. Consequently, the proposed method yields significant performance gains across various downstream tasks, including turn-span classification and semantic parsing, by utilizing semantic inference capabilities. Experimental results highlight the effectiveness of our pre-training strategy for dialogue understanding. The code is available at: https://github.com/alexpaulin/semantic-due. Furthermore, we aim to release checkpoints, which can be accessed here: https://drive.google.

Algorithmic interpretability is essential for establishing trust in AI systems, ensuring accountability, and verifying ethical and legal compliance. However, the field currently lacks a formalized definition for this concept. This study addresses that gap by adopting algorithmic learning as a framework for interpreting AI models. We propose a formal definition of interpretability grounded in human learning theory and introduce the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS) as a metric to quantify it. The CCS evaluates the information content within training data relative to the sequence complexity of the training process, which reflects the cognitive demands placed on the learner. We outline the development of this score and its associated algorithm, demonstrating that the CCS effectively captures existing algorithmic interpretability characteristics. Furthermore, a human study was conducted to validate the proposed framework and to explore the relationship between human-perceived interpretability and the cognitive complexity of the learning process. Finally, the paper concludes by identifying key areas for future research. (Our source code and data are available at: https://github.com/ailab-fudan/cognitive-score). Our findings can be accessed at: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.01009.pdf. The paper was originally submitted as: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01009. Unsupervised anomaly detection is a critical task across numerous domains, yet it often struggles in scenarios characterized by weak supervision, unsuitable feature spaces, or the need for energy-efficient algorithms. Isolation Forest (iF) stands out as a leading solution, particularly for weak supervision, yet it remains underutilized in other critical areas. This work addresses three specific gaps: first, by proposing TiWS-iForest, a novel variant optimized for weak supervision that enhances performance in tabular data by mitigating the impact of irrelevant features; second, exploring the iF family to identify models best suited for anomaly detection on extremely small datasets (fewer than 10,000 instances); and third, analyzing iF's hardware footprint to develop energy-efficient versions suitable for edge computing. TiWS-iForest represents the first adaptation of iF to handle irrelevant features in tabular datasets. Our findings indicate that the TiWS-iF family outperforms the standard iF family in anomaly detection on tabular data when features are unavailable or of low quality. Specifically, TiWS-iF enhances detection rates by 1.5% to 10% while reducing false positives. Furthermore, we observed that model complexity in iF can be significantly reduced without compromising accuracy, and that TiWS-iF is particularly effective for tiny ML tasks involving datasets with fewer than 10,000 instances. Additionally, TiWS-iF demonstrates superior energy efficiency compared to standard iF, making it ideal for edge deployment. These contributions collectively broaden the applicability of Isolation Forests in emerging fields such as tabular data analysis, small dataset learning, and edge AI. Experimental results across various datasets, including CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Caltech-101, validate these claims. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/fernandogarcia2001/TiWS-iForest}. This study introduces a novel parameterization tailored for threshold exceedances reparameterized through a lens on the shape parameter. In the standard Pareto/Generalized Pareto Model (GPM), inference on the shape parameter is often unstable due to the identification of scale and shape, as well as the difficulty of estimating the tail index when it approaches zero. By reframing threshold exceedances via the equivalent Poisson process using this new parameterization, we enable inference to be drawn from a point process score function. This score function is independent of the chosen threshold and relies on the difference between two consecutive event times. This approach facilitates the construction of a nonparametric estimator for the inter-arrival time distribution within the Generalized Renewal Model (GRM). This estimation method is fully nonparametric, incurs no additional degrees of freedom, and is optimal for the GRM as it avoids the unstable estimation of five GPM parameters. We develop a Bayesian nonparametric prior for the inter-arrival time distribution, allowing for the simultaneous estimation of the five GPM parameters. A simulation study demonstrates that this new parameterization, which focuses on the tail behavior of the Poisson process score function, yields more stable estimates of the tail index. Furthermore, we apply this method to a real-world dataset consisting of a time series of US S&P500 returns. The resulting estimator is fully nonparametric, avoids the unstable estimation of the GPM parameters, and is not biased by the selection of a cut-off point. Additionally, we derive a fully nonparametric estimator for the Value-at-Risk of the Poisson process, which is also applicable to the original GPM. This Poisson process score function can be viewed as a score function for a semiparametric model where the Poisson intensity is parametric up to a cut-off point and nonparametric thereafter. This score function is particularly effective for estimating the change-point in the Poisson intensity score function, a critical step in deriving the tail index. Finally, we propose a nonparametric estimator for the Poisson intensity that is also free from the unstable estimation of the GPM parameters. This research falls under the domain of Bayesian nonparametric estimation. The paper introduces the problem of optimizing the selection of experimental data to determine the average total cross section for pion-particle interactions. It demonstrates that extending the analysis of pion-proton interaction cross sections to high energies yields a value of $5b$, which exceeds the diffractive disk limit of $4b$ predicted by the optical model. Similarly, high-energy pion-nucleus cross section data can be selected to optimize average total cross section values, resulting in an asymptotic upper limit of $A \cdot 4b$ for nucleus-particle interaction cross sections at high energies, where $A$ represents the nuclear mass number. This result aligns with the optical model's prediction for such interactions. The study considers two scenarios for the target: one where it possesses the same stationary average total cross section as the pion-particle system, and another where it exhibits the maximum possible stationary value. For both scenarios, appropriate experimental data selection regions are identified, characterized by the average momentum transfer and the selection interval. The optimal selection interval is determined by the condition that the selected total cross section average remains constant and equal to the target's value. Furthermore, the influence of the selection region on the final average total cross section value is examined, revealing that while the selection region impacts the result, it does not alter its value. Finally, the methodology is extended to determine selection regions for other diffractive processes, such as elastic scattering and charged particle production, utilizing the corresponding optical potentials. The derived regions for these other processes are analogous to those for total cross sections, defined by momentum transfer and a selection interval determined by the optical potential's imaginary part. The average value for total charged particle production cross sections is calculated as $2(A-1)b$, whereas for elastic scattering, it is $(A-2)b$. The former is derived by subtracting elastic data (with a maximum value of $4(A-1)b$) from the total value ($5Ab$), and the latter follows the same subtraction logic but using an average total value of $5Ab$ and an elastic average of $4(A-1)b$. The maximum value for nucleus-particle interaction cross sections is confirmed as $12b(A-1)$. Additionally, a novel method is proposed to experimentally verify the proposed selection regions and optimize data selection to calculate stationary average total cross sections. This involves measuring the total cross section as a function of the selection interval and identifying regions where the average value remains constant. The current work focuses on pion-nucleon and pion-nucleus

This work outlines the data reduction pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey, a comprehensive survey of star-forming regions conducted with the HIFI instrument on the Herschel Space Observatory. The pipeline incorporates data quality checks, frequency channel calibration, and flux calibration, with a specific emphasis on addressing 158 GHz water vapor absorption effects and integrating them into the calibration workflow. We have conducted a spectroscopic analysis of 11 first-interaction blue stragglers in the globular cluster NGC 2808, utilizing spectra from the UVES and UVES-FOURSEE instruments at the ESO-VLT. By employing a line-by-line analysis method, we determined precise and reliable radial abundances for these stars. Our results indicate that the derived abundances align closely with the cluster's average metallicity, with no significant variations among individual stars. This finding definitively rules out any substantial spread in metallicity for the population's second blue stragglers, thereby confirming that such a spread does not exist within the first blue stragglers either. Consequently, the observed spread in metallicity previously reported for blue stragglers in NGC 2808 is now understood to originate primarily from a minority component of second blue stragglers, while the majority of these stars exhibit abundances consistent with the cluster mean. This conclusion further invalidates the hypothesis that a significant fraction of first blue stragglers are the products of mergers. Our study also demonstrates the exceptional quality of the UVES and UVES-FOURSEE spectra obtained from these faint stars (at a distance of 2.2 kpc and with a mean magnitude of $V \sim 19.5$), showing that high-precision abundances can be derived. Finally, we demonstrate that a high-resolution spectrum of a single star can yield a comprehensive set of radial abundances, including C, N, O, Na, Al, K, Ca, Fe, and Ni. We conclude that UVES spectra offer high-precision radial abundances for all elements, while UVES-FOURSEE spectra provide high-precision radial abundances for Fe and the alpha-elements Mg, Ca, and Ni. These findings are highly relevant for future large-scale spectroscopic abundance studies of globular clusters using the ELT and its instruments. Future work will extend this analysis to other stars in NGC 2808. Additionally, we will investigate the implications of these results for the evolution of blue straggler stars and the specific mechanisms responsible for their formation. Classical Bayes' rule, which governs belief updating in classical statistics, encounters a fundamental conflict when applied to quantum mechanics due to non-commuting observables. Specifically, sequential measurements of non-commuting operators yield the same probability distribution as a single joint measurement, a result that contradicts the application of classical Bayes' rule between the two observations. This discrepancy highlights a critical issue in inferring quantum states from measurement data, a problem that has led to various proposed solutions. In this work, we demonstrate that a set of consistent state update rules can be derived by extending quantum mechanics with a set of non-trivial, non-unitary state evolution. This framework allows for the rigorous application of classical Bayes' rule to a non-commuting pair of observables, effectively resolving the inconsistency inherent in inferring quantum states from measurement outcomes. Furthermore, this proposed extension offers a novel approach to the longstanding challenge of defining quantum joint measurements. A specific implementation of this scheme is also proposed that is feasible within the context of a realistic quantum optical setup. Finally, we explore the broader implications of this proposal for the general foundations of quantum mechanics. The code utilized in this study can be found at https://github.com/SeokminKoo/QBayes. Additionally, we have developed a user-friendly, open-source Python package named QBayes, available at https://github.com/SeokminKoo/QBayes, which provides practical methods for inferring quantum states from measurement data. This package supports three distinct state update schemes: the standard von Neumann projection rule, the measurement-based rule proposed in this paper, and the continuous variable quantum filtering approach. These schemes are compared to illustrate the distinct characteristics of quantum measurement. QBayes is designed to be accessible to both experimental and theoretical researchers in the quantum information community. It includes an intuitive, step-by-step example that aligns with the theoretical proposal, with all associated numerical simulations performed using the provided Python code. Additionally, we have created a practical, step-by-step example that mirrors our theoretical proposal, enabling users to explore the implications of QBayes in real-world scenarios. This example is highly accessible to experimentalists, as it can be run on existing quantum hardware. We anticipate that QBayes will serve as a valuable resource for researchers in quantum state and process tomography, quantum feedback control, quantum filtering, and quantum field theory. The package is freely available for download. We hope that QBayes will facilitate further research into the foundations of quantum mechanics and assist experimentalists in extracting meaningful information

This study reports initial findings regarding finite volume corrections to the equation of state, trace anomaly, and speed of sound for two specific models: a self-interacting, massless scalar field representing the non-perturbative vacuum of QCD, and pure $U(1)$ QED. Regarding the scalar field model, we evaluate two scenarios: one where the field is strictly confined within the box, and another where it can propagate outside via massless Goldstone modes, with the box size governed by an arbitrary mass scale. For $U(1)$ QED, we examine both even and odd spatial dimensions. In the context of the equation of state, we investigate how finite size effects influence the crossover scale and whether these findings can be extrapolated to QCD. Additionally, we examine the ultraviolet behavior of the trace anomaly and speed of sound in small volumes. Finally, we outline potential extensions of these models to the confined phase and discuss future research directions. Our results indicate that for $U(1)$ QED, finite volume corrections are substantial, whereas for the self-interacting scalar field, these corrections are negligible. Consequently, small systems such as quark-gluon droplets may not exhibit significant thermodynamic fluctuations relative to mean field theory predictions. Ultimately, this research paves the way for developing new theoretical tools to explore the QCD phase diagram. Specifically, it offers a pathway to address longstanding questions regarding the location and nature of the QCD critical point. Finally, our approach may facilitate the development of novel theoretical tools for analyzing the QCD phase diagram. Specifically, this could facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of the location and characteristics of the QCD critical point. Finally, our methodology may contribute to the development of new theoretical tools for navigating the QCD phase diagram. The recent discovery of numerous intergalactic supernovae has significantly advanced our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution and the early universe. However, these transient events are challenging to study because they are obscured by neutral hydrogen, which blocks the detection of Lyman continuum radiation. This study introduces a novel approach to observing intergalactic supernovae by detecting the ionizing radiation they emit. We present the design of a new broad-band filter, termed the "Lyman-alpha filter," alongside an optical prototype. This device is intended for integration with optical, reflective telescopes to capture Lyman-alpha emissions from these transient objects. By employing this innovative filtering method, we aim to discover new intergalactic supernovae and investigate the nature of their progenitors. Additionally, this method may help resolve the long-standing mystery of the missing far-ultraviolet photons. We anticipate that a single night of observations with the new Lyman-alpha filter will yield hundreds of intergalactic supernovae, a number comparable to the total count of events observed over the past decade. Furthermore, we propose that a dedicated small telescope equipped with this filter could enable the detection of thousands of intergalactic supernovae per year. The rapid identification of these objects would facilitate detailed spectroscopic analysis, potentially revealing whether they originate from massive Population III stars or stellar remnants. This paper introduces a distributed algorithm designed to address two graph-symmetric optimal control problems within a multi-agent system that communicates via a directed graph. These problems encompass unconstrained graph-symmetric $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ and $\mathcal{H}_2$ control, alongside the computation of graph-symmetric feedback gains for linear systems using graph-filter-based distributed state estimation. To achieve graph symmetry, the distributed computations are enhanced through a centralized, high-order graph-filter-based distributed innovation propagation mechanism. This mechanism enables each agent to independently calculate its optimal control input by processing only its local measurements and control algebra. Simulation results are provided to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

**Index Terms:** Multi-agent systems, distributed optimal control, graph symmetry, graph filters, optimal control computation.

Image text is frequently used for browsing and retrieval. This paper presents a novel framework for creating an image database where the textual description is not merely passive or manual but is instead actively generated by a text-generation language model. This approach enables new capabilities, such as enabling text-modified image encoders to serve as generators for text-image encoders and facilitating interactive agents that can free-form their textual descriptions through continuous human-agent collaboration. We evaluate this method using two datasets: COCO and Concept12K. On the Concept12K dataset, our method achieves a top-k recall of 0.621 at 100k captions per image, surpassing the second-best method by a significant margin. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of our method to enable interactive agents to utilize active text indexing for reliable text-image retrieval. For instance, when provided with a few unstructured English sentences or even basic commands like "show me a picture of a dog," the agent can iteratively refine the text-image index to reliably retrieve the target image. This ability to handle diverse input types, from structured queries to open-ended instructions, represents a significant advancement in text-image search capabilities. The code is available at: https://github.com/IDEA-Research/AktiveImages.
Keywords: text-image search, text-image retrieval, text-guided image search, text-modified image encoder, interactive text-image search.

This study investigates keyless authentication for the Gaussian channel, where the server and the legitimate user share a long, low-rate training sequence that is subsequently discarded. In this framework, a user attempts to authenticate by sending a short message on a channel where a malicious user may also transmit a different message. The authorization decision is based solely on whether the received signal is more similar to the server's message or the malicious one. We derive the key capacity, defined as the maximum probability of correct authorization, and compare the keyless authentication channel to the classical channel coding setting. Furthermore, we demonstrate a fundamental gap between the key capacity and the capacity to transmit the authorization result, indicating that the number of training symbols required for authentication scales exponentially with the key rate. Finally, for the angle-modulation channel, we derive a closed-form expression for the key capacity as a function of the training rate, key rate, and training symbol energy. Additionally, for a restricted class of channels, we prove that the key capacity equals the capacity to transmit the authorization decision. Simulations validate our theoretical findings and assess the performance of a practical authentication code. Specifically, for the angle-modulation channel, we derive a closed-form expression for the performance of the optimal authentication code, which deviates from the theoretical key capacity due to the need to control false authorization rates. We analyze the performance trade-off between the theoretical key capacity and the practical achievable key capacity for this channel.

**Index Terms**—Keyless authentication, training-aided authentication, key capacity, angle modulation.

This study re-examines the dispersionless transport of particles within a ratchet potential, specifically addressing the Brownian ratchet proposed by Smoluchowski and the AC ratchet proposed by Poynting. The research highlights the critical influence of initial conditions on both ratchet mechanisms. It is demonstrated that the smRatchet fundamentally relies on a non-zero temperature gradient applied across the particle, whereas the poRatchet requires the particle to originate from a thermal equilibrium state. These findings are verified through two-dimensional particle simulations, which also reveal the significant impact of the initial spatial extent of the particle's wavefunction. Consequently, the paper concludes that designing an AC ratchet necessitates careful consideration of the particle's wave-like properties. Finally, the study briefly outlines the implications of these results for quantum pumping phenomena. Finally, the paper provides an overview of the broader historical and conceptual context of the smRatchet and poRatchet. Specifically, the text details Smoluchowski's original proposal of a "molecular motor" driven by a temperature gradient across a particle trapped in a sawtooth potential, as well as Poynting's suggestion that a time-varying electric field across a similar potential could also induce a net current. The discussion further elaborates on the "ratchet mechanism" originally described by Smoluchowski in 1912, which posits that a temperature gradient causes asymmetric Brownian motion, leading to a net current. The poRatchet is then explained as a purely electrical phenomenon that, under specific conditions, breaks spatial inversion symmetry in a periodically driven system, resulting in a current that opposes the average force exerted by the time-varying field. The text then outlines the specific conditions under which each ratchet operates. For the smRatchet, a "molecular motor" requires a temperature gradient across the particle to generate a net current, with the particle's position in the potential being "fuzzy" due to Brownian motion. For the poRatchet, the particle must be in thermal equilibrium to exhibit particle-like behavior, whereas the "Poynting effect" involves the particle being "too fuzzy" for a single force to be defined, necessitating a statistical description of its behavior. We present a flexible local projection (FLP) model as an alternative to traditional OLS-based estimation of vector local projections (VLP) for impulse responses. While VLPs impose strict constraints on the data-generating process (DGP), such as linearity, the FLP model accommodates a broader range of dynamics by allowing nonlinearities. Furthermore, we extend the impulse response to the entire distribution via quantile local projection (QLP) and evaluate the finite sample performance of these methods. Finally, we apply the framework to identify the impulse responses of monetary and fiscal shocks to the U.S. economy, finding that VLP and the FLP model yield similar results. However, the QP framework reveals that the impulse response to monetary policy shocks is not fully characterized by its mean, mode, or median. Specifically, while both approaches agree on a significant negative mean response, the FLP model indicates a distribution where some firms experience positive responses. Additionally, the FLP results suggest a more gradual response to monetary shocks compared to the VLP case. In contrast, the response to fiscal shocks remains largely unchanged across all three frameworks. These findings underscore the value of incorporating flexibility into local projection models. As the demand for cloud computing services grows, so does the need for more efficient load balancing techniques. Virtualization has become a widely adopted technology in cloud environments, enabling the deployment of virtual machines (VMs) on physical hosts. However, as the number of VMs grows, load balancing becomes a critical issue. This paper introduces a novel method called "Prepartition," which allocates a specific portion of a host's resources to each VM. This strategy ensures that a VM can always access its dedicated resources, even under heavy load, thereby preventing performance degradation. We present an experimental comparison of Prepartition against two traditional load balancing approaches: Static Load Balancing (SLB) and Dynamic Load Balancing (DLB). Our findings indicate that Prepartition outperforms both SLB and DLB. Furthermore, we demonstrate that resource partitioning is a more effective load balancing solution than the conventional SLB and DLB methods. Additionally, we analyze the execution time of Prepartition relative to SLB and DLB. We implemented this proposed method in the OpenNebula cloud platform. We believe this novel approach will be valuable for future VM reservations. To facilitate further research and development, we are making the Prepartition code available on GitHub. Game theory offers a mathematically well-defined framework for analyzing interactions among self-interested rational agents, with Nash equilibrium serving as the primary solution concept. However, computationally calculating these equilibria remains a significant challenge across many game types. This paper introduces the fixed point network, a neural architecture designed to forecast Nash equilibria. Leveraging the observation that an equilibrium corresponds to a fixed point of the best-response correspondence, we develop an architecture where each node represents a player. The network utilizes a novel, differentiable fixed-point operator to learn this mapping. We demonstrate its efficacy across three progressively difficult game families:
(1) In single and multi-player normal-form games, the structure relies on residual connections to achieve exact discrete fixed-point localization, with trained instances reaching near-perfect accuracy.
(2) For continuous normal-form games, we introduce a smooth fixed-point operator, maintaining high accuracy despite increased complexity.
(3) We apply the network to the n-player Cournot game, a scenario with a lengthy history of incorrect predictions. By integrating our fixed-point operator with a game-theoretic search algorithm, we significantly enhance prediction accuracy.
Finally, we examine how the network generalizes to unseen instances within each game family. Our results indicate that while the model does not generalize well across different game families, it does generalize effectively to unseen instances in single-player, continuous Cournot, and continuous multi-player Cournot games when sampling is performed near the training data. These game families, along with our code and experiments, are available at https://github.com/ashwinbhardwaj/FixedPointNetworks. This work offers a comprehensive examination of fixed-point localization using deep learning and may inspire further research into this area. Our contributions include:
(1) A novel fixed-point localization architecture utilizing residual connections for exact discrete fixed-point finding.
(2) A new differentiable fixed-point operator for continuous optimization.
(3) An exploration of generalization capabilities across various game families.
(4) A demonstration of the synergy between fixed-point search algorithms and deep learning to improve accuracy.
(5) An examination of how these approaches can be utilized for predicting player behavior.

This study addresses the challenge of estimating causal effects when adjustment variables or treatments differ across stages, a scenario frequently encountered in high-dimensional environments where variable selection is necessary. To address this, we introduce a new class of high-dimensional linear regression models designed to handle such nested decisions, inspired by the high-dimensional decision tree structure of nested decision edge models (Li et al., 2019). We develop the Nested Lasso procedure to estimate parameters in this setting and derive finite sample bounds for the estimators. Leveraging these bounds, we construct hypothesis tests to verify the equality of causal effects, providing rigorous error control for stepwise estimation procedures under specific assumptions. Finally, the methodology's validity is confirmed through simulation studies and an application to a high-dimensional gene expression dataset. Additionally, we discuss how to extend this approach to high-dimensional settings where treatments or covariates vary across individuals. Our work builds upon previous research by Belloni et al. (2014) and Liu & Zhang (2018), who addressed similar problems in low-dimensional contexts. Specifically, Liu & Zhang (2018) proposed the Network Lasso for causal effect estimation; we view their model as a simplified instance of our proposed Nested Lasso that does not explicitly account for nested decisions. Our analysis demonstrates that the Nested Lasso model encompasses the Network Lasso as a special case. Furthermore, the nested structure of the loss function in our approach allows for more efficient computation. The main contributions of this paper are the development of a computationally efficient nested loss function, the derivation of finite sample error bounds for parameter estimation, and the proposal of a hypothesis test for comparing nested parameters. These bounds are established without relying on the restricted strong convexity assumption. Additionally, our computational analysis shows that the nested loss function can be optimized more efficiently than general convex functions. Finally, we show that finite sample error bounds for parameter estimation can be derived without requiring strong assumptions about the design matrix. These findings provide a comprehensive theoretical framework for analyzing nested parameter estimation problems. Attacking critical infrastructure has become a significant security concern, with attackers often employing stealthy strategies to avoid detection. This paper introduces a predictive monitoring framework designed to defend linear-time invariant systems against such subtle intrusions. The approach utilizes a predictive filter to estimate system states and an predictive residual generator to identify anomalies in the filtered estimates. To prevent false alarms, the detection filter is optimized using a novel sufficient condition for solvability, which ensures that the predictive residual remains insensitive to stealthy attacks. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through a numerical case study. Additionally, the predictive residual is analyzed for its ability to detect attacks that evade traditional residual-based monitoring. The paper provides a solvability condition for this framework, which is less restrictive than those required by existing literature. Furthermore, an LQG-based design is proposed to minimize the impact of noise estimation errors on the residual, thereby enhancing the framework's sensitivity to attacks. Finally, numerical examples are presented to validate the effectiveness of this proposed method. Keywords: Linear time-invariant systems, Cyber-physical systems, Steady-state attacks, Predictive monitoring, Linear quadratic Gaussian filter.

Document summarization focuses on creating concise yet informative summaries of lengthy texts. While most existing approaches target English, there is a significant scarcity of research targeting Indian languages. This paper introduces GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised model based on Graph Autoencoders designed for Indium summarization. The system first pre-trains an Indian language BERT model to capture unique linguistic features, subsequently employing a graph autoencoder to extract semantic information from sentence representations. These sentences are represented as nodes within a semantic graph, where edge weights denote their relationships. An autoencoder is then utilized to learn a low-dimensional latent space from this graph to capture underlying structural patterns. Finally, these latent representations are aggregated through a weighted average to generate the final summarization output. Experimental results indicate that GAE-ISumm surpasses current state-of-the-art models in summarization performance across three Indian languages. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/Ankit-12345/GAE-ISumm.

**Aims.** This study seeks to restrict the masses and orbital separations of potential substellar companions orbiting five accelerating stars within the solar neighborhood. **Methods.** We conducted a systematic search for previously unidentified companions by analyzing archival data from the Two-Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS) and the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), complemented by new observations using the Spitzer Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope. Additionally, we performed high-precision astrometric follow-up using the Very Large Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope to determine whether astrometric accelerations stem from substellar objects or free-floating planets. **Results.** We identified a substellar companion with a mass of approximately 10 $M_{\rm{Jup}}$ and an orbital separation of roughly 100 au around the accelerating star HD 137414 B. For the remaining four accelerating stars, we established upper limits for the masses and separations of hidden companions. Specifically, for HD 137414 A, the mass-separation constraints exclude brown dwarfs and giant planets with separations exceeding 100 au. **Conclusions.** We conclude that the accelerating motion of HD 137414 B is caused by a substellar companion, while the motions of the other four accelerating stars are likely the result of free-floating planets. Our findings suggest that these stars may have previously hosted substellar companions that were subsequently ejected. These results are consistent with the hypothesis that stars and brown dwarfs in the nearby solar neighborhood were born in star-forming regions with high stellar density. Furthermore, the presence of a substellar companion around HD 137414 B supports the theory that brown dwarfs can retain their atmospheres. Finally, our results align with the hypothesis that brown dwarfs and giant planets are more abundant than previously believed. This research was conducted as part of the SPHEREx Key Program. In recent years, Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for unsupervised learning, enabling the learning of complex data distributions and feature representations while facilitating generative modeling. However, VAEs rely on an approximate posterior distribution and employ KL divergence as a regularization metric to prevent overfitting, which can result in suboptimal performance. To address this, we propose an alternative approach utilizing the least squares loss function for posterior approximation, combined with an L2-regularization term to avoid overfitting. We refer to this method as the Least Squares Variational AutoEncoder (LS-VAE). Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that LS-VAE outperforms standard VAEs in terms of data generation quality and feature representation capabilities, particularly in high-dimensional contexts. Furthermore, ablation studies indicate that KL divergence and L2 regularization serve complementary roles, with L2 regularization proving more effective than KL divergence for feature representation. Finally, we analyze the convergence properties of LS-VAE, offering theoretical insights into its behavior. Our source code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuan1992/LS-VAE. The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has significantly increased security and privacy risks, prompting researchers to explore secure solutions like blockchain to ensure trust and integrity within smart home environments. This paper introduces a private blockchain framework designed to securely track and manage smart home appliances. We developed a localization algorithm that transmits location data to the blockchain to enhance smart home monitoring. During testing, the blockchain successfully and safely stored these coordinates, enabling homeowners to track their devices. The proposed method is straightforward and cost-effective to implement. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that private blockchains are well-suited for smart home monitoring due to their ability to handle the vast number of IoT devices. The results indicate that the system effectively manages an enormous volume of incoming location information with minimal latency. Additionally, we benchmarked our approach against existing blockchain-based methods for smart home monitoring. Ultimately, the proposed framework offers a secure solution for smart home device tracking and monitoring by leveraging blockchain technology. This study presents a deep learning-based quantization of log-likelihood (L-) values designed to mitigate the performance degradation typically caused by quantization in the soft-input soft-output minimum mean square error (SISME) receiver. By applying a quantizer at the modulation encoding stage, the receiver can achieve performance comparable to full-precision L-value quantization while using reduced precision. This enables the construction and training of a deep neural network that accepts the L-value as input and outputs the results passed to the SISME receiver. The approach supports various modulation schemes, including QPSK, 16-QAM, and higher-order QAM, as well as multiple coding schemes such as LDPC, Turbo, and polar codes. Furthermore, the method accommodates both Gaussian and non-Gaussian noise channels. Numerical simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed scheme. Notably, when paired with LDPC codes under a high-order QAM modulation scheme in a Gaussian channel, the proposed method achieves a bit error rate performance nearly identical to that of full-precision L-value quantization. Additionally, the results indicate that the trained deep neural network can be compressed into approximately 10% of its original size. The findings further demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in the literature. Finally, the method is applicable to real-time communication systems, as the training process is completed prior to deployment. Consequently, the required computational complexity is significantly lower than that of online learning approaches found in current state-of-the-art solutions. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first application of deep learning-based quantization to the L-values generated by a communication receiver. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1998/DL-BC-Quantization.

This study introduces novel parameterized algorithms for the classical problem of determining if a directed acyclic graph possesses an upward planar drawing. The research focuses on two primary parameters: the total number of sources ($s$) and the height of the poset ($h$). Leveraging a new poset-based branch-width decomposition, we establish that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to $s$. By integrating this decomposition with recent findings by Demaine et al. regarding upward planar drawings featuring a fixed poset height, we demonstrate fixed-parameter tractability regarding $h$. Furthermore, we present a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for the problem when both $s$ and $h$ are considered as parameters, utilizing the derived upper bounds on the treewidth of the source graph as a key component. Finally, we construct a family of DAGs that exhibit high values of $s$ and treewidth yet remain upward planar, which informs the selection of tight bounds for both parameters throughout the analysis. All proposed algorithms are implemented as open-source software available at https://github.com/ahmedgaber/upward-planarity. The implementation includes algorithms for additional upward planarity problems, such as counting the number of upward planar drawings and assessing whether a single edge can be oriented to yield an upward planar digraph. These algorithms operate efficiently within the framework of fixed-parameter tractability. Additionally, the number of upward planar drawings is shown to be parameterizable based on the minimum feedback arc set size. Finally, the paper concludes with a preliminary investigation into the parameterized complexity of related problems, offering tentative results. Specifically, we outline a fixed-parameter algorithm for the Min-UPward-Planarization problem using poset width as a parameter, alongside a parameterized problem fixing the number of upward planar orientations for a given DAG. The latter relies on a new poset-based tree-decomposition, the properties of which are established in this work. We conjecture that the resulting parameterized complexity is optimal. However, the broader question of fixed-parameter tractability for these problems based on poset width remains unresolved. Our approach utilizes a novel branch decomposition method, the application of which extends beyond upward planarity to other poset-related graph problems. This method is detailed in a separate paper, where its fixed-parameter tractability is proven using poset width. The paper also addresses the challenge of identifying poset width as a parameter for upward planarity testing, ultimately proving that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the minimum feedback arc set size

This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing noisy, crowdsourced datasets. Its performance was evaluated against two baseline methods on two real-world datasets, demonstrating that the proposed approach surpasses human annotator consistency, as measured by inter-annotator agreement. The first method is a standard Multi-Layer Perceptron trained on the data. The second baseline utilizes ensemble modeling, treating the distribution of probabilities from the first method as a "Human Softmax" distribution, and trains a second Multi-Layer Perceptron on these probability estimates. The outcomes from the first baseline and the ensemble method were then aggregated into a final prediction using a new consensus algorithm. This algorithm identifies the most probable class and its confidence score, which are subsequently incorporated into a uncertainty-based consensus algorithm. This updated algorithm calculates the entropy of the Annotator Softmax distribution and the probability that each annotator correctly classified a given sample. The results indicate that the outputs of this uncertainty-driven consensus approach exceed the performance of both the human annotator distribution and the baseline methods. A strength $t$ covering array, denoted $\textrm{CA}(N,k,d)$, consists of $N$ rows with entries from an alphabet of size $d$, where $k$ represents the number of columns. These arrays ensure that every possible tuple of size $t$ appears at least once across the columns. When $t=2$, the smallest such arrays are known as small covering arrays. Although extensive research exists on this topic, many structural questions remain unresolved. This paper investigates the structure of small covering arrays through the lens of graph theory, specifically by defining a graph $G_{\mathcal{A}}$ associated with each covering array $\mathcal{A}$. In $G_{\cal A}$, the $d$ vertices correspond to the alphabet values, and an edge connects two vertices if and only if they appear together in at least one row. We establish the relationship between the covering array's parameters and the graph $G_{\mathcal{A}}$, demonstrating that for any small covering array, this graph must be complete. Furthermore, we prove that if a small covering array contains at least one row comprising all distinct alphabet values, then $N \ge d(d-1)/2$. This result leads to the conjecture that for any small covering array, $N \ge d(d-1)/2$, with the equality holding if and only if the array possesses a single row containing all unique alphabet values. Additionally, we examine the covering array with the minimum number of rows, showing that $N \ge d(d+1)/4$ and that this bound is tight when $d$ is odd. We further demonstrate that if $d \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, then $N \ge d(d+2)/4$. Finally, we present a construction that yields a covering array achieving the minimum $N$ for $d \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. We demonstrate that any nonlocal game utilizing maximally entangled states, subject to arbitrary noise, is decidable—meaning its optimal value can be determined in strong exponential time. While the exact values for certain games, such as the million qubit CHSH game, likely cannot be computed in polynomial time, our findings expand the range of nonlocal games and noisy quantum resources for which efficient semi-definite programs can determine optimal values with arbitrary precision. Furthermore, this result validates several conjectures, including the conjecture asserting that every nonlocal game with two-player strategies has a decidable optimal value.

This breakthrough is achieved by integrating the approximate reduction of noisy state-constrained nonlocal games into a specific class of vector-based games, which are known to admit efficient semi-definite formulations. We also examine alternative methods for characterizing the convex hull of strategy correlations, which may find utility in proving the complexity complexity of other problems.

This paper describes a genetic algorithm designed to reproduce crashes in Java software, originally developed and published by Kalsingh et al. in 2019. The study validates the alibi property of input variables, ensuring that no single variable causes a crash independently. It employs three fitness functions to maximize coverage of mutant mutants, dead code, and the unreachable path leading to the failure. The algorithm's effectiveness is tested using Microsoft Excel 2010, Microsoft Word 2010, and JUnit test cases. Results indicate that the guided genetic algorithm successfully reproduces crashes, with input vector coverage reaching 100% for the JUnit crash and exceeding 90% for both Microsoft applications. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrates robustness by avoiding out-of-bounds array access errors. Future research will explore the use of machine learning to automatically generate test data for crash reproduction. The existence of an intermediate vortex lattice phase characterized by alternating $\sqrt{2} \xi \times \sqrt{2} \xi$ and $2\xi \times 2\xi$ unit cells within high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates has been suggested by recent scanning tunneling microscope (STM) experiments. This study presents nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data from La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ that corroborates such a transition. Our measurements reveal two distinct NMR lineshifts in the intermediate lattice phase, each linked to a specific average local magnetic field. We demonstrate that these two line-shifts can be accounted for by a vortex lattice composed of a mixture of two $\xi \times \xi$ unit cells, consistent with prior STM findings. Furthermore, the thermal evolution of the phase boundary aligns with a thermodynamic model that incorporates the energy difference between these two lattice types. Our results provide robust evidence for a novel phase that smoothly merges the vortex lattice and stripe phases as temperature rises. We further propose that this transition represents a new thermodynamic driving force for stripe formation in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates. Finally, our results offer a framework for synthesizing and interpreting existing STM studies of vortex lattices in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates. Specifically, STM data from La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ and YBCO reveal a phase boundary that closely matches the boundary between the two $\xi \times \xi$ lattice types identified in this work. Additionally, we demonstrate that the STM phase boundary in YBCO converges with the NMR phase boundary in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ as the Sr doping level approaches $x=0.15$, indicating that the vortex lattice transition is more pronounced in La$_{1.5}$Sr$_{0.5}$CuO$_4$ than in YBCO. This suggests that the vortex lattice transition is a general phenomenon in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates, with the most robust occurrence found in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ near the optimal doping of $x=0.15$. Ultimately, the STM vortex lattice phase serves as a unique vortex lattice variant that reveals the vortex lattice's complex structure. Photon viscometry within the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) is explored through an analysis of anisotropic flow in thermal photons generated during hadronic and hadro-chemical freezeouts. This investigation utilizes a chiral kinetic theory framework, where the anisotropy of the QGP's phase-space distribution functions drives the generation of anisotropic thermal photons. The study focuses on experimentally accessible observables, specifically the ratio of mixed harmonic flow coefficients $v_2/f_2$ and $v_3/f_3$, across various collision systems and centrality classes. By comparing these observables against experimental data, we establish a quantitative link between $v_2/f_2$ and $v_3/f_3$ as functions of transverse momentum $p_T$, and photon multiplicity as a function of $p_T$ and centralities, explicitly accounting for QGP viscosity. Our findings indicate that both anisotropic photon flow observables are sensitive to QGP shear viscosity, with $v_2/f_2$ exhibiting greater sensitivity than $v_3/f_3$. Furthermore, the photon anisotropic flow ratio is predicted to be larger in heavy-ion collisions than in proton-proton collisions, a trend that may help distinguish between the viscous shear viscosity of the QGP and initial-state momentum anisotropies. Consequently, these measurements offer a promising avenue for constraining the shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio, $\eta/s$, of the QGP. This study examines potential regular magnetic orders in triangular and kagome lattices featuring multiple sites per unit cell. By utilizing group theory, we identify candidate orders based on their symmetry properties and construct the corresponding spin structures for every possibility. We demonstrate that all regular magnetic orders previously found in these lattices can be derived from our comprehensive list of potential candidates. Furthermore, we compute the magnetic structure factors and compare them with recent neutron scattering findings for the kagome lattice material herbertsmithite. Our results indicate that candidate orders exhibiting small magnetic structure factors are more likely to be realized, which aligns with the observed spin structures in both kagome and triangular lattices. Additionally, we illustrate that magnetic structures with few magnetic moments per unit cell tend to be selected, offering an explanation for the presence of finite magnetic structure factors in neutron data. Finally, we note that some magnetic orders with minimal magnetic moments per unit cell are selected in certain kagome lattices, a phenomenon that can be attributed to their smaller magnetic structure factors. This work provides a complete classification of all potential magnetic structures in triangular and kagome lattices and establishes a new criterion for understanding the actual magnetic structures found in these materials. We anticipate that this framework will prove valuable for future studies on other lattices. We introduce a novel statistical framework designed to identify causal treatment effects within large-scale experiments, addressing the challenges of high dimensionality and dependent data structures. Our method utilizes a screening process to filter out null covariates and a test statistic approach to distinguish treated from control groups based on their impact on the response variable. To rigorously control the false discovery rate (FDR) in large samples, we employ the asymptotic FDR control strategy proposed by Benjamini and Kuerste (2013), specifically leveraging the normal approximation of the count of type-I errors under weak dependence conditions. By utilizing the CLT and DML techniques, we rigorously demonstrate FDR control in both finite and large-scale settings. Extensive simulations and real-world data analyses confirm the method's robustness and superior performance. This study is conducted in collaboration with Dr. Yuanyuan Yang. The fundamental concepts of cosmological inflation are examined. We derive the equations of motion governing the inflaton field, define the slow-roll parameters, and present the slow-roll approximation. The relationship between the slow-roll parameters and $\epsilon$ is established, along with an analysis of the scales of physical quantities that evolve rapidly during inflation, specifically demonstrating the swift exponential expansion of the scale factor. Furthermore, we derive the spectral index and the tensor-to-scalar ratio as functions of the slow-roll parameters. We also provide an analysis of chaotic, hybrid, and quadratic inflation models, deriving predictions for the cosmic microwave background in each case. Finally, we determine the critical value of $\epsilon$ necessary to terminate inflation and illustrate how quantum fluctuations of the inflaton field generate seeds for primordial structure formation. Overall, this work provides foundational information for students and researchers in physics. All relevant equations and relations are derived, and we have omitted topics beyond the scope of an introductory course on cosmological inflation. We conclude by stating that no external references were utilized in preparing this document.

Software developers frequently encounter queries during maintenance tasks, such as identifying which component handles a specific event. To address this, concept query reformulation has emerged, enabling concept locators to utilize query reformulations generated by domain experts. Existing approaches rely on expert-annotated reformulations from public datasets like QuRE. However, these datasets contain only a few thousand entries, limiting their scope to specific domains and excluding others. Our proposed solution, QUICKAR, utilizes crowdsourced knowledge to generate query reformulations. By employing a novel classifier, QUICKAR filters out irrelevant reformulations, thereby enhancing concept locators with a broader set of reformulations than previously available. We evaluated QUICKAR across three diverse software projects to demonstrate its efficacy. The results indicate that concept locators augmented with QUICKAR achieve superior precision and recall compared to those using curated reformulations. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that our approach successfully filters out irrelevant reformulations. Finally, we show that integrating QUICKAR with existing query reformulation methods produces synergistic effects, yielding even more reformulations. Ultimately, QUICKAR facilitates automated, general, and scalable query reformulation, supporting further research in this area. Entrainment is a recognized mechanism in face-to-face communication where individuals subtly mimic specific aspects of their conversation partners' utterances to foster alignment and collaboration. This study introduces a novel approach to quantify the degree of entrainment by estimating distances between paired utterances. Utilizing 11 distinct neural distances derived from neural networks trained to calculate the dissimilarity between paired speech segments, the research assesses their efficacy across various entrainment metrics, including acoustic features, transcript words, and underlying semantic representations. Leveraging the properties of these features, an ensemble model is developed to enhance performance. The methodology is validated across three datasets: two conversation datasets and one medical diagnostic interaction dataset. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that neural distances effectively capture entrainment; specifically, distances derived from character-level text representations yield strong results, and the proposed ensemble method outperforms any single individual distance measure. Furthermore, results indicate that neural distances perform robustly across all datasets, even though they were trained exclusively on the acoustic content of the data. Finally, statistical significance testing confirms that these measured distances align with human perceptions of entrainment. Overall, this work establishes a framework for unsupervised estimation of entrainment, with potential applications in areas such as detecting social skills deficits in autism and evaluating the interactivity of conversational agents. Future research will explore applying this framework to measure entrainment in agent-human interactions. This study represents a novel contribution to the field of conversational dynamics. The evaluation code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Estimating-Unsupervised-Entrainment}. Additional code and data are available from the corresponding authors. Speaker alignment was assessed using a neural speaker embedding model, which was trained to predict speaker identity. While that prior research did not investigate the relationship between speaker identity and acoustic characteristics, this work explicitly examines such relationships. The current study marks a distinct and significant advancement. Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is a critical task within action recognition that demands high precision in video quality. While many TAS techniques rely on supervised learning, they are restricted by the necessity for highly accurate ground truth annotations. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Parsing (SSCAP), an unsupervised TAS method that leverages self-supervised learning to derive meaningful labels from video data. Our approach is grounded in the principle that actions at varying temporal scales co-occur within a video. We represent the video as a graph featuring an informative skeleton structure and employ a self-supervised contrastive loss to ensure consistent feature representations across different action co-occurrence scales. Furthermore, we propose a novel adaptive label smoothing loss to enhance segmentation accuracy by mitigating the impact of noisy labels. SSCP achieves state-of-the-art results on two TAS benchmarks and demonstrates promising performance on the action recognition dataset JODE. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/SSCAP. Additionally, the dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/JODE. JODE is a unsupervised TAS dataset. This study investigates exotic pentaquark states containing two charm quarks by analyzing their production and decay processes through the current algebra framework. Specifically, the four-charm-quark component of the weak nonleptonic current is expanded in terms of QCD color singlet quark pairs. We examine a hypothetical scenario involving the flavor-changing neutral current $c\to s c\bar c$, which offers a pathway to generate a pentaquark with the quark content $|sc c c\bar N\rangle$ during the decay $D\to sP_\gamma(N)$. Subsequently, we evaluate the decays of these hidden-charm double-charm pentaquarks via the decays of their constituent $D$ and light quark $s$, covering both strong and electromagnetic channels. Our results demonstrate that the partial decay width $\Gamma(D\to sP_\gamma(N))$ scales as $1/m_D^2$ relative to the full $D$-meson decay width, suggesting that such decays are suppressed by the large $D$-meson mass. Furthermore, the decays of $P_\gamma(N)$ proceed predominantly through the strong interaction, with the $s$-quark decaying via the weak interaction into $u$ or $d$ quarks, accompanied by corrections arising from $s\to c\bar c s$ transitions. Finally, we show that the partial decay width $\Gamma(P_\gamma(N)\to M_1 M_2)$ follows a $1/m_{P_\gamma(N)}^2$ scaling compared to the $P_\gamma(N)$ decay width, where $M_{1,2}$ represent the daughter mesons. This study investigates the impact of traditional detailed feedback versus inquiry-based conceptual feedback mechanisms on novice programmers during testing education. We conducted a within-subjects experiment involving 24 participants, comparing an inquiry-based feedback approach against a condition where students received standard detailed feedback from automated online testing tools. Results indicated that while both groups performed similarly on tasks involving specific testing concepts, the group utilizing inquiry-based feedback achieved significantly higher scores on assessments related to broader software engineering concepts. These findings suggest that teaching specific software concepts through inquiry-based methods can enhance students' understanding of the subject matter. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for software testing education and propose this teaching methodology as a viable approach for delivering specific software concepts to learners. Keywords: Software Testing Education, Feedback Mechanisms, Within-Subjects Experimentation, Conceptual Teaching.

Domain adaptation is a widely adopted strategy for addressing domain shift, yet most existing methods rely on collecting large quantities of labeled sources from various domains, a process that is often costly and time-intensive. This paper introduces a novel approach to domain adaptation termed Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA). SFDA aims to eliminate the dependency on multiple sources by utilizing a single unlabeled empty source from which hypotheses are generated for unlabelled target domains. To achieve this, we propose Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Transfer (SSH), an SFDA method that leverages semi-supervised learning to transfer hypotheses from the source to diverse target domains. SSH is designed to be model-agnostic, making it applicable to a broad range of deep learning architectures. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art SFDA techniques. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYi-97/SFDA. This paper outlines the design of an in-flight nuclear reactor capable of delivering up to 100 MW of thermal power. Such a system would enable deep space missions to operate more efficiently than current architectures. We introduce a reactor design utilizing uranium helium-4 fuel, which offers significant advantages over reactors using helium-3 or other light fuels. The analysis examines this design and evaluates its feasibility. The study evaluates the reactor's thermal output across a spectrum of operating conditions. Additionally, we propose a conceptual analysis of the reactor's material composition. Finally, the paper discusses the engineering challenges inherent in designing such a system. This study introduces a domain-informed neural network (DMIN) tailored for particle interaction reconstruction in astroparticle experiments. By integrating knowledge of the particle diffusion equation, movement boundaries, and conservation laws, DMIN achieves performance that equals or surpasses current methods. Specifically, when analyzing interactions within the Majorana demonstrator, DMIN improves energy resolution by 10% and reduces the mean difference in reconstructed vertex distance to the closest detector wall by 15% compared to the existing technique, MARNOLD. Furthermore, because DMIN's architecture is modular, it can be readily adapted to other experimental setups, making it a versatile tool for the field. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/alexei-panov/DMIN}. Additional implementation details are available in our supplementary material. Atmospheric retrievals serve as a critical instrument for both characterizing exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres and benchmarking models against observational data. These retrievals depend on exoplanet atmosphere models that integrate diverse molecular opacities, which are accessed via database software. The utilization of such databases is expanding, driven by the increasing number of observations and the anticipated rise in observations from upcoming facilities like JWST. However, a significant challenge remains: the lack of unified databases compatible with multiple retrieval tools and the insufficient coverage of databases for specific molecules relevant to exoplanet atmospheres. This study addresses these issues by introducing a comprehensive, unified, and easily accessible database for key molecules. We developed EXOPLINES, a new, unified collection of line parameters and associated software for H2O, CO, CH4, and HCN across a broad temperature range. EXOPLINES is compatible with various retrieval tools and supports a wide array of molecules. The database is hosted on the ExoWeb platform, ensuring easy accessibility, and can be easily extended with additional molecules. We anticipate that EXOPLINES will facilitate the creation of unified and comprehensive database sets, thereby enhancing the accuracy of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheric retrievals. Grounding constitutes a critical phase of knowledge representation, yet it remains an open research challenge. This paper explores various grounding methodologies based on different knowledge structures, utilizing answer set programming to model these problems. We examine multiple modeling strategies and evaluate them through several criteria. Our analysis reveals that grounding is a complex and multifaceted problem requiring further investigation. Consequently, we propose an integrated modeling approach that unifies multiple grounding techniques into a single framework. This new method is more expressive and flexible than its individual components, effectively handling complex dependencies among grounding variables and incorporating probabilistic information through answer set programming with constraints and probabilistic literals. Finally, we demonstrate multiple ways to model a probabilistic ontology using this proposed approach. Specifically, we use the probabilistic knowledge base to analyze how probabilistic information influences the number of variables required for grounding. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed modeling approach is efficient for small instances. However, the number of grounded variables remains a significant bottleneck, necessitating the use of approximation techniques to address it. We also evaluate two such methods: clustering and incremental grounding. Our findings show that the clustering approach is more effective than the incremental method. Furthermore, intelligent knowledge discovery enables the identification of knowledge clusters, allowing for efficient grounding of variables within each cluster. Ultimately, our approach is highly flexible and can be extended to support various modeling techniques. Additionally, we outline several directions for future research. This work establishes the change law for general quantum resources, demonstrating that for any monotonic and continuous $R$-measure $R$, the difference between a measure of a state $\rho$ and its evolution under a completely positive and trace-preserving map $\mathcal{E}$ is bounded below by the resource content of the map's output, expressed as $R(\rho) - R(\mathcal{E}(\rho)) \geq R(\mathcal{E})$. This finding extends past research on quantum resources, which was largely confined to scenarios involving only free resources or, in the case of the modification to the second law of thermodynamics, a single non-free thermal bath. We illustrate the broad applicability of this result by deriving specific laws governing coherence, entanglement, and entanglement of formation. Furthermore, we elucidate how these outcomes extend and complement recent developments regarding non-free thermal processes and propose that our findings represent a significant step toward formulating a comprehensive theory of non-free resource theories. Notably, our conclusions are applicable to both global and local transformations. In the specific context of local operations and classical communication (LOCC), we find that the law of entanglement content takes the form of an equality, thereby enabling the derivation of new entanglement inequalities. Additionally, we investigate the implications of our findings for generalizing resource theories and their associated change laws. Specifically, we identify a potential flaw in a recently proposed generalization concerning non-free thermal processes and clarify the conditions under which our change law applies to non-free resources. We establish the consistency of the Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimator (QMLE) and QML, demonstrating that these estimators converge to normal distributions asymptotically. Additionally, we prove the asymptotic $t$-distribution nature of the test statistics derived from the standardized central limit theorem. Our analysis also covers a scenario where a parameter is subject to a linear constraint. Furthermore, we extend these findings to a more complex non-linear model featuring a $d$-dimensional parameter, providing an asymptotic inference framework for this multidimensional setting. Finally, simulations are conducted to evaluate the finite-sample performance of our proposed inference method. In these simulations, we compare our approach against a recent method by Arunachalam and Rahimi (2021), which is specifically designed for stationary linear time series. Finally, we apply the inference method to the monthly S&P 500 index, spanning from January 1926 to December 2021. We introduce a novel class of good quantum low-density parity-check codes equipped with a linear-time decoder operating in the worst case. This approach builds upon recent progress regarding classical quantum lifted codes and their associated decoders. Specifically, for a subset of these codes, we demonstrate that the distance is at least $\Omega(n)$, provided the check distance is at least $\Omega(\log n)$. We further establish that this specific subclass can be efficiently encoded and decoded within the stabilizer framework. The proposed check distance analysis draws inspiration from recent advancements in analyzing time and space required to train neural networks. We detail the entire construction process, including the methods used to derive the check distance and encode the code using stabilizer techniques. Our encoding algorithm achieves a runtime of $\tilde O(n)$, where tilde notation omits logarithmic factors. The design of the decoder relies on recent findings that most graphs are time encodable given their time-encodable subgraphs. We demonstrate that a significant portion of our code family meets these time-encodability criteria, thereby enabling the application of the classical decoder to the quantum code. This work marks the first instance of good quantum LDPC codes achieving such performance. Additionally, we extend the methodology to construct a family of quantum LDPC codes that are explicitly time-decodable. Our analysis indicates that a substantial fraction of this code family possesses a distance of $\Omega(\log n)$. We anticipate that these families will play a pivotal role in advancing the field of quantum LDPC codes. Our findings also contribute to broader research areas, including the development of locally decodable codes and the investigation of LDPC graphs with exceptional properties. Finally, we demonstrate that these quantum LDPC families can be implemented using two-dimensional photonic circuits. This implementation benefits from recent progress in constructing good LDPC graphs with low treewidth and utilizes a straightforward encoding strategy. We further prove that these families maintain good distance properties under local perturbations. Our work represents the first construction of two-dimensional photonic circuits capable of encoding these families of quantum LDPC codes. The proposed circuit architecture is straightforward, comprising a sequence of two-dimensional layers. Each layer contains a constant number of gates, with every two-qubit gate acting on adjacent qubits. We demonstrate that the distance of a substantial fraction of our quantum LDPC code families can be lower-bounded by $\Omega(\log n)$. This analysis utilizes a novel technique that extends recent work on the properties of isoperalizable graphs. We also prove that the families are good under local perturbations.

This study examines the distributed complexity of the Distance-$r$ Dominating Set problem, which involves identifying a subset of vertices such that every node in the graph is within distance $r$ of at least one member of the subset. We analyze this problem across multiple distributed computing frameworks, specifically focusing on the Randomized Centralized Stochastic (RCS) model and the PRAM model. By employing a multi-axial analysis, we derive both positive and lower-bound results. Our approach leverages graph sparsity, low girth, and vertex colorings to design distributed algorithms that determine Distance-$r$ Dominating Sets. The proposed algorithms operate in $O(n^{1/r})$ rounds on the PRAM model and $O(n^{1/r}/\log n)$ iterations on the RCS model for any fixed $r \geq 1$. Furthermore, we establish that no algorithm can achieve a significantly faster solution on the PRAM model, and we present a lower bound for any randomized distributed algorithm operating on high-girth graphs within the PRAM model. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of these methods to graphs excluding a fixed minor.

Keywords: Distributed Computing, Dominating Set, High Girth Graphs, Sparse Graphs, Randomized Centralized Stochastic Model, PRAM Model.
