We conducted a survey of the Rho Ophician cloud using the 100 and 486 GHz lines of $C^{18}O$ and the [CII] 100 $\mu$m recombination line, alongside new observations of the PDR fine structure lines [NII] 205 $\mu$m and [OI] 63 $\mu$m. These data were gathered with the IRAM 30m and NOEMA telescopes, along with the SOFIA and Herschel Space Observatory, to map the distribution of ionized, atomic, and PDR gas surrounding the SMM source S1 in the Rho Ophician cloud. Our analysis reveals a compact molecular core at the base of the S1 SMM source, which is enveloped by a large-scale atomic cloud. Additionally, we detected a narrow layer of PDR gas enveloping the ionized gas. The [CII] 100 $\mu$m recombination line indicates a size of approximately 0.1 pc for the S1 SMM source, a dimension consistent with observations in $C^{18}O$ and NII 205 $\mu$m. The [NII] 205 $\mu$m line exhibits a blue-shifted velocity of roughly -1 km s$^{-1}$ relative to the molecular core, while the [CII] profile shows a slight red-shift of about 1 km s$^{-1}$. This suggests that the ionized gas is expanding away from the source at a velocity of approximately 2 km s$^{-1}$. The PDR gas displays a red-shifted velocity of about 1 km s$^{-1}$ relative to the molecular core, indicating that the PDR layer is expanding into the ionized gas. We propose that the S1 SMM source is a compact, expanding HII region, with the PDR layer situated at its boundary. The [OI] 63 $\mu$m line is detected at the periphery of the HII region, where the radiation field is weaker, consistent with expectations. The [OI] 63 $\mu$m line is approximately 10 times fainter than the [CII] 100 $\mu$m recombination line, implying that the [CII] 100 $\mu$m recombination line is a more reliable tracer of the HII region's edge. The remarkable success of transformer-based machine learning (ML) models has spurred extensive research and development across numerous domains. In computer vision, these models have surpassed traditional convolutional architectures, achieving state-of-the-art results in tasks ranging from image classification to complex scenarios like panoptic segmentation and video prediction. This survey comprehensively reviews the adoption of transformers in vision applications, focusing on surveying 111 papers published between 2020 and 2022. We categorize these works into four primary areas: vision transformers, vision transformers enhanced with convolution, vision transformers applied to time-series data, and large-scale vision transformers. Our goal is to deepen the understanding of transformer-based computer vision for both practitioners and researchers. This study evaluates two factor models, TVFM and IVFM, for short-term mortality forecasting using US data from 1900 to 2018. In the TVFM framework, factor loadings are allowed to vary over time via a smoothing method, whereas in the IVFM, loadings remain constant throughout the series. We estimate both models and forecast mortality rates for the US, comparing their performance against the CaviModel, a widely used benchmark. Our analysis reveals that, on average, the TVFM generates forecasts as accurate as those from the CaviModel. Furthermore, we examine the evolution of forecasting accuracy over time and identify a shift occurring between 1960 and 1970. Finally, to enhance prediction quality, we propose a model-averaging approach that linearly combines the forecasts from both frameworks. This averaging technique improves TVFM and CaviModel forecasts during the period 1970–2018, while also yielding superior results for IVFM forecasts from 1900 to 1960. These results underscore the value of model averaging for short-term forecasting applications. All code and data utilized in this research are publicly accessible. For additional details, please consult our website or contact the corresponding author. Keywords: mortality forecasting, factor models, model averaging. JEL Classification: C58, I12.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) offers a promising method for automatically designing neural networks for image classification by exploring a search space of architectures. To reduce the time required for this exploration, researchers often restrict the process to a subset of the search space, a strategy known as one-shot Search Space Restriction (SSR). SSR aims to identify a specific subset where performance is maximized while interference between architectures is minimized. This study provides the first in-depth analysis of interference within NAS search spaces. We characterize it based on the relationship between an architecture's performance and that of others in the space, distinguishing between beneficial interference (where high performance is maintained) and harmful interference (where performance drops). SSR is shown to be an effective approach for mitigating this interference. Our research demonstrates that this technique can further be enhanced by incorporating the concept of interference into the design of network components, the selection of search spaces, and the formulation of optimization methods. Additionally, we introduce a novel SSR method called Hierarchical Search Space Restriction (HSSR), which restricts the search space for each network layer to a subset of the overall search space. This work not only offers a deeper understanding of interference in NAS search spaces but also establishes a new framework for mitigating it. Experiments on image classification tasks within the ENAS search space validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongzhixu/interference_analysis_NAS. Furthermore, the HSSR method is available for research use in the Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) framework at https://github.com/zhongzhixu/hssr. The results of one-shot SSR and HSSR are also included. This research was conducted during an internship at the Microsoft Research OneStopShop. We provide specific, "infinitesimal" criteria ensuring that a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space possesses a semistable fundamental group at infinity. These criteria are applicable to certain classes of spaces arising from low-dimensional topology. In the second part, assuming a mild condition on fundamental groups, we demonstrate that a CAT(0) space with non-positive curvature possesses a semistable fundamental group at infinity precisely when its boundary comprises two ends, each homeomorphic to an Euclidean building of dimension one or two. This result relies on the recent finding by D. Löh and J. Pettersen that fundamental groups of CAT(0) spaces are amenably dominated by their ends if and only if the space possesses two ends. Furthermore, we establish the reverse of this statement for spaces with an Euler characteristic of one. The final section offers examples illustrating the reverse implication and highlights the significance of the assumption requiring that cyclic subgroups be compactly contained within the space. Our findings extend the work of D. Löh and J. Pettersen, building upon the connection between the amenability of ends and the properties of isometry groups in CAT(0) spaces with positive curvature. Additionally, we present examples demonstrating how the nature of ends and amenability in CAT(0) spaces with positive curvature can differ from those with non-positive curvature. The second and third parts of the article specifically address geometric group theory and group actions. These parts extend the recent work of D. Löh and J. Pettersen on amenability and ends in non-positively curved spaces with Euler characteristic zero, building on their findings regarding spaces with Euler characteristic one. The paper concludes with an outline of future research directions. We first develop a Bayesian model designed to address the challenge of translator reliability assessment. Subsequently, we demonstrate how this same model can be utilized to calculate the probability that specific MT outputs fall within a certain range of automatic evaluation scores, as well as the probability of their recombination. These capabilities enable planners to determine optimal thresholds for post-editing. The study's effectiveness is validated through a case analysis of professional translators. Ultimately, this research underscores the significance of Bayesian approaches in driving the development of Computer-Assisted Translation technologies. By facilitating reliability assessment and aiding the planning of post-editing operations, this method supports the broader objective of establishing an effective Total Quality Management system. Furthermore, it assists in refining the design of translation services to meet client requirements. Given the widespread adoption of MT services, there is a pressing need to accurately assess both translator and MT reliability to ensure that the adoption of such services is justified. In systems characterized by random scattering, the deposition matrix transforms an incident wavefront into an internal field distribution throughout a target volume. These eigenchannels of the matrix represent an orthogonal set of independent scattering modes, each resulting in distinct spatial energy distributions within the target. This study demonstrates that sum rules governing these eigenchannels can be derived from the scattering properties of a single specular reflection, providing a straightforward generalization of the universality inherent in diffuse eigenchannel statistics. Additionally, it is shown that while sum rules for eigenchannels with real eigenvalues apply universally to any shape or size of a randomly scattering object immersed in a random medium, sum rules concerning eigenchannels with complex eigenvalues rely on the geometric details of the specific object. Finally, applications of these findings to problems involving small and large particles are explored. The necessary generalizations are also provided to address problems where the scatterer is immersed in a non-uniform background. These results are supported by applications to a randomly scattering sphere and a randomly scattering slab. Finally, a numerical simulation of a randomly scattering square demonstrates the validity of the sum rules. This work was conducted in collaboration with J. B. Davies, M. P. P. Musgrave, and J. R. Pruning techniques have emerged as a promising approach for reducing the computational demands of deep neural networks. This study investigates the capacity of pruning to extract the features necessary for high-accuracy performance on the MNIST and CIFAR100 image classification tasks. By utilizing the recently introduced Dynamic Sparse Pruning (DSP) algorithm, we demonstrate that both Fully Connected (FC) networks and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can be pruned to retain the essential features for training. Our findings indicate that, even with an equivalent number of parameters, the sparsity achieved in FC networks exceeds that of CNNs. This result underscores the critical role of convolutional kernels in efficiently extracting features within CNNs compared to the architecture used in FC networks. Consequently, we conclude that CNNs are likely the winning lottery ticket among all possible networks composed of FC layers. This insight offers a valuable perspective for designing sparse neural networks that maintain accuracy while minimizing computational requirements. This study investigates maximizing the expected return of a lottery ticket by addressing two fundamental questions: the optimal pricing for sales and the ideal conditions for purchase. To solve this, we formulate two corresponding stochastic dynamic programming models. We then derive optimal policies, derive key properties of the value functions, and establish the necessary conditions under which purchasing becomes advantageous. Finally, we explore the computational complexity associated with calculating the optimal pricing strategies. A Python implementation utilizing the JAX library is made available to ensure reproducibility. Additionally, we introduce two new algorithms capable of solving the proposed stochastic dynamic programming problems. Our numerical experiments employ two distinct scenarios: one involving discrete random variables and another involving continuous random variables. For the continuous case, we utilize two methods: a computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulation and a computationally efficient piecewise constant approximation. These simulations demonstrate that: (i) our algorithms effectively solve the models for both continuous and discrete variables; (ii) stochastic demand significantly impacts the optimal pricing strategy; and (iii) the optimal selling period is contingent upon the price at which tickets are offered. Furthermore, numerical results indicate that our models can yield substantial returns, ranging from 10% to 30%. This paper serves as a foundation for future research aimed at extending our models to capture more realistic demand dynamics. Specifically, we aim to model demand as a random variable dependent on previous winning numbers, thereby creating a more realistic framework for lottery pricing. This approach would also enable the analysis of potential market manipulation risks. Our future work will focus on developing appropriate mathematical models to investigate these scenarios. Our methodology is applicable to various lotteries, including those with continuous random variables, such as the French Loto, which uses a $[1, 90]$ range. This application is highly relevant for public policy, as it can assist regulators in setting appropriate prices to prevent market manipulation. Furthermore, our findings can guide regulators in establishing reasonable minimum and maximum price limits. The methods developed in this work can also inform decisions regarding the introduction of new pricing strategies or the implementation of discounts. The material presented herein can thus assist regulators in making informed decisions concerning pricing strategies in the lottery market. Finally, our findings may assist consumers in determining the optimal times to purchase tickets. The methodologies developed in this work can also assist consumers in making informed decisions about when to buy. These outcomes could enhance the consumer experience and promote responsible participation in the lottery market. The valley Hall effect and related valley Hall resistivity phenomena have been widely investigated in two-dimensional materials. These features typically stem from specific electron-phonon-avalanche mechanisms triggered by high-energy phonons, which necessitate a specific crystal structure and strong valley separation. However, certain mechanisms can operate without requiring these strict conditions, thereby expanding the range of potential materials for valley physics. This study demonstrates that both the valley Hall effect and valley Hall resistivity can arise solely from nonlinear electron-phonon coupling. This approach eliminates the need for high-energy phonons, a specific lattice geometry, or distinct valleys, thus broadening the scope of materials suitable for valley Hall phenomena. The resulting mechanisms can produce substantial valley Hall resistivity even in systems with minimal valley separation. Furthermore, these effects persist in three-dimensional materials and can be enhanced through thin-film engineering. These findings provide a foundation for investigating additional valley-related phenomena and enable the development of valley-based devices in thin films of conventional non-two-dimensional materials. The proposed mechanisms can also be harnessed for thermoelectric applications by exploiting nonlinear valley-dependent phonon scattering. Finally, the computational framework employed facilitates the calculation of complex many-body interactions, significantly accelerating the discovery of new materials for valley physics. This research investigates the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model, where an impurity interacts attractively with a Fermi sea of particles under zero-range conditions. We present diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DMC) findings for both the polaron binding energy and wave function normalization constant across a range of coupling strengths. Our DMC binding energy results align well with recent variational density-matrix quantum Monte Carlo (DMQMC) data for the coupling range of $U = [-0.5, -0.1]$. Additionally, we offer a theoretical explanation for the discrepancy between our binding energy results and those from the density-matrix approach. Finally, our results support the hypothesis that a quantum phase transition from a polaron to a molecule occurs at $U = -0.25$. This hypothesis is derived by comparing polaron properties with molecule properties calculated using the same DMC technique. To address the slow convergence issue in computing the normalization constant, we introduce a novel algorithm designed to significantly enhance the convergence rate in this specific context. Using the new algorithm, we determine the normalization constant for $U = -0.25$, finding it to be $Z = 0.11(1)$. This value indicates that the polaron transforms into a molecule at $U = -0.25$, consistent with the analysis of the binding energy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the binding energy and normalization constant can be accurately represented by a power-law function near the critical point, with critical exponents of $\nu = 2$ and $\nu(2-\eta) = 1$, respectively. These exponents correspond to the 2D Ising universality class. Finally, we examine the limitations of the DMC method in calculating the decay rate of an unstable polaron into a two-particle state. Specifically, for strong coupling ($U < -0.2$), the decay rate proves to be sensitive to the number of diagrams included in the DMC calculation. Graph polynomials constitute a significant and rapidly developing field, with researchers actively seeking methods to connect them through diverse approaches. This work examines two distinct methodologies for defining families of symmetric polynomials based on graph invariants. The initial approach utilizes generating functions to establish polynomials through their initial coefficients, whereas the second approach defines polynomials recursively using elementary symmetric polynomials. The objective is to determine whether the resulting generating functions exhibit a relationship. This study investigates these frameworks across a wide array of examples, demonstrating that while no general equivalence exists, numerous relationships do arise. Specifically, we identify that for many natural families of graph polynomials, the recursively defined version is simply a scalar multiple of the generating function version. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this scalar relationship in the context of the graph reconstruction conjecture. Finally, we establish a new connection to the reconstruction conjecture by analyzing the relationship between the polynomials derived from our second approach and the polynomial $\pi(G)$ introduced by Kocay and Lowe. To facilitate this analysis, we derive an explicit formula for $\pi(G)$ that accommodates a broader class of graphs than previously addressed in the literature. Additionally, we provide an efficient algorithm to compute $\pi(G)$ for any given graph. Our findings indicate that $\pi(G)$ is closely linked to polynomials generated by the first approach; however, unlike the scalar relationship observed between the two approach-based polynomials, the relationship between $\pi(G)$ and the first-approach polynomials involves an infinite set of scalar factors. We conclude by outlining several open questions regarding these relationships. Finally, we demonstrate that polynomials generated by the second approach can be efficiently computed for any graph. Specifically, we present an algorithm with $O(|V(G)|^2)$ complexity to calculate these polynomials, where $|V(G)|$ denotes the vertex count of $G$. This represents a substantial improvement over the naive algorithm, which exhibits exponential complexity relative to the graph size. We also propose a conjecture concerning the existence of an $O(|V(G)|)$ complexity algorithm for this purpose. Finally, we detail an algorithm for computing the coefficients of these polynomials that relies on a generalization of the rotation distance between binary trees. These algorithms are implemented in the Sage mathematical software system, and we provide a comprehensive suite of computational experiments utilizing this implementation. All code is available on our GitHub repository. We contend that these algorithms hold significant potential for future research applications. This work provides an explicit formula for the pullback of the Hitchin connection from the moduli space of genus two curves to a ten-fold cover of a Teichmüller curve identified by Veech. Furthermore, we derive an expression using iterated integrals for the monodromy representation associated with this connection. As a consequence, we establish quantum representations for infinitely many families of mock theta functions. In the final section, we explore various applications, including methods for computing holomorphic differentials on genus two curves and their automorphism extensions, as well as techniques for determining holomorphic invariants of the Hitchin connection. Specifically, we derive explicit basis formulas forgenus two logarithmic inflectional Jacobian sections and calculate previously unknown monodromy matrices. Additionally, we present a novel family of genus two vector bundles on $\mathcal{M}_{0,5}$ that cannot be realized as logarithmic inflectional Jacobians. This approach also yields a new family of solutions to the Painlevé 6 equation, linking it to the universal family of moduli spaces of curves with marked inflection points. This aligns with recent independent findings by Bostan et al. regarding mock theta functions and their connection to Hitchin connections and PDEs on $\mathcal{M}_{0,5}$. Furthermore, this methodology recovers the work of Jones and Kauers on the hypergeometric solution of the Hitchin connection over $\mathcal{M}_{0,4}$ and recovers the results of Chenen and Zudilin, who linked mock theta functions to the pullback of the Hitchin connection over the Veech curve. In the final section, we outline several interesting directions for future research. Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, numerous organizations have transitioned to fully remote work, significantly altering team dynamics. This shift introduces various challenges, including heightened feelings of isolation, difficulties in virtual communication, and an increased risk of burnout. These issues can negatively impact remote teams, particularly those utilizing the Scrum framework, potentially reducing their effectiveness.

This study investigates how remote work influences Scrum teams. Through a multiple case study involving 20 teams across 10 organizations, we collected 101 in-depth interview responses. Our analysis identified three primary factors affecting remote work with Scrum: (1) challenges in adapting to a fully remote environment, (2) the impact of health and safety protocols, and (3) the effects of organizational and cultural mindsets.

To address these identified issues, we examined how teams mitigated their negative impacts by reviewing literature on Scrum and high-performing groups. This review revealed six strategies for enhancing remote Scrum teams: (1) fostering a strong team culture, (2) ensuring regular communication, (3) managing virtual meetings effectively, (4) simplifying processes, (5) encouraging virtual socialization, and (6) implementing flexible work schedules.

Finally, by synthesizing our case study findings with literature on remote work and Scrum, we developed practical guidance for organizations aiming to transition their projects to a fully remote model. This structured approach assists organizations in successfully adopting remote work for Scrum initiatives. Additionally, for teams already remote, it offers a foundation to improve their current operational state. We conclude by outlining key recommendations for transitioning to fully remote Scrum projects. Furthermore, we suggest prioritizing the development of remote work practices during the product backlog refinement process. To our knowledge, this is the first study to comprehensively analyze the effects of fully remote work on Scrum projects. Finally, we outline opportunities for future research. This work demonstrates how Scrum can be adapted to the remote work environment, offering valuable insights for practitioners. Additionally, it provides practical guidance for organizations managing remote software projects, contributing to the broader understanding of remote work dynamics. This research also offers practical value to practitioners by presenting a list of recommended practices for transitioning to fully remote Scrum projects. Additionally, it offers guidance for organizations managing remote software projects. Finally, this study contributes to the multi-disciplinary field of fully remote work. Specifically, it addresses the knowledge gap regarding the effects of fully remote work on Scrum projects. Furthermore, it offers practical guidance for transitioning to fully remote Scrum

This study examines elliptic flow ($v_2$) arising from beauty hadron decays, utilizing a dataset of Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV from the ALICE detector at the LHC, with an integrated luminosity of 35 $\mu$b$^{-1}$. By analyzing the $p_T$ distributions of dimuons originating from beauty hadron decays, we derive $v_2$ values for beauty hadrons across a transverse momentum range of 2 to 10 GeV/$c$. Our findings indicate that, when normalized to yield a $R_{AA}$ value of 1, the $v_2$ of beauty hadrons exceeds that of prompt light hadrons at low $p_T$ but is suppressed at high $p_T$. To interpret these results, we compare our data against two distinct models: one incorporating beauty-quark coalescence and another relying solely on fragmentation. Both approaches suggest that beauty quarks interact more weakly with the quark-gluon plasma than light quarks, a conclusion supported by a recent hydrodynamic model. Furthermore, we observe that beauty quarks experience less interaction than light quarks within the same medium, a discrepancy difficult to reconcile with current theoretical frameworks. This paper introduces a categorization method designed to integrate the advantages of formality and flexibility in data auditing. The process begins by constructing a knowledge base using formal concept analysis, derived from raw data through abstraction. Subsequently, an object's categories are represented via belief functions, with their basic belief assignments calculated using Dempster-Shafer theory. The final step employs the Pignistic transformation to facilitate decision-making. The study demonstrates the algorithm through a concrete case study and includes a sensitivity analysis to evaluate its stability. Ultimately, the paper provides an algorithm that is both easy to implement and effective for auditing tasks. The proposed method is particularly advantageous in scenarios where an object possesses diverse attributes, as this diversity translates into multiple beliefs. A key benefit is its ability to handle incomplete information, thereby enhancing the reliability of categorization. The paper concludes that this approach is well-suited for data auditing applications. Additionally, the framework is extensible; for instance, it can be adapted for e-auctioning by substituting the scoring function with a bid function. The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) is a quantum framework designed to both preserve quantum mechanics at high energy scales and incorporate gravitational effects. This study extends the GUP to the classical domain and analyzes its impact on both Lorentz and Galilean transformations. The primary innovation of this work is the derivation of GUP-modified Lorentz transformations (GLTs) that maintain the Lorentz group's algebraic structure. These GLTs are applicable to localized states whose spatial extent is significantly larger than the Planck length. A key advantage of the proposed GLTs is their ability to linearly encode Planck-scale physics, thereby avoiding the unnecessary deformation of the Lorentz group. Furthermore, we derive Generalized Galilean Transformations (GGTs) from the GLTs, demonstrating that these GGTs can integrate gravitational effects while preserving the classical Galilean group's structure. Finally, we apply the GGTs to define GUP-modified velocity and establish its upper limit. This limiting velocity, which depends on the scale factor of a hypothetical universe, may offer insights into phenomena such as dark energy. Additionally, we examine how Planck-scale influences affect the equivalence principle and the constancy of the speed of light. We conclude by suggesting that future research should explore how these GUP-modified transformations affect energy-momentum relations and quantum field theory. A companion paper will address these GUP effects within the context of quantum field theory. In that follow-up study, we will employ the GUP-compatible coordinate system and GUP-compatible derivatives to construct a GUP-modified energy-momentum tensor. This will enable us to derive generalized Einstein field equations that incorporate quantum gravity effects, a topic explored in this article. We anticipate that these modified field equations will provide a framework for investigating how gravitational effects interact with quantum gravity. Multitasking scheduling encompasses scheduling systems where processing resources support multiple execution modes, such as single-mode and multi-mode configurations. In single-mode systems, only one task can be processed at any given time. Conversely, multi-mode systems allow for task sharing, where multiple tasks can share a single processing resource, though typically only one task can be completed at a time. This sharing incurs a penalty known as the switch loss. This paper addresses multitasking scheduling across various multi-mode characteristics, focusing on minimizing the total weighted completion time. We consider three distinct resource-sharing scenarios: (i) general multi-mode resources, (ii) branch-and-stock resources, and (iii) stock resources. For each scenario, we examine multiple task types and multiple objective functions. Our analysis demonstrates that the computational complexity of optimal scheduling varies significantly based on whether the primary goal is minimizing the total weighted completion time or the total weighted earliness-tardiness. Furthermore, we compare the performance of heuristic approaches against optimal solutions. Notably, for certain scheduling problems, our computational experiments indicate that a simple heuristic often yields optimal results. Additionally, we introduce a set of exact algorithms that utilize linear programming to either determine optimal solutions or derive strong lower bounds. Finally, we present a multiobjective optimization model to address multiple goals simultaneously, enabling a direct comparison of performance across various criteria. To our knowledge, no such comprehensive overview of multitasking scheduling problems and solutions currently exists. This work aims to stimulate further research into this area. Given the shared nature of multitasking scheduling, it is highly relevant to numerous real-world applications. For instance, branch-and-stock scheduling models are applicable to manufacturing environments where machines transition between raw material processing and product storage. Stock scheduling, where resources are not required for storage, serves as a preliminary step in supply chain management. Furthermore, storage-related issues in cloud computing and data centers can also be effectively modeled using multitasking scheduling frameworks. This study serves as a foundational overview of multitasking scheduling, offering a solid basis for future research in this domain. We have also developed a Python-based software library to support the proposed methodologies. The library is available at: https://github.com/SebastianSchulze100/Multitasking-Scheduling. It includes a heuristic algorithm, a mathematical model, a computational framework, and a suite of examples. We intend to use this library to facilitate the comparison of alternative solutions. This paper introduces a reduced-order model for the dynamics of a monopod machine, designed to simulate dynamics on yielding terrain and to plan and optimize energy-efficient hopping trajectories. The reduced-order model effectively replicates the behavior of multi-link systems, enabling the derivation of an optimal trajectory that maximizes hop distance for a specific energy source. Furthermore, reduced versions of the system are presented to facilitate distance and energy calculations, alongside a trajectory optimization framework utilizing a multiple-shooting method to generate the most energy-efficient trajectory for a prescribed distance. Numerical simulations confirm the model's efficacy in generating distance-maximizing trajectories, while a physical prototype validation demonstrates its accuracy in both distance estimation and trajectory planning. Ultimately, this model facilitates the design of energy-efficient hopping trajectories for monopod machines operating on deformable surfaces. Additionally, the proposed model has been adapted for a two-legged robot, where it serves to predict travel distance, energy expenditure, and to generate energy-efficient hopping trajectories. A simulation study supports these assertions. This research is a collaborative effort between the authors and their former institution, the University of Freiburg. Corresponding author: Dr.-Ing. Alexander Kellner (alexander.kellner@tue.mpg.de).

Internet of Things (IoT) systems are becoming increasingly prevalent in both public and private sectors, driving the demand for robust security and dependable communication protocols. A critical security measure for these systems is the regular update of firmware to mitigate vulnerabilities. However, delivering firmware updates to vast networks of IoT devices presents significant challenges, particularly in wireless environments where updates are large data packets susceptible to packet loss, retransmissions, and interference. This paper reports on the performance analysis of a firmware update mechanism designed for IoT networks, specifically focusing on IoT gateways that facilitate communication among numerous devices. The study's primary objective is to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism for large-scale deployments. To gather data for this analysis, we implemented the mechanism on a real IoT gateway supporting 3COM AXE-1000 devices organized in a star topology. Results from this analysis will assist mechanism designers and administrators in making informed decisions when updating extensive IoT networks. Additionally, the paper provides a preliminary discussion comparing the proposed mechanism to a widely adopted alternative, TFTP, in the context of this specific deployment. Future research will involve a more thorough performance analysis, potentially utilizing simulation tools to model various network conditions. This approach aims to facilitate updates across diverse environments, including those with long-distance mesh network topologies, thereby enhancing the flexibility of IoT network management. Specifically, the analysis will investigate how network latency, packet loss, and retransmissions influence the mechanism's performance. Finally, the paper will detail the specific modifications required to adapt the proposed mechanism for mesh network conditions, with an emphasis on how routing protocols impact its efficiency. By addressing these factors, the research seeks to improve the flexibility of IoT networks, enabling easier and more efficient management of large-scale device populations. This, in turn, will contribute to the broader adoption of mesh network topologies in future IoT deployments. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews related work on various update mechanisms; Section III outlines the proposed mechanism and its implementation details; Section IV presents the analysis results and compares them with the existing TFTP mechanism; and Section V concludes the paper and suggests several avenues for future research. This research was conducted as part of the authors' internship at 3COM, a leading manufacturer of IoT gateways and devices. The internship took place during the summer of 2019, following the authors' graduation from the Computer Science Department at the University of Haifa. The internship was conducted under the supervision of Mr. Shlomo Shalev, the Chief Information Officer of 3COM.

We provide an analytical explanation for this scaling, showing that the localization length variable is directly proportional to the inverse of the two-point correlation function exponent, denoted as $\eta_s$. We further clarify that this scaling holds true on average for the localization length, even if the correlation function does not maintain a consistent amplitude on the localized side. We conclude by proving that the function describing the scaling of the localization length is indeed multifractal at the transition. Additionally, we confirm that the spectral form factor displays the same multifractal scaling in a one-dimensional spin model, which is well-established as a many-body localized system. Interactive search for multiple targets has recently gained significant attention for its broad practical applications. In this framework, a searcher engages with an oracle that returns a "Yes" or "No" response to each query, aiming to identify all target instances while staying within a limited budget of queries. This paper focuses on a scenario where targets are distributed according to an unknown prior. We demonstrate that a specific instance can be resolved in a number of queries that does not exceed the support size of this prior. This upper bound is achieved through an algorithm that requires only a single pass over the prior in expectation. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound matching this estimate, thereby resolving an open question posed by Liang et al. [2021]. This study examines Steklov eigenvalues for three-dimensional domains that are nearly spherical. Building on prior research demonstrating that these eigenvalues are analytic functions of the domain perturbation parameter, we calculate the first-order terms of the expansion for Steklov eigenfunctions, spectral activity intervals, and Steklov eigenfunctions relative to small deviations from sphericity. As an application, we derive an isoperimetric-type inequality: the solid angle subtended by a nearly spherical domain at an interior point $x$ is maximized when the domain is spherical, with the first-order perturbation term dependent on $x$. Specifically, for a perturbation comprising a small bump, we provide an explicit expression for the coefficient and employ it to compute the change in the solid angle subtended by the perturbed boundary from points within the bump. Furthermore, we identify the analytic expression for the derivative of a Steklov eigenvalue with respect to the bump's size and its critical points, showing that this derivative vanishes at $-1+\sqrt{2}$, approximately $-0.414$. These findings are supported by numerical computations and visualizations of normalized eigenfunctions. Ultimately, we contend that the derived expressions for perturbed Steklov eigenfunctions and spectral intervals offer a more direct and insightful framework for isoperimetric-type problems regarding Steklov eigenvalues than the corresponding expansions for spectral activity intervals. Additionally, we provide explicit formulas for the first-order corrections to the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $1$ in the unit sphere's Steklov spectrum and for the derivative of a one-parameter family of such eigenvalues, expressing both in terms of spherical harmonics. Conformance checking involves comparing the behavior of modeled processes against observed process behavior captured in event logs. Alignments represent a versatile method for identifying, locating, and quantifying deviations, with recent research introducing infix and postfix alignments to capture temporal variations in activity sequences. However, existing algorithms for computing these alignment types struggle with noise and incompleteness in event data, a scenario common in real-world business process monitoring where events are often recorded as fragments. To address this, we propose a conformance checking technique that evaluates event fragments by inserting dummy activities into observed sequences. We demonstrate that this approach can be extended to compute infix and postfix alignments for fragments with only polynomial increases in both time and space complexity relative to standard alignments. Experimental results indicate that these proposed alignments for fragments yield superior noise tolerance and completeness compared to the corresponding classical alignments. Furthermore, we show how to extend prefix alignments to handle fragments in a computationally efficient manner, thereby filling a gap in the current research literature. Finally, we introduce a new hybrid alignment measure based on the integration of infix and postfix alignments for fragments, which offers an optimal balance regarding noise tolerance, computational efficiency, and conformance quality. This new infix/postfix alignment for fragments outperforms both traditional infix/postfix alignments and the recently developed prefix alignment for fragments in terms of conformance quality and noise tolerance. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the computational complexity associated with calculating various alignment variants for fragments. Accurate radio propagation modeling is essential for the planning and optimization of wireless cellular networks. While traditional models are typically built using empirical or physics-based approaches, this paper introduces a novel deep convolutional neural network model that learns site-specific radio propagation characteristics directly from measured data. When trained on a relatively small dataset, the proposed model delivers superior prediction accuracy compared to both traditional models and machine learning alternatives. Furthermore, this new model is capable of handling the sparse data often found in cellular network measurements, which contain minimal or no a priori knowledge. By leveraging this rich data, the model can be fine-tuned for each cellular site, allowing it to adapt to site-specific propagation features and thereby achieving even greater prediction accuracy. Experimental results based on field measurements from a university campus demonstrate that training the model on as little as 100 samples per sector yields state-of-the-art performance. This model is particularly well-suited for cellular networks with low base station heights and dense deployments, such as those found on university campuses. Future enhancements could incorporate additional data sources, including user equipment measurements and maps of relevant environmental features. Additionally, the model's ability to predict radio conditions for new base stations using only geographic information makes it ideal for site selection in cellular network planning. This represents a significant departure from current state-of-the-art methods, which rely on physics-based or machine learning-based approaches that require extensive data collection and lack the ability to provide site-specific predictions. We introduce a straightforward and compact semantics for temporal planning, which is formally developed within the logic of the Isabelle/HOL interactive theorem prover. Based on these semantics, we develop a validation algorithm for linear temporal plans and demonstrate, through formalization in Isabelle/HOL, that the algorithm correctly identifies invalid plans. Our fully formal proof utilizes a coinductive argument. Additionally, we examine various design choices made during the development of this proof. Finally, we demonstrate that both the plan validity and a specific form of soundness for our verification procedure can be formally established using a more detailed specification of the planning domain. To our knowledge, this represents the first fully and machine-checked proof of correctness for a validity problem in temporal planning. We conclude by outlining several directions for future research. Finally, we present a more comprehensive and detailed discussion of the many design choices involved in developing a verified solution for temporal planning. This study systematically tests the sensitivity of such models to costs associated with generation, storage, and flexibility measures. Our findings indicate that while the optimal capacity of generators and storage units is highly sensitive to cost variations, resulting in highly variable investment plans, the costs associated with these installations remain relatively insensitive. Furthermore, the system's overall cost exhibits only moderate sensitivity to these parameters. Consequently, investors seeking stable returns should anticipate significant fluctuations in power plant utilization, whereas power system operators must prepare for cost variations that are not significantly higher than the optimal sensitivity level. Finally, given that the optimal sensitivity exceeds the actual sensitivity for costs within the considered range, we conclude that optimal investment plans are not uniquely determined by the given data. This insight necessitates a more comprehensive approach to accounting for data uncertainty in power system costs. To address this, we introduce a novel uncertainty set for power system costs and propose a new two-stage stochastic optimization framework for power system expansion planning. This new model demonstrates only a minor increase in computational effort compared to the deterministic version while generating data-driven, robust, and therefore unique investment plans. We provide numerical results to demonstrate this. Additionally, we discuss the broader implications of this planning approach for other sectors, such as housing, agriculture, and transport, where data uncertainty is a critical issue. This paper presents STRICT, a novel approach designed to mitigate the graph density issue that hinders the effectiveness of existing concept location techniques based on code retrieval. This density problem arises because concepts, particularly those that are uncommon, are rarely encountered in typical retrieval queries. STRICT addresses this challenge by reframing code retrieval as a natural language processing task, specifically leveraging information retrieval. To accomplish this, STRICT pre-trains a transformer model on a vast collection of Python codes and their corresponding search terms, sourced from the FuzzyMatch dataset. During actual concept location tasks, the model computes similarity scores between a target concept and various function candidates by comparing them against a latent search term. Subsequently, a deep graph learning model analyzes the resulting search result graphs to identify concepts with low intra-node similarity and high inter-node similarity. STRICT was evaluated using a manually annotated test dataset, and experimental results demonstrate that STRICT surpasses both state-of-the-art code retrieval models and prior work in this domain. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/11111111/STRICT. Our source code, data, and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/11111111/STRICT.

Colloidal gels, characterized by their unique and tunable rheological properties, are extensively employed across various scientific and technological fields. This study introduces a new rheo-acoustic method for manipulating the structure of colloidal gels through ultrasonic vibrations. By applying specific frequencies and amplitudes, we can adjust the system's mechanical and flow properties. Our findings indicate that a gel formed at an ultrasonic strength (US) of 30% retains its structure when exposed to low acoustic intensities (US < 50%). However, intensities between 50% and 70% induce structure remodeling, and a threshold at US = 75% leads to complete destruction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ultrasonic vibration can restore a disrupted gel to its original state by selecting an appropriate acoustic intensity. These results provide a new pathway for controlling gel properties and highlight a novel technique for their characterization. Additionally, we offer insights into the mechanisms governing these structure changes, which can be modeled using effective medium theory. This approach utilizes the complex modulus of the original gels and the colloidal particles as inputs to calculate the percolation fraction, defined as the ratio of the liquid fraction to the total volume fraction of the gel. This newly developed rheo-acoustic methodology holds significant promise for future applications in materials science. Specifically, it may facilitate the creation of new functional materials, such as "smart" gels capable of responding to external ultrasonic stimuli. Additionally, this technique could enable the fabrication of complex gel structures, including those with internal patterns, by applying spatially varying ultrasonic intensities. Finally, this approach offers a means to characterize internal patterns within 3D-printed gels. By printing a gel with an initial percolation fraction below the critical threshold and applying an appropriate ultrasonic intensity, the resulting pattern can be reconstructed to achieve a final percolation fraction equal to the critical value. This allows for the visualization of the internal gel structure using techniques like micro-CT scanning. Our results provide valuable insights into the interplay between ultrasound-induced forces and inter-particle forces within the gel. Let $X$ denote a separable Banach space equipped with the weak topology, and let $K \subseteq X$ be a compact set. Assuming the Continuum Hypothesis, we prove a generalized version of the Collatz conjecture, which asserts that any sequence of length $\mathfrak{c}$ within $K$ contains a subsequence that converges weakly to a limit located in the closed convex hull of the sequence. This result extends to sequences of length $\mathfrak{c}$ composed of weak-* null sequences of bounded linear functionals, or equivalently, sequences of signed measures on $\mathbb{N}$ with uniformly bounded total variation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the assumption of the Continuum Hypothesis is necessary. A comparable finding was previously established by G. Godefroy, J. Kalton, and A. Maestripieri, who additionally identified a shorter example illustrating the necessity of the Continuum Hypothesis assumption. We present two examples showing that the assumption remains necessary even for sequences of length $\mathfrak{c}$ in $c_0(\mathbb{N})$ and, respectively, in $c_0(\mathbb{R})$ and $\ell_\infty(\mathbb{R})$. The final example applies to separable Banach spaces $X$ where the dual unit ball consists solely of weakly compact elements. Additionally, we examine the case where the sequence length is $\aleph_1$, providing a counterexample for $\ell_\infty(\mathbb{N})$ and demonstrating that the conclusion fails for a specific class of separable Banach spaces. This class encompasses $c_0$, $\ell_1$, and the space of continuous functions on the Cantor set. For this class of spaces, the conclusion holds if and only if $\aleph_1 = \mathfrak{c}$. Finally, the necessity of the Continuum Hypothesis assumption is also proven for $\mathbb{R}$. This work investigates the reconstruction of a sparse signal using sparse quadratic measurements. We demonstrate that for random sparse vectors, there exists a threshold for the proportion of quadratic measurements; exceeding this threshold enables the guaranteed recovery of an arbitrary sparse signal of any sparsity level, provided it is unique. This finding generalizes previous research on linear and affine recovery and adds to the understanding of vector space sampling. Furthermore, we introduce a new algorithm capable of efficiently and reliably recovering the target signal. The study concludes with numerical examples that validate the theoretical results. These computations also indicate that the proposed algorithm is significantly faster than those relying on mixed norm convex relaxation. Additionally, the theoretical framework is applied to solve a specific problem in spectral analysis. This application considers spectra composed of peaks with unknown positions but known widths, where the peak locations can be accurately recovered from quadratic spectral data obtained via an interferometric instrument with a restricted field of view. A novel spectral recovery algorithm is developed, which is substantially faster than existing methods based on mixed norm convex relaxation. Notably, the proposed algorithm also outperforms convex methods in terms of robustness. This advantage is illustrated through a numerical example demonstrating the recovery of a sample spectrum from a star, highlighting how the algorithm effectively mitigates measurement noise. Finally, the paper begins to explore the connection between this approach and the concept of spectral super-resolution. This involves recovering the positions of narrow peaks from data generated by an instrument with low spectral resolution, which can be interpreted as a form of quadratic measurement. A new algorithm is derived from this perspective, offering advantages over current spectral super-resolution techniques regarding both theoretical and practical performance. The case study employed to illustrate this approach is the analysis of the atmosphere of the exoplanet HD 189733b. This case study exemplifies the growing significance of spectral analysis in astrophysics, where it is used to identify chemical reactions and trace the movement of planets within their solar systems. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that quadratic measurements offer new tools to address current challenges in spectral analysis. Specifically, it shows that quadratic algorithms offer new solutions to problems that are either unsolvable or only weakly solvable using linear or affine methods. These results are supported by numerical examples, and the discussion begins to explore the implications of these findings for spectral analysis. Keywords: Compressed sensing, sparse recovery, spectral analysis, uniqueness region, quadratic measurements, nonlinear measurement, peak recovery, super resolution.

Fusion approaches combining camera and LiDAR data have become increasingly popular in autonomous driving research. Nevertheless, conventional methods often suffer from complex fusion strategies, inefficient feature fusion mechanisms, and suboptimal performance. To address these issues, we introduce BEVFusion, a straightforward and robust fusion framework that projects camera features into LiDAR's bird's-eye view (BEV) representation for direct fusion. Our core innovation lies in a novel fusion module that unifies multi-source features within the BEV plane, enabling effective alignment and low-complexity fusion through a lightweight convolutional network. This architecture eliminates the need for additional learning modules to learn fusion weights, thereby enhancing model interpretability. We demonstrate that BEVFusion significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on widely used datasets, including KITTI and nuScenes, for detection and segmentation tasks. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that our approach is not only effective but also efficient, robust, and suitable for real-time applications. We provide a critical analysis of recent investigations into a purported connection between large-scale fluid turbulence and thermal noise, a phenomenon originally proposed by Forster, Leutheusser, and Hohenberg in 1980. Our assessment reveals significant flaws in the theoretical framework, casting doubt on the validity of the noise-turbulence link. Furthermore, we examine various experimental methods that have been proposed to detect this hypothesized connection. In a companion study, we explore alternative theoretical avenues that could restore the credibility of this idea. Additionally, we investigate a distinct form of dissipation-range turbulence that arises in the collective dynamics of active matter, independent of any involvement with thermal fluctuations. This phenomenon is supported by both numerical simulations and experimental evidence. We conclude by outlining several promising directions for future research in this field. Our overall perspective suggests that, given current findings, it is premature to assert that large-scale fluid turbulence exists within thermal noise. Instead, we propose that turbulence in active matter may represent a novel phenomenon that is fundamentally distinct from turbulence in conventional, non-active fluids. Specifically, the existence of large Reynolds number turbulence in thermal fluids might simply be impossible.

We provide a comprehensive numerical characterization of temperature distributions in liquid water, accounting for absorption depth, beam profile, and intensity, to support the prediction and analysis of experimental diffraction images. These distributions address a critical gap in current theory, which predominantly relies on uniform temperature approximations. By solving the steady-state heat diffusion equation, we demonstrate that thermal diffusion results in a nearly Gaussian modified input profile, whose width depends on intensity and thermal conductivity. Furthermore, we show that modifications to the Gaussian profile are most pronounced at low intensities and are enhanced by increased absorption. Finally, we illustrate how specific deviations from Gaussian behavior can be observed in diffraction patterns, enabling the extraction of the thermal diffusion coefficient and absorption depth. These findings establish essential parameters for future studies. Additionally, our methodology is transferable to other liquids and potentially to thermal self-induced diffraction phenomena in other nonlinear optical media. Developer comments on version control systems are a vital resource for software maintenance, enabling tasks such as requirement tracking, change impact analysis, and requirement Design-Build consistency checks. However, the inherent variability in human language makes it difficult to develop robust mining techniques that yield consistent results despite minor phrasing differences. This paper introduces a novel natural language model that addresses this challenge by ensuring conclusion stability. By leveraging semantic representations to measure the distance between developer comments and a specific target class, the model achieves high accuracy in assigning the correct target class to software requirements. We validate the model's conclusion stability through experiments, demonstrating that it significantly surpasses baseline approaches in both accuracy and stability. Furthermore, we detail how this model was applied to our dataset to evaluate Design-Build Consistency in Java code, with the results shown to align with industry practices. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedmohr/Conclusion-Stability. The accompanying dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/ahmedmohr/Conclusion-Stability-Dataset. It offers a unified programming model that handles streams, files, and streams stored in files, utilizing the distributed storage and computing framework to process data with scalability and efficiency. H-STREAM features a unified data processing pipeline capable of handling streaming data from sources like Apache Kafka and HDFS, as well as periodic batch loading from external sources such as Teradata and Salesforce. Ultimately, this work aims to address the limitations of legacy stream processing systems and accelerate the development of data pipelines for business analytics. Through this research, the authors seek to offer valuable insights and guidance for business analytics applications. Any inquiries or suggestions are welcome. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems translate knowledge base (KB) entity mentions by leveraging external KB data as context for enhanced generation. However, the standard NMT architecture, which relies on a fixed encoder-decoder framework, cannot accommodate a "copy" mechanism necessary for directly transmitting KB elements through the context. To address this, we propose a novel NMT model integrated with a copy mechanism that facilitates direct transmission of KB elements within the context while preserving the inherent NMT capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves improved translation quality by learning to copy KB elements within the context, and it exhibits superior performance in entity normalization tasks compared to the baseline approach. Furthermore, a human evaluation confirms that our model produces more accurate translations of knowledge-intensive sentences compared to the baseline. Finally, we apply our model to parallel conversation generation for question-asking tasks and obtain performance gains by learning to copy KB elements in the context. In light of these findings, we conclude that the copy mechanism serves as a highly effective tool for enhancing NMT models. We introduce a technique that assigns individual scores to research venues, offering a straightforward alternative to metrics relying solely on publication records. This approach integrates both local and global citation data to facilitate comparisons among authors within and across various fields. Our evaluation demonstrates that venue analytics correlate more strongly with author impact than traditional, venue-agnostic citation measures. Furthermore, we highlight several additional features that venue analytics provide, including the ability to compare authors in diverse disciplines and reduce career-risk bias linked to institutional reputation. We also outline significant distinctions between venue analytics and other citation-derived methods, such as field-normalized scores, which often suffer from comparability issues between venues and fields. Finally, we propose venue analytics as a fairer and more transparent supplementary metric that could potentially replace or complement existing alternatives to standard citation counts. The code required to reproduce these findings is available at github.com/venueanalytics/venue-analytics. Venue analytics can be applied to any citation dataset organized by publication venue; however, due to data limitations, comparisons between venues or fields are only reliable when the dataset includes sufficient cross-citations. Consequently, the code is accompanied by a Python library that enables users to easily apply venue analytics to any bibliography. This library is also being made open-source to support future development and experimentation with venue-specific adjustments. We anticipate that venue analytics will be valuable in a broad range of applications, including hiring, promotions, funding decisions, and editorial processes. To ensure transparency, we have made the code and data behind the calculations publicly accessible. Additionally, we have published an analysis of potential biases affecting venue analytics and their interaction with other metrics, which can be found in the paper "Bias Analysis of Venue-Annotiated Metrics" at doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7055050. This analysis is also hosted on github.com/venueanalytics/venue-analytics-bias-analysis. While venue analytics can be used independently, they serve as a valuable supplement to other established alternatives to standard citation counts, such as the Open Citation Impact (OCI) metric (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7055051). Although significant advancements have been achieved recently, verifying neural networks remains a challenging task. Since these networks are too complex for analytical solutions, verification relies on approximations that convert the check into a chaperized or relaxed form. This paper examines these techniques and their application in checking various neural network types. These approaches are particularly relevant to control systems, where analysis is essential for safety-critical applications. The discussion also covers related challenges in optimization and computation, as well as emerging research directions. Finally, we explore how these methods facilitate the safer deployment of neural networks within neural feedback control loops. Finally, we demonstrate the control advantages of utilizing interpretable networks like polytopes and Gaussian mixture models. Overall, this paper aims to inspire further research into safer, more robust, and reliable neural networks for contemporary and future control systems. We present a novel and more robust approach to functorial clustering. Traditionally, a clustering method assigns each element $x$ of a set $S$ to a specific cluster $C \in \mathcal{C}$, where $\mathcal{C}$ is a partition of $S$. In contrast, our method allows $x$ to belong to multiple clusters. Functorial clustering is inherently pushforward-compatible, meaning that if $f : S \to S'$ is a bijection and $\mathcal{C}$ is a clustering of $S$, then applying $f$ to every element yields a clustering of $S'$ without altering the original clusters. This property also applies to any injective map $f : S \to S'$, provided the clusters are considered as subsets. Conversely, partitions are not generally pushforward-compatible because the direct image of a cluster under an arbitrary map $f : S \to S'$ may not be a cluster. Our functorial clustering is defined by two maps: one from sets to sets and another from sets to the collection of clusters. This clustering remains pushforward-compatible for any map $f : S \to S'$ and is additionally pushforward-stable for any surjective map $f : S' \to S''$. We demonstrate that several established clustering techniques, such as single-linkage, are functorial and thus possess implicit algebraic and topological structures. Furthermore, we show that many methods previously thought to be non-functorial can be converted into functorial clusterings with unique advantages. For instance, average-linkage clustering with complete graphs yields a tight bound on the number of clusters. Additionally, hierarchical clustering can be made functorial by applying a functor to the hierarchy itself. Finally, we illustrate that functorial clustering can be made monoidal for any monoidal set $S$, resulting in a clustering whose number of clusters corresponds to the cardinality of the underlying monoidal structure. This offers a new monoidal framework for average-linkage clustering. Overall, this work provides a fresh perspective on methodological issues in clustering. As an example, we revisit monoidal clustering, a technique that has received limited attention. We demonstrate that it offers a tight upper bound on the number of clusters and facilitates a more efficient algorithm. Furthermore, monoidal clustering exhibits a complementary functorial property, enabling the definition of many functorial clusterings that surpass even the single-linkage bound. Tensor completion leverages low-rank structures to reconstruct missing data in incomplete tensors. While streaming tensor ring completion (STRC) is designed for continuous, patch-by-patch recovery of visual data, it suffers from a significant issue: it cannot accurately recover new, unseen local patches because it relies on a limited set of basis elements that fail to capture the infinite variability of new patches. To address this, we propose a novel tensor ring model driven by patch tracking. This model utilizes patch tracking to effectively capture the structural information of new, unseen local patches, thereby significantly enhancing the ability of tensor ring completion to recover these unseen regions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in visual data recovery. Furthermore, we validate the proposed patch tracking mechanism's effectiveness on a new dataset featuring local patches with high variability. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1992/PatchTracking-based-STRC. Source: 2021 IEEE Access.

This study provides a classification of Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V)$ derived from specific $G$-gradings $V$ of the standard representation $V_G$ of classical groups $G$, where $G$ belongs to the set $\{A_{n},B_{n},C_{n},D_{n},E_6\}$ and $G$ is not $D_4$. Furthermore, we establish that $\mathcal{B}(V)$ is finite-dimensional if and only if it is of Heckenberger's type 1. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Nichols algebra $\mathcal{B}(V)$ associated with the $G$-grading $V$ of the standard representation of $D_{4}$ is also finite-dimensional and of Heckenberger's type 1. Consequently, this confirms that every $G$-grading of the standard representation of a classical group $G$ yields a finite-dimensional Nichols algebra of Heckenberger's type 1. This result completes the classification of Nichols algebras arising from $G$-gradings of the standard representations of classical groups $G$, where $G$ is subset of $\{A_{n},B_{n},C_{n},D_{n},E_6\}$ and $G$ excludes $D_4$. Specifically, it resolves two questions posed by Heckenberger regarding whether finite-dimensional Nichols algebras of Heckenberger's type 1 exist for $G$-gradings of the standard representations of $C_{n}$, $B_{n}$, or $E_6$. This paper introduces a class of iterative graph normalization techniques, offering a comprehensive analysis of their properties and establishing a link between these algorithms and Markov chains. The study investigates the characteristics of normalized graphs once algorithmic convergence is reached. Additionally, efficient methods for identifying fixed points are introduced, along with a detailed examination of the algorithm's behavior relative to independent set polytopes. The paper further explores an application connecting iterative graph normalization to the greedy approach for solving the maximum weight independent set problem. Finally, the study addresses the computational complexity of these problems and their associated decision variants.

This study investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of monolayer graphene subjected to both perpendicular magnetic fields ($B$) and electrical modulation. The primary objective is to analyze how electrical modulation influences these thermodynamic properties. To achieve this, the Grand Canonical Ensemble is employed, utilizing the exact analytical expression for the density of states derived by P. Peiers and V. Perelov. The analysis reveals that electrical modulation transforms the linear energy dispersion of the Dirac fermions into a parabolic energy band, thereby restoring the Pauli exclusion principle. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that both heat capacity and compressibility exhibit oscillatory behavior as functions of $B$, with the oscillation amplitude reaching a maximum at $B=0$ and diminishing as $B$ increases. These findings suggest that applying electrical modulation at a bias voltage of $V_s$ can facilitate the detection of the half-integer quantum Hall effect in graphene, even in the absence of an external magnetic field. Additionally, it is noted that heat capacity displays oscillations as a function of modulation frequency, while compressibility shows periodic variations with changes in modulation wavelength. The results indicate that heat capacity oscillations are more pronounced for higher values of $B$, whereas compressibility oscillations are more significant for lower values of $B$. Ultimately, these conclusions provide valuable insights for designing and developing efficient electronic and thermoelectric devices based on modulated graphene. Finally, it is observed that heat capacity attains its maximum value at $V_s=0$, whereas compressibility is maximized at $V_s=2\hbar eB/h$. These outcomes are expected to facilitate the measurement of Landau level spacing and the effective mass of carriers in graphene. Moreover, the calculated heat capacity and compressibility for modulated graphene are compared with those of three-dimensional free electron gases. Based on these comparisons, it is concluded that parabolic band graphene exhibits superior thermoelectric performance relative to a three-dimensional free electron gas. Consequently, electrical modulation of graphene holds significant promise for advancing thermoelectric technology. Additionally, it is established that the quantum nature of graphene's thermodynamic properties is enhanced by applying electrical modulation. These findings are anticipated to contribute to the design of efficient thermoelectric devices utilizing modulated graphene. Finally, it is demonstrated that parabolic band graphene exhibits the highest thermoelectric performance when a specific value of $V_s$ is applied. We report on low-frequency observations of the M dwarf binary system CR Draconis across a 14-year span, conducted at 165 MHz and 230 MHz. These data reveal that M dwarf flares are characterized by prolonged radio emission lasting several hours. Specifically, CR Draconis exhibits maser emission at 165 MHz that persists for approximately 4.5 hours, a duration significantly exceeding typical solar maser events. This finding suggests that M dwarf masers may have a longer intrinsic lifetime than their solar counterparts. Furthermore, the observed frequency of maser activity in CR Draconis is substantially higher than that seen in the nearby M dwarf GJ 1002. The detection of maser emission at 230 MHz during this observation marks the first instance of such a flare being detected across a broad frequency range for an M dwarf system. Additionally, we determined the system's distance to be 28.1 ± 0.3 parsecs, a value consistent with prior distance estimates. We also present a comprehensive analysis of the M dwarf's magnetic field, including its evolution, topology, and energy. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for understanding M dwarf magnetic activity and its potential impact on the habitability of any planetary systems orbiting these stars. This study is part of a broader investigation into the low-frequency properties of M dwarfs, with several related papers currently in preparation. The observations were conducted using the LOFAR Low-Frequency Array. CR Draconis is a well-known M dwarf binary hosting a close-in planet, and it is also a target of the upcoming EXO-LFAR project. The paper includes a dedicated section detailing the EXO-LFAR initiative. Customized neural rendering has recently emerged as a leading approach for creating photorealistic avatars by synthesizing new views from captured video and pose data. However, current methods face two major hurdles: first, they depend on 3D models like SMPL, which restricts rendering in cases with inaccurate 3D poses or diverse body morphologies; second, they struggle to produce realistic micro-expressions. To overcome these challenges, we present a articulated neural renderer (ANR) that achieves high-quality, real-time avatar synthesis using only 2D keypoints. Our model comprises a 2D pose encoder, a neural point cloud representation, and a neural renderer. By directly mapping 2D pose data into 3D point clouds, we eliminate reliance on 3D pose accuracy and accommodate varied human shapes. Additionally, we represent 3D heads as multi-layer perceptrons to capture micro-expressions, enabling realistic rendering of these subtle facial cues. We evaluate our method across a wide range of human morphologies, including scenarios with incorrect 3D poses and expressive faces. Furthermore, our approach supports real-time rendering on a single GPU. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. For code and video demos, please visit https://chrisyyli.github.io/ANR/. Supplementary materials are available at https://chrisyyli.github.io/AVATR/. Finally, our code is released under the terms of a commercial license. Contact the authors at chem.christopher@tudelft.nl. Recent research has examined the impact of image transformations on both human and machine performance, with recent efforts specifically targeting extreme transformations. This study investigates how such extreme modifications affect perception in vision models compared to human observers. We evaluated a diverse range of image transformations across three visual tasks: denoising, out-of-distribution detection, and object localization. Our results indicate that while machines often rely on a single cue to solve these problems, humans utilize multiple signals. Furthermore, humans demonstrate superior performance, particularly in addressing out-of-distribution issues. These findings suggest that current computational models may fail to capture essential aspects of human vision. To address this gap, we propose a collection of axioms that any solution to extreme transformation problems must satisfy. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for future research in this field. A comprehensive set of image transformations, along with solutions to the evaluation tasks, is available at https://github.com/arielkay/Extreme-IT-Affects-Humans-and-Models-Differently. The code for this evaluation can be accessed at https://github.com/arielkay/Extreme-IT-Affects-Humans-and-Models-Differently-Evaluation. Utilizing the Edwards and Anderson mapping, these spin models are transformed into hard-core dimers on a four-color lattice featuring specific self-avoiding constraints. By extending the quantum Monte Carlo technique originally developed by Sandvik for frustrated Ising models on four-color lattices, we analyze the thermodynamic properties of two representative trimer lattices. Our analysis reveals the critical temperatures and the temperature-dependent evolution of the dimer weight distribution for both trimer systems. Furthermore, our findings suggest the presence of a finite-temperature phase transition at the critical temperature, which aligns with previous theoretical predictions. Additionally, we examine the effects of symmetry-breaking fields on the phase transition. Finally, we discuss the potential for these methodologies to address various other spin models.
