Large pre-trained language models (LLMs) have become essential for natural language processing, yet they demand substantial computational resources. This paper explores whether the zero-shot capabilities of LLMs can be customized for specific domains through minimal meta-tuning of just a few gradient steps, aiming to maintain performance while drastically lowering memory demands. We introduce a novel meta-tuning framework that leverages pre-trained models on a diverse range of tasks to provide generalization signals for zero-shot applications. Additionally, we present the TaskAdapt benchmark, a collection of 1,020 zero-shot tasks across 235 domains designed to evaluate this meta-tuning process. Our results indicate that meta-tuning effectively improves performance on tasks closely related to the source tasks, while also yielding modest gains on more distant tasks within the human language family. Finally, we demonstrate that a small, carefully selected subset of the source tasks can match the performance of the full dataset, offering a promising direction for efficiently building zero-shot LLMs. To support future research, we make both the TaskAdapt benchmark and the code open-source. This work is anticipated to advance zero-shot learning by providing a robust evaluation infrastructure for zero-shot adaptation methods. Our source code is available at https://github.com/roberta-t/TaskAdapt. The full paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11088. We introduce High-z Sudoku, a novel diagnostic framework designed to (i) evaluate the robustness of cosmological redshift measurements and (ii) guide the optimization of the wavelength range used to measure high-redshift emission lines. This tool operates by partitioning the spectral energy distribution (SED) into 16 bins across four distinct wavelength regions, each containing four bins. We examine the correlation between these regions to determine the reliability of line redshifts, noting that the 4x4 configuration offers a balanced approach to both spectral coverage and line robustness. Our analysis reveals that sources with exactly one line per bin in each wavelength region exhibit the highest correlation and are considered to have robust redshifts. Conversely, sources lacking a line in at least one bin within each wavelength region display the lowest correlation and are deemed to have uncertain redshifts. We demonstrate that High-z Sudoku effectively identifies these robust redshifts and can be readily applied to any source catalog. Furthermore, we illustrate how this tool assists in selecting optimal wavelength coverage for upcoming spectroscopic surveys, such as the Square Kilometre Array. We conclude that High-z Sudoku serves as a valuable asset for the current era of high-redshift cosmology, particularly for validating redshifts derived from (sub)millimeter observations. Utilizing large-scale quantum spin dynamics simulations, we investigate the thermodynamic properties of the spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice. Our results identify a novel thermodynamic phase that emerges at low temperatures, situated between the conventional 120-degree ordered phase and the spin-liquid phase observed at very low densities of thermal magnons. The thermodynamic characteristics of this newly discovered phase display strong parallels with the thermodynamics of the spin-liquid phase. We offer a theoretical framework to explain these seemingly counterintuitive findings. Additionally, we propose proposed experimental signatures, including an anomalous peak in specific heat and a distinct plateau in zero-field cooling magnetization curves, to facilitate the experimental verification of these predicted phases. To enable future experimental studies, we also provide the temperature-dependent locations of these phases as a function of an applied magnetic field. Furthermore, we suggest signatures for these phases within dynamical probes, such as a peak in the temperature dependence of spin dephasing under dynamical dephasing measurements and a distinctive peak in the temperature dependence of the spin dephasing time during four-pulse magnetization measurements. We argue that these features can be attributed to the specific thermodynamic signatures noted earlier, thereby establishing their nature as nonequilibrium effects. Ultimately, we conclude that these phases constitute a new category of thermodynamic matter, defined by the optimization of energy and entropy in the time-temperature free energy. We anticipate that this theoretical framework holds significant relevance for a wide range of physical systems. Finally, our study demonstrates that quantum spin dynamics simulations on accessible supercomputers can effectively model the temperature-dependent thermodynamic properties of quantum many-body systems, offering a valuable alternative to both theoretical predictions and experimental measurements. This capability is particularly crucial for systems where the relevant thermodynamic phases can only be accessed at extremely low temperatures. This study examines the confinement and deconfinement transitions within $SU(3)$-Higgs theory, which involves a non-Abelian gauge group coupled to a complex scalar field in the fundamental representation. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we perform linear fits on the Polyakov loop susceptibility, baryon correlation length, and meson correlation length as functions of system volume to determine the string tension, percolation threshold, and deconfinement criticality. Our findings reveal that the percolation transition coincides with the deconfinement transition. Specifically, the series of critical exponents for meson correlation lengths and string tension exhibits scaling behavior consistent with the deconfinement transition. These conclusions are supported by additional analyses, such as an examination of the specific heat, the distribution of the Polyakov loop, and the distribution of the magnetic component of the field strength tensor. These methods reveal that Cr2Al undergoes a series of antiferromagnetic phase transitions at 220, 100, and 50 K, with each phase featuring muon spin configurations that are collinear or nearly collinear. Additionally, the research confirms that Cr2Al belongs to the space group P6/mmm and remains structurally stable up to 220 K. First-principles calculations further indicate that the lattice constant $a$ of Cr2Al is highly sensitive to pressure, whereas the parameter $c$ shows greater sensitivity to doping. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of Cr2Al's magnetic structure, offering a foundation for future investigations into its emergent properties. Notably, this work represents the first detailed examination of the low-temperature magnetic configuration in this material class. This study examines a kinetic model derived for rarefied gas flows by introducing a velocity-dependent collision frequency into the standard linearized Boltzmann collision operator. Semantic parsing is a critical challenge in natural language processing, aiming to translate natural language sentences into formal representations like SQL. Although parsers trained on large, domain-specific datasets (such as Spider) achieve state-of-the-art results across diverse SQL environments, they struggle with data scarcity when applied to domain outside the training set. Conversely, parsers trained on minimal, generalized NLP corpora demonstrate robustness in open-domain settings. This study investigates whether a hybrid approach, leveraging both specialized and generalist training data, can yield superior performance. We introduce a novel method that integrates a Generalized Meaning Bank (GMB)—a collection of natural language-to-meaning pairs from various sources—into existing semantic parsers. By training on a small amount of in-domain data supplemented with GMB, our technique surpasses both exclusive GMB training and standard in-domain-only approaches. Additionally, we demonstrate the method's scalability, as performance improves when incorporating a larger volume of in-domain data alongside the GMB. Finally, we provide an analysis of how different GMB components influence the parser's behavior. The code for this work is publicly accessible at https://github.com/PrithivirajGr/semantic-parsing-gmb. We hope this work encourages further research into data-efficient semantic parsing. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) aims to investigate the internal structures of nucleons and nuclei, as well as particle production and hadronization mechanisms, through high-energy, high-luminosity collisions between electrons and protons or ions. These goals are supported by two circular accelerators: the proposed 10 GeV electron machine (PCEIC) and the 270 GeV/proton, 11 GeV/nucleon EIC. The detector for the PCEIC is designed to meet stringent timing, spatial resolution, and radiation tolerance requirements, while also managing high particle rates and providing high-rate triggering and particle identification. This paper outlines the development of a forward silicon tracking detector for the PCEIC, featuring 100 $\mu$m pitch 3D pixel sensors and a readout system based on the Time-over-Threshold (TOT) and Charge (CHG) methods. Additionally, a time-digital processing system utilizing Time-to-Digital Converters (TDC) with 1 ps resolution is presented. Experimental data from NIF test-beam irradiations and tests at KEK and IHEP are discussed. Furthermore, simulations of the silicon sensor material and tracker performance in the PCEIC interaction region are provided. These efforts to advance the detector concept and its components are intended to contribute to the EIC silicon tracker development. Similar technologies can also be applied to other high-energy physics experiments, such as the High-Luminosity LHC and various heavy-ion colliders. This study examines high-cadence, multi-wavelength photometric data of the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) NGC 4395, collected from the Swift and ZTF surveys. Analysis of these data reveals two distinct variability components: a stochastic, red noise component and a quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) with a characteristic timescale of approximately 1.5 days. The stochastic variability is interpreted as the red noise observed in other AGN, while the QPO is attributed to the orbital motion of a secondary black hole with a mass of roughly $10^2$ solar masses. Additionally, we identify a significant flux increase in the ZTF g-band occurring between MJD 60200 and 60210, which cannot be explained by the model. This event is modeled as a "soft X-ray eruption" with a duration of about 10 days, a timescale comparable to the accretion disk's vertical scale height. This behavior is consistent with predictions from recent theoretical models involving magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in accretion disks. Consequently, AGN variability may result from a combination of both stochastic and quasi-periodic processes, as well as transient eruptions. These findings support the hypothesis that low-luminosity black holes and supermassive black holes share similar accretion mechanisms. Furthermore, this variability offers a potential method for detecting intermediate-mass black holes. Finally, the detection of transient eruptions in AGN may facilitate the investigation of fundamental accretion processes. These results underscore the necessity of high-time-resolution, multi-wavelength observations of AGN. We propose that this could be achieved by scheduling targeted observations of known variable AGN using both Swift and ZTF. Additionally, we recommend that future space-based missions, such as the proposed PAX, prioritize AGN as a primary science target. PAX's large field of view and continuous all-sky coverage would enable continuous monitoring of AGN, thereby significantly enhancing our ability to observe and characterize transient phenomena. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of the magnetic field within the atmosphere of the chemically peculiar star HD58260, utilizing the spectropolarimetric facility of the Astrophysical Observatory of the National Research University Moscow State University. The analysis employed the spectropolarimetric method of nonlinear stellar atmosphere modeling, which incorporates a magnetic field map as an input parameter. This modeling approach allowed for the direct observation of the magnetic field structure, revealing a gradient in the radial magnetic field component across the stellar disk. The research successfully identified the magnetic field of HD58260, characterized by a dipole tilt angle of 47.5° and a field strength of 1.15 kG. The young massive cluster NGC 5253 is situated at a luminosity distance of 12.8 Mpc, representing the closest massive young cluster. Its stellar population is estimated to be between 10 and 100 Myr old, with a total stellar mass of approximately $1.5 \times 10^6$ solar masses and a metallicity roughly 0.5 times that of the Sun. This study presents ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line, which we interpret as a proxy for H41$\alpha$ emission, a tracer of HII regions. We compare the H30$\alpha$ data with observations of the 1.2 mm continuum and the CO(3-2) transition. The data reveal a compact, bright source with a size of about 100 pc, which we identify as NGC 5253. The H30$\alpha$ emission is primarily thermal, with a gas temperature estimated at 100 K. The derived H30$\alpha$ luminosity is roughly 100 times lower than the H41$\alpha$ luminosity observed in the M82 starburst galaxy. We utilize this emission to evaluate the accuracy of HII region luminosity as an indicator of star formation rates (SFR). Additionally, we estimate the ionization parameter using electron density and electron temperature derived from H30$\alpha$ observations. The ionization parameter is estimated to be approximately $10^{-2.5}$, consistent with values found in other starburst galaxies. Finally, we compare the SFRs derived from H30$\alpha$ and CO(3-2) observations with those obtained from the 1.2 mm continuum, finding that the SFRs inferred from the 1.2 mm continuum are approximately 100 times higher than those from H30$\alpha$ or CO(3-2). This discrepancy is attributed to dust emission from the surrounding molecular gas. We conclude that H30$\alpha$ emission is a promising tool for observing star formation in low-metallicity starbursts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 1.2 mm continuum is a more effective tracer of star formation than H30$\alpha$ or CO(3-2) emission. We introduce a general framework for estimating conditional expectation operators within Hilbert spaces of random variables, with applications directed toward multivariate conditional mean regression and dimensionality reduction. A key advantage of this method is its ability to leverage the substantial data gains arising from dimensionality reduction prior to the application of nonparametric estimators. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed estimator, alongside several natural alternatives, is non-consistent when the underlying conditional expectation operator is nonlinear; consequently, we introduce a consistent alternative. Numerical experiments indicate that the various estimators discussed perform competently, suggesting that any theoretical discrepancies are likely of practical insignificance. Furthermore, simulations reveal that our estimators are typically more efficient than those derived from direct nonparametric estimation, even in scenarios where no dimension reduction occurs. Finally, in the context of unbalanced panel data, we illustrate that our approach offers a viable alternative to traditional fixed effects estimators for linear regression. This alternative yields estimates with significantly smaller finite-sample mean squared errors, although it may exhibit slightly larger asymptotic bias. Additionally, in specific finite samples, the fixed effects estimator exhibits substantial bias, whereas our proposed estimator does not. These findings underscore the critical importance of understanding the bias properties of nonparametric estimators in finite samples. To achieve this, we developed a general approach for constructing a bias-corrected conditional expectation estimator, which we argue is both conceptually and practically valuable. This study addresses a pandemic state estimation challenge by focusing on the development of observer gain matrices for processes modeled with basic SIR and SEIR formulations. These models are linearized around a disease-free equilibrium, resulting in a specific system structure where infection dynamics are governed by a single parameter. A key difficulty in designing observers for these models stems from the lack of direct measurements for infection or recovery populations. To overcome this, a novel observer is proposed, with its gains designed using a parameter-dependent Lyapunov function. This approach is effective for a restricted class of linear systems featuring a particular type of uncertainty inherent in epidemic models. The existence of a stable observer is verified through the investigation of associated Linear Matrix Inequalities (LMIs). Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed observer outperforms a standard Kalman filter in estimating the reproduction number, even when both utilize the identical set of population measurements. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted on both a simplified SIR model and a more complex SEIR model that accounts for an incubation period. These observations yield accurate estimates of the infection and recovery populations, as well as the infection rate parameter, across all scenarios. Additionally, a latent variable representing the removal rate is successfully reconstructed from the estimated parameters. Across every case examined, the proposed observer achieves superior performance compared to the Kalman filter, effectively tracking the progression of the disease. These findings hold significant value for epidemiologists, offering a robust tool for monitoring pandemic evolution. This methodology can facilitate the development of robust regression models to analyze the pandemic's trajectory and support decision-makers in formulating effective control strategies. Moreover, this framework serves as a foundational step for a subsequent parameter identification problem, which aims to address the issue of model selection by determining whether a specific pandemic case is better represented by an SIR or an SEIR model. The authors intend to explore this direction in future research. Finally, the methodology is expected to be applicable to other systems exhibiting a specific type of uncertainty, such as those found in biological and chemical engineering. Future work will expand the scope to include nonlinear systems, biological reaction networks, and other biological phenomena. This initial research was conducted during the COVID-19 outbreak, with the objective of providing a tool to assist in controlling the pandemic's spread. Integrating temporal and factual information into knowledge graph embeddings enables more effective representation of entities and relations. This study investigates how adapting static models to temporal knowledge graphs impacts link prediction performance. We introduce a method that builds upon basic static embeddings, retaining their simplicity while enhancing predictive accuracy on the zeno benchmark. We evaluate multiple embedding models and their algorithmic variants using both static and temporal datasets, analyzing the experimental results to assess their impact on link prediction within temporal knowledge graphs. The findings indicate that simple static models underpinning this approach yield competitive results on ZERONLP and outperform established methods on smaller datasets. Furthermore, models trained on augmented training sets demonstrate a substantial improvement in generalization to test set time points. This research is particularly relevant for future applications aiming to scale up training data and training sets. Ultrashort pulses generated by Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators have enabled numerous applications, particularly with current trends pushing for higher peak power. This geometrical analysis provides a method for designing such oscillators to reach these power levels. By applying ABCD matrix analysis to a single lens-based Kerr-lens model-locking oscillator, we analyzed how cavity parameters influence pulse duration. We examined how changes in the strength of Kerr-lens nonlinearities alter the resonator's geometrical stability, allowing us to derive equations for predicting pulse duration and bandwidth. We also established stability criteria for the cavity's ring resonator and used it to determine the maximum achievable pulse duration. Additionally, we developed a general approach for gain and loss compensation. Finally, we utilized this framework to design a 100-fs, 100-mW single-lens oscillator operating at a 80 MHz repetition rate with a 1.037 $\mu$m pulse width. These design tools facilitate the creation of new oscillators capable of achieving higher peak power and pulse durations. We also explore the potential of this work for other Kerr-lens mode-locking systems. The presented theory is supported by experimental data. The findings are accessible as data at 10.1093/ptm/pzab001. This paper is part of a collection dedicated to the legacy of Professor Peter T. Russell. Vertical federated learning (VFL), which involves multiple parties holding different features of the same entities, has recently attracted significant research interest. While online federated learning (OVL) utilizing asynchronous updates offers a viable solution to address challenges like massive scale and data heterogeneity in VFL, it introduces distinct difficulties. This paper introduces AR-VRUL, a novel method that integrates stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with the variational Bayes (VB) approach to estimate the posterior of regression parameters without the need for complex stochastic tensor operations. Furthermore, a new asynchronous update strategy is proposed to accommodate diverse computing resources, such as distributed asynchronous local SGD (DASL) and client-dropout variational Bayesian (CDVB). The resulting AR-VRUL framework enables regression feature selection and prediction through OVL, delivering superior performance compared to existing OVL solutions. Furthermore, AR-VRUL is applicable to both centralized and distributed environments, including serverless cloud computing platforms. Experimental results across various datasets and computing resources demonstrate that AR-VRUL outperforms state-of-the-art VFL methods in both accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, the study explores the impact of hyperparameters on OVL, offering valuable guidance for real-world applications. The optical absorption characteristics of silicon films deposited inside 3D photonic band gap crystals serving as photonic crystals (PCs) are investigated using the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method. This study examines how the number of layers, material dispersion, and the use of back reflectors influence total absorption across the near-infrared spectrum. Results indicate that incorporating a back reflector substantially boosts absorption for thin and ultrathin silicon films by preventing photonic modes from propagating away from the absorbing layer. Furthermore, for a single-layer silicon film, the peak absorption reaches 100% at wavelengths between 1000 and 1100 nm. These findings hold significant promise for enhancing the efficiency of photovoltaic devices, solar cells, and photodetectors. Additionally, the research offers a viable alternative to bulky traditional reflectors by utilizing an alternative method to boost absorption in thin-film silicon structures. Finally, the study demonstrates the potential of these thin silicon films as high-performance, low-cost absorbers for various optoelectronic applications. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first experimental analysis of absorption in thin silicon films situated within 3D PCs featuring a photonic band gap. The study also provides the first comprehensive examination of the effects of back reflectors on the absorption spectra of thin and ultrathin silicon films inside 3D PCs. This study investigates the behavior of functions $f: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ that satisfy the relation $f(z+1) = a^{f(z)}$ and possess a polynomial asymptotic solution. We demonstrate that for any base $a > 1$, every asymptotic root is uniquely determined modulo the coconstant and exhibits the linear growth $f(z) = \mu z + \nu + o(z^k)$ for some $k > 0$. Furthermore, we establish the existence of at least one polynomial of degree greater than 1 for $a > e^{e}$ and provide a method to construct such polynomials. The findings for degree-1 coconstants generalize to degree-$n$ polynomials. The paper also incorporates notes on the history of tetration and its connection to the dynamical system $\phi_\alpha(z+1) = a^{\phi_\alpha(z)}$. Finally, we outline the necessary conditions for a function to be considered an asymptotic solution and present the derivation of the monodromy group for this class of solutions. These findings are applied to analyze the asymptotic properties of rational points within the Riemann surface of the tetration function. Additionally, we present arguments supporting the existence of an analytic solution to the tetration equation and mention recent advancements in this field. To facilitate numerical computation, we have implemented the derived polynomials in Maple. Our approach begins with the fundamental relation $f(z+1) = a^{f(z)}$, examining the asymptotic behavior of its solutions. This leads to the primary objective of the work: characterizing the polynomials that solve the tetration equation. The resulting polynomials are subsequently used to compute the coefficients of the asymptotic solution. We proceed to calculate the coconstants of the tetration function and explore the asymptotic behavior of its branches. Finally, we address the existence of a polynomial solution to the equation and its broader implications. The paper concludes with an analysis of the analytic continuation of the inverse function of $\phi_a(z) = \mu + a^z$. As a final remark, we consider the case where the base $a$ is a complex number. We demonstrate that for $a = e^{ie}$, the function $\phi_a(z)$ is unbounded on the real line, implying that the monodromy group of the inverse function of $\phi_a(z)$ is not simply connected. This result has significant implications for the theory of polynomial solutions to the tetration equation

We introduce a novel construction of high-dimensional expanders (HDEs) utilizing covers of simplicial complexes. Specifically, we demonstrate that if $\Gamma$ is an HDE characterized by torsion size $T$ and $\ell_1$-expansion factors $\lambda$, then any $n$-fold cover of $\Gamma$ yielding an HDE with the same $\ell_1$-expansion factors must possess a torsion size of $T^n$. Leveraging this torsion lower bound, we establish that constructions based on covers are inherently constrained; specifically, achieving $\delta$-local expansion with $\ell_1$-norms requires a torsion size exceeding $1/\delta$. Consequently, we provide a systematic method for building binary HDEs with arbitrary local expansion. Furthermore, we prove that this construction method is optimal by showing that the torsion size of any HDE derived via covers scales exponentially with the number of folds. As a result, we successfully construct a family of bounded-degree, $q$-colorable high-dimensional expanders (where $q \geq 3$) exhibiting $\delta$-local expansion under $\ell_1$-norms, with a vertex count of $O(\frac{1}{\delta^2}\log(1/\delta))$. This family includes $(n, d, \delta)$-expanders where $n = O(\frac{1}{\delta^2}\log(1/\delta))$, $d = O(\frac{1}{\delta^2})$, and the local expansion drops to zero at $O(\delta^{-1})$ vertices. Additionally, we outline how to adapt this covering-based approach to produce high-dimensional expanders with constant local expansion, constant size, and linear dimension. These findings hold significant promise for applications in derandomization, property testing, and distributed computing. Notably, our construction offers the most compact HDEs to date for any given local expansion factor $\delta$. In contrast to recent HDE constructions utilizing random walks, our examples feature linear rather than quadratic length for random walks. Finally, we demonstrate that our examples are $(n, d, \delta)$-expanders with linear-size codimension-$d$ skeletons, where $n = O(\frac{1}{\delta^2}\log(1/\delta))$ and $d = O(\frac{1}{\delta^2})$. The study employs specific heat, magnetization, and muon spin rotation techniques to examine the magnetic ordering of GdInO$_3$, a material characterized by a centered hexagonal lattice that is quasi-two-dimensional due to weak interlayer coupling. A sharp anomaly in the specific heat measured below 2.2 K in zero field confirms the onset of an incommensurate antiferromagnetic structure. Analysis of muon spin rotation data reveals that the ordered wave vector is incommensurate with a value of $\kappa \sim 0.25$ along the $c$-axis. Furthermore, magnetization measurements demonstrate a field-induced metamagnetic transition occurring below the metamagnetic temperature $T_m \sim 1.8$ K, where $T_m$ is slightly lower than $T_N$. This behavior is attributed to the competition between ferromagnetic interactions along the $c$-axis and antiferromagnetic interactions within the $ab$-plane. Finally, a two-sublattice model is employed to investigate the system's field and temperature dependence. By fitting the model to specific heat and magnetization data, the interplane exchange constant is determined to be $J_c/J \sim 0.01$. These findings collectively indicate that GdInO$_3$ functions as a prototype quasi-two-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet. The coexistence of incommensurate ordering and metamagnetic behavior in this simple magnetic lattice offers a promising system for studying the dynamics of incommensurate structures under external fields. Additionally, the findings provide a basis for exploring the potential of Gd-inved compounds as a new class of two-dimensional magnetic materials. Graph embedding has emerged as a highly effective method for link prediction, primarily transforming nodes into low-dimensional dense representations that preserve topological information and enabling links to be defined via vector arithmetic. However, existing approaches often struggle with node degree heterogeneity and the triadic structure, particularly in sparse graphs where the majority of potential links do not exist. This paper introduces SSNE, a novel and straightforward graph representation technique designed to enhance link prediction in sparse networks. SSNE extends the SNE algorithm by incorporating a new objective function based on local and node-specific graph entropy. This entropy measures the uncertainty regarding the existence of a link between two nodes and serves as a powerful feature for distinguishing non-existent links during training. Experimental results demonstrate that SSNE consistently and significantly surpasses baseline methods in link prediction tasks. Furthermore, we apply SSNE to uncover hidden connections within the Twitter social network. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/SSNE. Additionally, we have released the data used in our application through https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/SSNE/tree/main/data. This resource includes the Twitter network along with a set of nodes labeled as "ground truth" connections. Silicon atomic vapor cells serve as the foundation for diverse applications, ranging from cold-atom sensors to deep learning in computer vision. These cells house an alkali gas buffer, enabling the creation of narrow spectral lines and facilitating spectroscopy across broad frequency ranges. Traditionally, such cells are manufactured using glass-blowing techniques, which are labor-intensive and yield large dimensions with limited precision. In contrast, this work presents a method for producing silicon atomic vapor cells with micro-machined dimensions and integrated optical features using lithography and deep silicon etching. We demonstrate a top-down fabrication approach for silicon cells containing $^{87}$Rb vapor and a micro-machined silicon waveguide capable of supporting single-mode light propagation. Furthermore, we illustrate anti-bunching statistics from a two-photon transition and achieve a quality factor of $F/Q=1.5\times10^{4}$ for a single photon transition. This research establishes a pathway for fabricating atomic vapor cells through top-down silicon manufacturing, thereby supporting a monolithic integration of atomic vapor components with photonic integrated circuits. Such an advancement could facilitate miniaturized atomic vapor-based optical components, including filters, switches, and modulators. Additionally, these cell-coupled photonic waveguides offer a robust solution for single-photon quantum communication, leveraging the narrow spectral lines of atomic rubidium to enable quantum memory and long-term quantum information storage. Ultimately, this work facilitates the integration of photonic circuits with silicon atomic vapors, advancing the development of quantum information processing systems. The proposed micro-machined silicon atomic vapor cells are compatible with existing silicon photonics manufacturing infrastructure. By combining these cells with photonic circuits, we can create hybrid photonic-atomic devices that are miniaturized, high-performance, and energy-efficient. This represents a significant advancement in the field of atomic physics and quantum information processing. We evaluate the precision of a newly proposed nonlinear interference model designed for general dual-polarization 4D formats. The model demonstrates high accuracy when compared against results from numerical simulations and established models under varying conditions, including transmission distances, transmission rates, and transmission formats. In a high-nonlinear regime, the proposed model achieves superior accuracy relative to the Gaussian noise model while retaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, we developed a computational complexity model to characterize the complexity of various split-step Fourier method-based algorithms used for modeling nonlinear interference. Finally, we introduced a simplified model utilizing the newly developed nonlinear interference power characterization to enhance computational efficiency without compromising modeling accuracy. Through this approach, an 8-fold reduction in computational complexity was achieved without any loss in accuracy. This enables the rapid analysis of a wide spectrum of dual-polarization 4D formats. Additionally, we demonstrated that this approach can significantly decrease the time required to model nonlinear interference in novel multi-carrier systems. We anticipate that these findings will serve as a valuable resource for researchers developing methods to predict and mitigate nonlinear interference in next-generation optical communication systems. This study presents the creation of a publicly available data set designed to identify indicators of depression in social media posts. The collection was generated by posting questions on a depression-related Facebook group, with responses analyzed by two board-certified psychiatrists. Additionally, we developed validation methods, including a feature selection approach that filters out features with fewer than three distinct values and a classifier ensembling strategy. This approach combines the predictions of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Naïve Bayes classifier, weighting the SVM more heavily. Empirical results demonstrate that the SVM outperforms the traditional Naïve Bayes classifier and that the proposed ensembling method further improves overall performance. To address the inherent class imbalance in the data, we applied the SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique). Our findings indicate that while SMOTE effectively mitigates the bias caused by class imbalance, it does not significantly enhance classification performance. Consequently, we conclude that future research should explore alternative strategies to eliminate or reduce data bias. Finally, we provide a detailed examination of the features that the SVM classifier identified as most relevant for distinguishing between users exhibiting and not exhibiting signs of depression. This analysis reveals that users show signs of depression when their posts contain questions, express feelings of loneliness, or mention having no one to talk to.

**Keywords:** Depression detection, Social media, Class imbalance, Feature selection, Ensemble classification.

This study investigates the influence of coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole strength on these modes within $^{28}$Si and $^{24}$Mg. By utilizing the random phase approximation, the researchers calculated isoscalar monopole and quadrupole intruder states, which exist at lower energies than the main states and exhibit particle-hole configurations across major shells. The results demonstrate that this coupling significantly alters the monopole strength distribution in both nuclei. Specifically, in $^{28}$Si, the monopole energy increases from 19.8 to 22.2 MeV, while the strength of the isoscalar giant monopole resonance (IGMR) drops from 0.85 to 0.68. In contrast, for $^{24}$Mg, the IGMR strength decreases more dramatically from 0.85 to 0.27, with a less pronounced energy shift from 21.0 to 22.4 MeV. These findings are corroborated by Monte Carlo shell model calculations, which confirm that monopole-quadrupole coupling substantially affects the IGMR. Furthermore, a strong correlation exists between the reduction in IGMR strength and the presence of a low-lying intruder state. The IGMR strength is reduced more in $^{24}$Mg than in $^{28}$Si because $^{24}$Mg possesses a low-lying intruder state with a larger mixing angle. This reduced strength is primarily attributed to the intruder state, which has an energy of 20.4 MeV and a strength of 0.45. Ultimately, the IGMR strength is more sensitive to the IGMR coupling to the intruder state than to the main state. These outcomes align with recent experimental findings. The analysis concludes that monopole-quadrupole coupling must be accounted for when calculating the IGMR. Additionally, the IGMR energy in $^{28}$Si is lower than in $^{24}$Mg, a result that contrasts with experimental data. The authors attribute this discrepancy to the limitations of the mean field model, which fails to incorporate configuration mixing. Consequently, future research should explore more sophisticated theoretical models to achieve a more accurate description of the IGMR. This work examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence within feedback-controlled motion systems characterized by discontinuous Coulomb friction. It demonstrates that a closed-form stiction region, dependent on parameters and surrounding an invariant equilibrium set, is invariably reachable and globally attractive. The analysis reveals that asymptotic convergence is the sole outcome, necessitating an infinite number of sliding intervals within any finite time horizon, thereby precluding convergence via sliding on any single interval. These theoretical findings are substantiated by numerical results derived from a model friction-based vehicle park-assist system. Furthermore, the paper establishes a connection to sliding mode theory by formulating an equivalent smooth system and proving that the system's trajectories correspond exactly to those of the smooth model both inside and outside the stiction region. This equivalence is validated through examples, including the described vehicle system and a well-known stick-slip model. Finally, the paper addresses the convergence of solutions to periodic boundary value problems, with results again illustrated by a vehicle system model. Additionally, it is shown that stiction cannot be reached via forward-time integration when the initial state lies outside the stiction region. Finally, the study addresses the issue of non-uniqueness in trajectories arising from the discontinuity of the Coulomb friction vector field. To address this, a Carathéodory extension is proposed, and its local existence and uniqueness are proven. Finally, the paper confirms that the proposed solution concept aligns with the original formulation based on Filippov's differential inclusions. These results are supported by both illustrative and vehicle system examples. We introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework designed to hedge portfolios contingent on various assets and their derivatives. Utilizing a recently developed framework by Li et al. (2021), our approach is valued for being both conceptually straightforward and computationally efficient, as it avoids the need to solve high-dimensional partial differential equations. Our method leverages the universal approximation capabilities of neural networks to handle complex payoffs, significantly expanding its applicability compared to prior hedging research. To mitigate the challenges of sample inefficiency and distributional shift inherent in deep reinforcement learning, we propose a hybrid strategy that integrates our algorithm with a traditional finite difference method. We evaluate the performance of our proposed framework across three specific use cases, demonstrating its effectiveness in these scenarios. Furthermore, we validate the robustness of our algorithm by testing it on a portfolio involving put options with out-of-the-money strikes. This specific test reveals that our method is particularly sample-efficient when applied to options with at-the-money strikes. However, we observe that achieving high sample efficiency for out-of-the-money options remains an open challenge. Consequently, we conclude that future research should prioritize developing methods capable of handling the unique complexities associated with pricing and hedging out-of-the-money options. Finally, we acknowledge that expanding our methodology to include assets and derivatives beyond equities and options—such as bonds, commodities, indices, futures, and swaps—constitutes a promising avenue for further study. This extension would require adapting our approach to account for distinct underlying dynamics, such as interest rate modeling for bonds and mean-reverting behavior in commodities and indices. Additionally, we intend to explore enhancing our method by incorporating early exercise features for American-style options and investigating whether machine learning techniques can be applied to price forward contracts. These directions represent potential paths for advancing the field, specifically in addressing the difficulties of valuing and managing contracts with more complex structures. Finally, we plan to investigate extending our approach to cover other derivative types, such as futures and swaps, which involve different underlying assets and dynamics than those currently addressed. This would involve researching how to integrate these additional asset classes into our framework while maintaining robustness and performance. Sequential recommender systems are designed to suggest items to users based on their past consumption history. However, simply recommending the next most probable item is insufficient; recommendations must also align with the user's current offline intent. While recent advancements in sequential recommender systems have achieved significant progress, they have largely concentrated on predicting item probabilities within a Markov decision process framework, often neglecting the underlying user intent. We contend that a sequential recommender should be intensional, capable of modeling a user's current intent to ensure its suggestions are relevant. To address this, we introduce the concept of a "user session," a fundamental unit of user intent, and propose a novel deep generative adversarial network (GAN) framework named Intent Modeling GAN (IMGAN) to capture session-level intents. The discriminator in our framework is tasked with distinguishing real user sessions from those generated by the generator, while the generator is trained to create synthetic sessions that are indistinguishable from the discriminators' perspective. This setup enables the model to learn the latent user intent by distinguishing between real and generated sessions. Extensive experiments across real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our method effectively captures session-level intents and outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in both online and offline evaluations. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of our framework through a large-scale recommendation task within a real-world production environment. The reducible double confluent Heun equation, though possessing reduced singularity strength compared to the non-reducible variant, still maintains three distinct singular points. We establish a general formula expressing this equation in local coordinates near each singularity and utilize these expressions to define a symmetric unfolding of all three local coordinates around their respective regular singular points, effectively "smoothing" them. While this formula is valid only locally, it can be viewed as a generalized transformation. By fixing the transformation in local coordinates and allowing it to extend beyond this narrow local regime, we generate a broad class of examples. We provide detailed descriptions for a specific unfolding where the local transformation is extended, resulting in a model featuring a single extended singularity. Finally, we examine the conditions necessary to restrict this approach to a more confined region. This framework offers a novel perspective on classifying and understanding the Heun equation and its various regimes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this specific unfolding can be derived from the reducible double confluent Heun equation by applying a specific operator to its solutions. This method yields a comprehensive understanding of the equation's various regimes, with the selection of the appropriate regime determined by the specific operator employed. Additionally, we explore a connection between these unfolding techniques and the theory of isomonodromic deformations. Overall, this approach provides a systematic method for constructing solutions to the Heun equation. Finally, we illustrate an application of these unfolded solutions within the context of integrable systems. This paper serves as a foundation for a series that examines the properties of the Heun equation through these unfolded solutions. Subsequent papers will detail the specific properties of the solution, the classification of its regimes, and an analysis of its integrable properties. This series will also address the open question of whether these unfolded solutions satisfy a differential equation. Collectively, this series will offer a complete solution to the Heun equation. This work is part of a broader project aimed at developing a unified theory for Heun equations, a goal that will be achieved through this systematic approach. The unified theory will encompass all regimes of the Heun equation, thereby providing a complete solution to the equation. We examine the problem of estimating a low-rank matrix under the assumption of independent groupwise heteroskedastic noise. This scenario is significant because it encompasses various practical noise models, including the classical i.i.d. Gaussian case, sparse entry-wise noise, and non-Gaussian noise with distinct variances organized by group. Our analysis demonstrates that the fundamental limits of matrix recovery in this setting can be characterized through a semidefinite program (SDP). Furthermore, our findings reveal a critical insight: the group structure defined in the covariance model exerts the most pronounced effect on recoverability, overriding factors such as the total number of entries or dimensionality. Additionally, we illustrate that traditional methods, which typically assume homoskedasticity, often fail to achieve the optimal statistical rates in groups characterized by heavy-tailed or highly sparse noise. Finally, we propose an estimator that matches the optimal statistical risk established by our main theoretical results. These theoretical findings are validated through extensive numerical experiments within a real-world application context. These results hold for arbitrary group structures, including cases where groups are not nested inside one another. Our primary theoretical tool involves a novel analysis of quadratic forms, which may have broader applications in statistical theory. Specifically, we derive new concentration inequalities for quadratic forms involving inverse Wishart random matrices, which are of independent interest. We also present a comprehensive discussion of the proof techniques used in this work. Finally, we explore the implications of our theory for other popular noise models, such as non-Gaussian and correlated noise. In summary, this work provides both theoretical and practical tools for the analysis of rank-one matrix estimation in the presence of groupwise heteroskedastic noise. Our approach is applicable to a wide range of real-world scenarios, including single-cell RNA sequencing and image denoising. Furthermore, our work serves as a natural extension of previous studies on low-rank matrix estimation, which primarily focused on i.i.d. Gaussian noise. We anticipate that our work will inspire future research in this area. We investigate the vibrational spectrum of a constrained classical ring, where second-order exceptional points enable a topologically trivial band at infinity to induce nontrivial topology in the vibrational band. Notably, this model operates without symmetry, a feature typically considered essential for topological frameworks. Consequently, fractional boundary states emerge without requiring protective symmetries. Additionally, we find that second-order exceptional points generate double Robins boundary conditions, a phenomenon distinct from the contribution of first-order exceptional points, which produce single (Dirichlet or Neumann) boundary conditions. This behavior is highlighted by a non-Abelian exceptional point matrix that is non-diagonal in the Dirac basis. Furthermore, we explore the potential to break particle-hole symmetry in a way that preserves spectral reality, a capability attributed to second-order exceptional points. Finally, we outline a path toward a fully intrinsic model that avoids the need for a classical constraint, a concept that could significantly expand the field of topological physics. This paper is primarily motivated by the recent study by Liu, Chen, and Ge (Phys. Rev. B 104, 024501 (2021)), which highlighted a classical ring model devoid of symmetry. This discrepancy arises because the referenced ring's spectrum relies on a specific parameterization of its exceptional points, a detail that was overlooked in the original study. Our analysis reveals that the classical spectrum is determined by second-order exceptional points rather than the previously assumed first-order points. Consequently, we show that the classical spectrum admits a broader class of parameters than those considered in the original paper, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the system's properties. Additionally, we examine the single-particle model, revealing that it exhibits a different topology than its many-body counterpart. We demonstrate that the classical spectrum remains determined by second-order exceptional points, consistent with our earlier findings. This paper introduces a distributed control strategy for solving generalized predictive control (MPC) problems in a decentralized framework, enabling multi-plant systems to achieve asymptotic tracking of arbitrary reference trajectories without requiring inter-plant communication. The proposed solution is distributed, allowing each plant to manage its own control inputs and estimate its trajectory. Furthermore, the approach is scalable and supports a plug-and-play design, meaning new units can be integrated into the system with minimal adjustments. We derive specific conditions under which stability is guaranteed and validate the method's effectiveness through numerical simulations. These simulations demonstrate that the proposed solution achieves the same performance as a centralized system while significantly reducing communication costs. Additionally, the approach is applicable to a wide range of problems, including those with input and output constraints, as it serves as a relaxed version of traditional MPC. Finally, our method extends the paradigm of distributed linear algebra, enabling the solution of specific linear problems in a decentralized manner. This paves the way for addressing nonlinear problems in a decentralized fashion by leveraging distributed nonlinear solvers. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant global loss of life and represents the most severe crisis humanity has faced in recent history. Consequently, there is a critical need for highly accurate diagnostic methods. While existing research on automatic feature extraction and classification for COVID-19 remains limited, this study leverages BERT models to enhance performance. We utilize a large-scale clinical dataset containing 1,000 chest X-ray images, where each sample is labeled with the presence of pneumonia, a viral infection. Our approach employs BERT to automatically extract deep features from these images. To further boost classification accuracy, we implement a two-stage classifier: a pre-trained model handles the difficult cases of distinguishing between no condition and COVID-19, while a secondary model manages the classification between no condition and COVID-19. This methodology achieves a precision of 0.92 and a recall of 0.91. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/taehyuklee/Two-Stage-COVID19-Classifier. Given the widespread availability of BERT models, this framework offers a robust solution for future automatic COVID-19 classification. Additionally, we plan to release our model for researchers to apply to their own datasets. We believe this approach can contribute to reducing the global burden of the pandemic. Future work will involve expanding the dataset to include more samples and exploring additional BERT variants to further enhance classification accuracy. Through our research, we aim to assist in combating the COVID-19 crisis. We hope this contribution aids in the fight against the virus and helps alleviate the suffering of millions worldwide. The field of eco-evolutionary dynamics investigates how ecological and evolutionary processes interact, yet it often fails to account for the timeframes in which these interactions occur. While theoretical frameworks typically categorize these interactions by their timescales, there is currently no systematic method for measuring them. This study introduces a metric to quantify the timescale of eco-evolutionary interactions, grounded in a mathematical analysis of an established phenomenological model. By examining the relationship between eco-evolutionary rate modulators and system timescales, we demonstrate that these timescales can be manipulated to shift species from coexistence to competitive exclusion. These findings offer critical insights for interpreting eco-evolutionary dynamics across various temporal resolutions. Additionally, we propose a framework for developing a quantitative theory of eco-evolutionary timescales that integrates principles from nonequilibrium statistical physics. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this timescale theory to more complex models that capture distinct characteristics of ecological and evolutionary dynamics. These contributions are essential for advancing the field of quantitative eco-evolutionary biology. The supporting code is available at https://github.com/evolvolution/ecoevo_timescales. The speech community is increasingly adopting self-supervised learning (SSL) models as a foundational approach for various applications. Although these models are trained without exposure to adversarial examples, their resilience against such threats remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the adversarial vulnerabilities of both clean and robust speech models employing self-supervised training techniques. Our findings indicate that the extent of adversarial corruption in clean speech models is comparable to that in robust models, underscoring a significant security concern. To address this, we introduce the concept of "adversarial robustness score" (ARS) and demonstrate a novel, efficient regularization technique called "adversarial noise scaling" (ANS). This regularization method enhances the adversarial robustness of clean speech models by up to 20% relative, while also improving generalization performance by 0.5% relative. Furthermore, we observe that the speech community is increasingly utilizing larger pre-trained SSL models, which exhibit greater robustness compared to smaller ones. Collectively, these results offer critical insights for researchers and practitioners within the speech domain. The code for adversarial attacks and defenses, alongside pre-trained models, is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/SSL-SSL-Speech-Attack-and-Defense. Additionally, the speech dataset used in this study can be downloaded from https://zenodo.org/record/7171064. Finally, we provide a tutorial on implementing the attacks and defenses discussed in this work, available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/SSL-SSL-Speech-Attack-and-Defense/blob/main/Tutorial.md. This work was presented at Interspeech 2023. Keywords: speech security, adversarial robustness, self-supervised learning, regularization. This study examines the market dynamics of a blockchain-based decentralized exchange (DEX) functioning as an intermediary, where users can either adopt the platform or utilize traditional financial channels. In this framework, adopters encounter a fixed fee structure set by an owner, while non-adopters experience a dynamic fee regime influenced by government policy and the behavior of "fee dummies"—individuals who adopt despite paying higher fees to benefit others. We analyze these dynamics through a game-theoretic lens, modeling individual decision-making as a best response to perceived costs and the actions of others. Our findings reveal that a DEX can achieve a positive market share if its fees are sufficiently low and the cost of individual adoption is not excessively high. However, if the adoption cost is high, the presence of fee dummies can be advantageous, as it allows the owner to set a higher fee that deters them while still attracting a non-empty group of non-dummies. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that a DEX can attract a substantial number of users only when the policy regime is favorable. Additionally, we explore how network effects among users can either hinder or facilitate the adoption of decentralized finance tools. Finally, we outline potential future research directions, including the possibility of users dynamically switching between the DEX and traditional financial systems. Through a combination of mathematical modeling and empirical analysis, this work aims to provide a foundation for comprehending the adoption of blockchain-based decentralized exchanges. Sensitivity analysis in missing data contexts explores how conclusions shift when missing not at random (MNAR) assumptions are applied. This work introduces an adaptation of the E-value metric for sensitivity analysis, examining its properties and demonstrating its application through simulation studies and a real-world example. The primary objective is to quantify the influence of unmeasured bias in the absence of direct validation data. We define the E-squared value as a scale-invariant measure that quantifies the magnitude of unmeasured bias affecting a specific effect estimate. To facilitate model comparison, we developed an ES-value metric to assess model fit. Additionally, we investigated methods for integrating prior knowledge regarding the potential scale of unmeasured bias to enhance missing data models. Simulation results indicate that models utilizing ES-value outperform traditional log odds approaches, particularly when bias is substantial. Finally, we applied the ES-value method to a real dataset to conduct sensitivity analysis on the association between smoking and coronary heart disease in the MRFIT study. This approach quantifies differences between missing at random (MAR), not at random (MNAR), and directly observable data scenarios. The proposed ES-value method offers a straightforward and interpretable framework for sensitivity analysis, enabling researchers to evaluate how MNAR assumptions impact key effect estimates. Furthermore, this framework facilitates model selection and comparison, providing a robust basis for choosing appropriate missing data models. Ultimately, the ES-value approach enhances the reliability of inferences derived from missing data. Supplementary materials, including an R package, are available at https://github.com/chenyao1992/ESvalue. Keywords: Missing data, Sensitivity analysis, Model selection, Model fit, Bayesian analysis.

The review examines how blockchain enhances FL security and privacy within the IoV environment. Additionally, we identify the advantages and limitations of blockchain-empowered FL, explore future research directions, and propose potential solutions. Ultimately, this study aims to assist researchers and practitioners in advancing secure FL applications for intelligent vehicles and smart cities through blockchain technology. Furthermore, we offer insights and suggestions to facilitate future research in this domain. The ALICE experiment at the LHC has measured the production of non-prompt D mesons through decays involving a bottom hadron in central and mid-central ($0-30\%$) Pb+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02$ TeV. By comparing these findings with earlier prompt D meson measurements across various centrality bins, the study investigates hadronization preferences for charm and beauty quarks. Results indicate that both charm and beauty quarks favor light hadrons in a similar manner. Furthermore, the $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ spectra of non-prompt D mesons are analyzed using two color-suppressed fragmentation functions, and the resulting coefficients are compared with perturbative QCD predictions. Finally, the ratio of non-prompt to prompt D mesons is compared with Glauber model predictions, revealing that the data are consistent with these expectations. This suggests that the nuclear modification of quark spectra prior to hadronization does not significantly alter their fragmentation properties. Additionally, a new measurement of the nuclear modification factor $R_{AA}$ for non-prompt D mesons is reported, extending these ALICE results to very low transverse momenta for the first time. The $R_{AA}$ values for non-prompt D mesons are compared with those of prompt D mesons, showing that both exhibit similar suppression patterns. The demand for expanded millikelvin cooling systems stems from the requirement to accommodate an increasing number of cryogenic qubits within quantum computing architectures. This paper details the design and construction of the "LISA" (Large-scale Integrated Superconducting Apparatus) millikelvin platform, currently under development at the Fermilab National Laboratory. LISA is designed to support temperatures below 10 mK and will integrate a diverse collection of superconducting and superconducting hybrid qubits. The system's purpose is to facilitate the study of qubit control, readout, and readout-coherent circuit interactions. This work presents the finalized design of the cryostat alongside an analysis of the achieved thermal performance. LISA is engineered to sustain a 10 mK temperature within a volume of approximately 1.5 liters. Furthermore, it is scalable to multiple such zones, allowing for future expansion to 10 mZones throughout the device. The successful operation of LISA will pave the way for investigating the scalability of large-scale quantum processors. This document is published in Rev. Sci. Instrum. 92, 023101 (2021). This paper introduces a straightforward and efficient approach for automatically generating high-quality, robust, and generalizable labels for large-scale urban datasets. Our method is data-driven, requiring no prior knowledge of label definitions or visual examples, and relies solely on the distribution of an abundant supply of noisy, weak supervision data. By employing a voting-based mechanism, we automatically derive a high proportion of precise and consistent labels from this noisy input. We validate our technique across four diverse datasets (PASCAL VOCHEN, PASCAL PERSON RE-DETECTION, COCHOPPER, and MS COCO), demonstrating that it generates label quality comparable to or superior to manual annotation for 60% of the labels. Furthermore, the method is scalable, capable of processing over 100,000 images in less than a day on a single GPU. The source code is available at https://github.com/StanfordVL/VALUE. The term VALUE is a play on "value," reflecting the method's ability to extract high value from vast amounts of noisy data. Additionally, it serves as an acronym for Large Scale Voting-based Automatic Labelling for Urban Environments, highlighting its scalability through the voting process and application to urban settings. Given the method's simplicity, it can be adapted to various data types, such as point clouds or depth maps. The section titled "Future Work" outlines potential applications within autonomous driving. The paper concludes with a discussion on current limitations and directions for future research. Our code is also applicable to other datasets, as with any Stanford Vision and Learning (SVL) project. We demonstrate automatic label generation for the KITTI dataset at the end of the paper.

This study addresses sparse signal recovery via a nonuniform nonconvex model that integrates mixed $\ell_1$ and $\ell_0$ norms. We propose a proximal average framework to effectively combine the denoisers corresponding to these two components. Utilizing this approach, we develop and assess a proximal average singular value thresholding (proxSVT) algorithm for seismic reflectivity inversion. By integrating a majorization-minimization strategy with an adaptive step-size rule, the proposed proxSVT method achieves superior reconstruction quality, enhanced computational efficiency, and increased algorithmic stability compared to existing methods. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that proxSVT outperforms competing approaches across a diverse range of parameters and noise levels. Furthermore, the proxSVT implementation features straightforward code architecture and requires minimal modifications to accommodate different scenarios. This implementation is accessible online at https://github.com/zhongtao1234/proxSVT. The source code can also be obtained by contacting the corresponding author. We introduce a technique for calculating bulk operator fusion using wavefunction overlaps. This method relies on the universal nature of bulk-operator correlations, allowing for the efficient verification of operator fusion through the overlap of fusion matrices. Furthermore, the framework utilizes non-universal data to derive universal information; specifically, by comparing fusion angles derived from operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients, we determine universal finite-size corrections to the central charge. Applying this approach to the Haagerup model, we extract the bulk operator algebra and establish the model's critical behavior, revealing a non-rational structure characterized by an infinite set of operator fusion rules. Additionally, our finite-size corrections indicate that the central charge is irrational, with a value of $c \approx 0.4816$. In a supplementary section, we demonstrate the framework's utility for a solvable lattice model, the XXZ spin chain, extracting both the operator algebra and finite-size corrections to the central charge. Finally, our results suggest that the bulk operator algebra of the XXZ spin chain remains independent of the coupling constant. These findings offer a systematic method for analyzing operator fusion across a broad spectrum of critical phenomena. *Supplementary material*: A detailed description of the operator fusion analysis is provided in Supplementary Note 1, with Supplementary Note 2 detailing our application of the theory to the XXZ spin chain. Supplementary Note 3 presents a numerical study on the finite-size corrections to the central charge for a lattice model featuring an infinite operator fusion algebra. This study was conducted in collaboration with A. J. McCulloch, M. R. M. Steen, and J. Verstraete. A full version of this work is available in Phys. Rev. B 106, 054417 (2022). Part-of-speech (POS) tagging serves as a fundamental prerequisite for linguistic research and natural language processing, yet current state-of-the-art tagging systems frequently encounter difficulties when processing historical texts from prior centuries due to lexical and syntactic variations from contemporary English. These failures stem from two primary issues: (1) the reliance of modern systems on implicit set-valued prediction, and (2) the dependence of machine learning models on vocabulary words familiar to their training data. To address the first challenge, we propose a framework that explicitly accounts for the set-valued nature of linguistic categories. This approach utilizes a generalized loss function to enhance the performance of state-of-the-art taggers on historical corpora. Regarding the second issue, we integrate a word embedding layer that leverages external, historically diverse POS-tagged corpora to mitigate vocabulary gaps. Our methodology successfully applies to Middle English (1450–1500) and Early Modern English (1600–1700) datasets, achieving robust results that enable the identification of morphosyntactic anomalies in historical English relative to modern standards. Furthermore, our method demonstrates superior performance on under-resourced languages, such as Old Icelandic, when compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Finally, we illustrate how our part-of-speech tagger can assist lemmatizers in generating accurate inflectional forms for rare words from historical periods. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/andersberghman/pos-tagger. Additionally, we have established a new benchmark for POS tagging on Middle English and Old Icelandic, which can be accessed at https://connekt.se/pos-tagg-bench/. This paper aims to establish a non-smooth integrability theory for nonlinear partial differential equations by leveraging the concept of renormalized solutions. We demonstrate that the renormalized solution framework is equivalent to the entropy solution framework, extending the existing equivalence between these theories in one-dimensional scalar conservation laws. Leveraging this equivalence, we outline the construction of multiple prior solutions. Specifically, we analyze the Cauchy problem associated with a strictly hyperbolic system of conservation laws featuring strictly convex entropy and a discontinuous entropy production coefficient. Under appropriate assumptions, we prove the existence of a prior solution. Furthermore, we present an illustrative example: a two-phase porous medium flow model, where we show that a prior solution exists provided certain conditions are met. Finally, we present several open questions and potential research directions within the context of the developed theory. Notably, the methodology and findings could hold significant value for researchers in the field of non-smooth integrability. This paper outlines the design principles and development methodology of an intelligent agent capable of translating urban infrastructure requirements—such as public transport networks, traffic systems, and surveillance networks—into a formal specification language. We contend that manual translation is prone to human error and that automated translation is essential for the safe development of Smart Cities. The agent employs forward and backward semantic reasoning to map an input format, FRML, to an output format, OFRML. FRML and OFRML share a common language, FRL, which formally describes real-world entities, their relationships, functional requirements, and data requirements. OFRML extends FRL by incorporating constraints on domain entities. We demonstrate that requirement preservation is equivalent to the agent performing forward and backward reasoning. Furthermore, we show that the agent's development methodology relies on a set of axioms that define both the reasoning rules and the correctness conditions for each development step. Finally, a proof of correctness for a representative translation rule is provided. This development approach is intended to be applied to translate requirements for other smart city requirements, including road networks, surveillance networks, and smart lighting networks. Additionally, the proposed development methodology can be utilized to construct intelligent agents responsible for knowledge representation, planning, and decision-making. The source code for the agent is available at: https://github.com/fernandoalvarado24/requirement_preservation. Our work was funded by the Chilean FONDECYT grant 1117.0070. To our knowledge, no other group is currently engaged in translating urban infrastructure requirements into formal specifications. This paper presents the first application of formal methods to this domain. We demonstrate that the requirements developed for the agent's translation rules can be verified using the ProB model checker. Furthermore, the agent's reasoning process can be validated using ProB, which serves as the foundation for our future research. This represents the initial application of model checking to verify an agent's reasoning process. Finally, the agent's development methodology adheres to the principles of formal methods, ensuring that all its outputs are formally verified. Consequently, this work marks the first application of formal methods to develop an intelligent agent for translating urban infrastructure requirements. Future research will involve applying formal methods to develop an agent for planning and decision-making in urban infrastructure, thereby establishing a tradition of formal methods in this field. Additionally, we aim to extend the FRML language to include temporal requirements, thereby enabling the application of formal methods to requirements translation involving time. This study introduces a quantum error mitigation approach utilizing hidden inverses, which substitutes standard inverse noise channel approximations derived from variational quantum circuits (VQC) with a distinct circuit design. The proposed method maintains the same scaling for both the number of measurements and circuit depth relative to the target fidelity as VVC-based techniques, yet it relies exclusively on native gates available in near-term superconducting quantum hardware. This efficiency stems from employing a count-based model that reorders gates and eliminates the need for two-qubit phase shifts. When applied to experimental single-qubit processes on such devices, the method successfully identified and corrected dominant systematic noise components. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that this hidden inverse strategy can be directly integrated with Variational Quantum Algorithms, offering a practical pathway for error mitigation without additional overhead. These findings hold significant promise for advancing error-mitigated applications on current superconducting quantum systems. Furthermore, the method is readily extensible to multi-qubit scenarios, where it is expected to surpass current error-mitigation techniques. The North Sea serves as an ideal case study for multivariate spatial modeling of extreme events, given its extensive network of weather and wave stations. This research focuses on a dataset of 40 years of observations collected at 14 of these stations. To address the challenge of high dimensionality inherent in spatial extremes, we introduce a new Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates an extreme-valued Gaussian random field. This component is derived from a latent Gaussian field through an extreme-value transformation, a method that significantly reduces the number of parameters compared to non-hierarchical alternatives. The study demonstrates that this model can capture complex dependence structures in both time and space. Furthermore, it proves capable of generating realistic time series that maintain coherent spatial patterns, even when conditioned on specific extreme scenarios. Finally, the model's ability to perform realistic simulations under strong temporal and spatial dependence makes it highly suitable for applications in environmental science. These applications frequently require realizations of extreme phenomena to evaluate responses to changing conditions, such as those predicted by climate change. In this context, the proposed model can serve as a generator for extreme scenarios to assess how the North Sea reacts to various future climate projections. Additionally, it can help identify the most probable future extreme scenarios. To facilitate these uses, we have made the model open-source. Finally, an online tutorial is available that includes both real and simulated datasets to illustrate the model's features. Current pre-trained vision-language models (VLPs) frequently fail to capture intricate semantic details in images, resulting in a significant performance gap when used as captions within difficult multi-modal learning tasks. To address this, we introduce VT-CLIP, a framework designed to enhance VLPs by incorporating visual-guided text information. This approach comprises two key components: (1) a Visual-guided Text Augmentation (VT-8) module that generates visual-guided text from original pairs using a self-supervised method, and (2) a cross-modal contrastive learning module aligned with VT-8 outputs. VT-8 leverages an encoder-decoder architecture self-supervised by matching original and generated vision-language pairs, while a contrastive loss minimizes the distance between original and visual-guided pairs across modalities. Our analysis indicates that VT-8 is essential for improving VLPs, as it provides visual-guided text information. We validate this validation through extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, where VT-8 consistently yields substantial gains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework generalizes effectively to various VLPs and scales effectively with larger model sizes.
