This paper introduces a novel network coding-based cooperative communication framework designed to minimize the energy consumption of a source transmitting a codeword to multiple destinations through direct and cooperative channels. To achieve this, the study jointly optimizes power allocation among source and relay nodes, determines the optimal power split for network decoding, and establishes a scheduling policy to reduce source transmission power. This approach leverages network coding's ability to generate multiple independent codewords within a single transmission, thereby decreasing the total number of required transmissions. By strategically selecting relays and allocating power based on these generated codewords, the system can further cut down on transmission counts. Consequently, a non-convex minimization problem is formulated to solve the joint optimization of power allocation and relay scheduling, aiming to minimize the source's energy usage. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed network coding-based cooperative communication system saves up to 40% more energy compared to a benchmark non-coding system. Additionally, the convergence of the network decoding power allocation algorithm is analyzed, and an exhaustive search is employed to determine the optimal scheduling policy. The results indicate that the source benefits from a reduced transmission power, with the optimal scheduling policy selecting relays that have the strongest channel to the destination. Furthermore, the study finds that the source should transmit a single codeword when a small number of codewords are generated, whereas a larger number of codewords is preferred when the count is high. Finally, an analytical expression for the optimal scheduling policy is derived, showing that the source should transmit with maximum power when a large number of relays are selected, while the power should be low when few relays are chosen. These findings are supported by simulation results. Ultimately, network coding-based cooperative communication emerges as an effective solution for green communications. A significant advantage of this approach is that it does not necessitate additional modifications to the source or relays, as these nodes can be reused without changes. This makes network coding-based cooperative communication a promising green communication solution. The paper concludes by outlining an agenda for future research in this area. Specifically, the network decoding power allocation algorithm is shown to converge to a local optimum, and future work will explore the development of a global optimization algorithm. Moreover, the optimal scheduling policy is derived under the assumption of a fixed number of selected relays; however, this fixed number is not necessarily optimal. Therefore, future research will investigate jointly optimizing the relay scheduling policy and the number of selected relays. Distribution to distribution (T2D) scan matching is a technique used for pose estimation in mobile robots. However, bias inherent to the algorithm can lead to suboptimal average estimation, making bias removal essential for high-precision applications. While distribution-to-distribution scan matching is robust against noise, it is highly sensitive to systematic range-finder bias. We introduce a differentiable D2D scan matching process incorporating a differentiable filter to eliminate bias. This process is trained using a supervised learning approach, where the differentiable filter is trained alongside it. The proposed method is evaluated against two alternative techniques and demonstrates superior performance. Our results indicate that the learned D2D scan matching process and differentiable filter perform effectively across various range-finder noise levels and demonstrate greater adaptability to different robot configurations. Additionally, the trained differentiable filter exhibits strong generalization capabilities for removing systematic errors in test data not utilized during training. Furthermore, the differentiable filter shows promising potential for application in other learning-based algorithms. We anticipate that this approach will facilitate the development of novel learning-based D2D scan matching algorithms. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/roboticslabtuda/d2d-scan-matching. Finally, we provide a tutorial on the implementation and source code for this task. The tutorial can be accessed here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=14422222222. Satellite imagery is frequently utilized to identify features such as roads, water bodies, and vegetation. This paper introduces a novel deep-agnostic approach leveraging the Hough transform and adaptive thresholding for edge detection in satellite photos. By integrating these techniques with a new original method, we develop a robust pipeline that operates without deep learning networks while maintaining high performance in edge detection. We evaluate this approach against HED, RDE, and U-Net—three prominent deep learning-based detectors—using two benchmark datasets: ISPRS Vaihingen and Pavia University. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed pipeline outperforms all compared deep learning methods, achieving a mean IoU of 0.62 compared to 0.53 for the best-performing network. Furthermore, we provide a generalizable framework for edge detection in satellite images that does not rely on network training, thereby eliminating the need for extensive datasets. Finally, we discuss how this approach can be integrated into edge- and object-based image analysis. We have open-sourced this framework to facilitate its adoption in the satellite imagery community. The code is available at: https://github.com/SebastianSchroeder1999/Deep-Agnostic-Edge-Detection. Our results are accessible here: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/360000000_Deagnostic_Edge_Detection_for_Satellite_Imagery. Additionally, we address how this framework can be incorporated into broader satellite image analysis workflows. Our approach enables the creation of object masks and the identification of land cover types, such as water bodies, vegetation, and roads, which are critical for various applications including disaster management, urban planning, and climate change research. By providing an alternative to deep learning methods, we aim to increase the diversity of techniques available for satellite image analysis and offer a framework for researchers to explore how our approach can be integrated into their specific workflows. We believe that by providing a general framework for satellite image analysis, we can facilitate the adoption of our approach in the satellite imagery community and enable researchers to explore how their specific workflows can be integrated with our approach. We introduce a rate-model framework to analyze time-resolved X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) data, specifically under high-intensity, non-linear pump-probe x-ray excitation conditions. This approach offers two primary advantages: it streamlines the number of physical parameters required for data fitting, and it elucidates the underlying dynamics of excited electronic states. By minimizing the parameter set, the model facilitates the identification and characterization of states that may be transient or difficult to access experimentally. Applying this technique to a series of time-resolved non-linear x-ray absorption spectra from cobalt metal demonstrates its effectiveness. The resulting outcomes provide a comprehensive understanding of electron population dynamics in cobalt, including findings that contradict current understanding regarding the states of excited electrons in transition metals. Furthermore, the high fluence employed in this study opens a pathway for conducting non-linear x-ray absorption experiments on transition metals, thereby enabling access to electron populations that are otherwise challenging to investigate. These experiments could yield novel insights into the dynamics of excited states in transition metals, a topic that has recently attracted significant attention. Additionally, we have integrated this rate-model into an open-source Python package, which is accessible on PyPI. This tool is designed to be adaptable for analyzing spectra from various elements. We anticipate that these findings will stimulate new experimental and theoretical research into the non-linear excitation of transition metals. Our analysis of the spectra was performed using the open-source PyXANES package. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have emerged as a resilient approach to automatic modulation classification (AMC), surpassing traditional methods in performance. However, these DNNs are highly susceptible to adversarial attacks, where adversarial samples are introduced to deceive the DNN into producing incorrect classifications. To address this, we propose employing a generative adversarial network (GAN) trained on both clean and cleanless data as a test-time defense mechanism. To enhance the GAN's ability to generate realistic samples, and by extension improve the classifier's robustness, we introduce a novel mixture GAN architecture for AMC. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed architecture effectively generates realistic samples, yielding superior adversarial robustness in AMC tasks compared to other GAN variants. Furthermore, the mixture GAN outperforms existing GAN-based AMC methods when trained exclusively on cleanless data. To further boost the GAN's realism, we also implement data augmentation techniques for AMC. Finally, we explore utilizing transfer learning to train the GAN, which results in significant performance gains. The source code for our AMC system is publicly available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/MixtureGAN-AMC. Our results indicate that the mixture GAN outperforms other GANs in AMC scenarios, producing more realistic samples that lead to a 10% increase in accuracy. Additionally, the GAN trained on cleanless data achieves performance comparable to methods trained on clean data. Overall, our approach offers a test-time solution for AMC, delivering state-of-the-art results without requiring modifications to the transmitter or knowledge of the adversary's strategy. This enables real-time AMC during attacks, even in the absence of prior adversary information. The results also highlight the potential of GANs for deep learning-based AMC. Deep learning models excel at segmenting brain tissue in neuroimaging, particularly for identifying Multiple Sclerosis (MS) lesions. However, a single model trained on one hospital's data often struggles when applied to others due to performance degradation. This issue is especially pronounced in MS lesion segmentation, where target datasets are small and vary significantly in imaging protocols. To address this, we introduce a novel continuous training approach that builds upon existing models, requiring less computational power and fewer annotations than training from scratch. We evaluated seven methods—comprising four that extend existing models and three that train from scratch—using data from the Lesion Segmentation Challenge 2022 across three source hospitals and one target hospital. Results demonstrated that continuous training yielded superior performance, particularly when multiple sources were utilized. Specifically, U-Net continuous training outperformed all other continuous training methods, while 3D U-Net trained from scratch achieved the best results overall. Our analysis indicates that 3D U-Net's success from scratch is likely due to the effectiveness of its large pre-training dataset. We also examined the characteristics of the target hospital's data to understand the challenge's root causes. Finally, we discuss the advantages and limitations of our proposed continuous training strategy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepBrainIA/Dual-MS-lesion-seg. Model error is a fundamental and persistent issue in the physics-based analysis of dynamical systems, particularly when interacting with data-driven methods. This paper introduces a framework that integrates model error with machine learning through statistical learning theory, specifically applying it to forecasting tasks in atmospheric science. The proposed approach is general, offering a method to incorporate a priori knowledge about model error into various machine learning algorithms. In our applications, we assume access to observations of dynamical variables from both a reference model and the target model, alongside the recognition that the reference model itself contains model error. We construct a general algorithm that utilizes the reference model to pretrain an initial machine learning algorithm, thereby leveraging prior knowledge to inform learning. Our statistical learning theory analysis demonstrates that this integration leads to a reduction in model error for both linear and nonlinear machines, with performance gains contingent upon the specific algorithm employed. We validate these findings using the simple GCM-1.0 atmospheric general circulation model, showing that the proposed method effectively learns and compensates for model error. Furthermore, we illustrate that this approach can enhance short-term forecast performance when utilizing a high-resolution climate model as the reference model. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for data assimilation and atmospheric modeling. We present high-resolution (0.01–0.1") dust continuum observations of the Dragon IRDC (G033.06+00.31) obtained with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, utilizing wavelengths from 0.8 to 1.3 mm to probe cold dust emission. By analyzing dust emission at 0.8 mm, we identified a filamentary structure extending over 1000 AU, which contains a core with an exceptionally high mass concentration of 100 M$_\odot$ per arcsecond. We reconstructed the three-dimensional structure of this core using dust emission at 1.1 and 1.3 mm, subsequently deriving the density structure via the Jeans equation. Our results indicate that the core's average volume density has increased by approximately an order of magnitude compared to earlier stages of evolution. This growth is driven by both the existing dense core and newly forming protostars, a mechanism that may facilitate the formation of massive stars. Furthermore, we detected a compact source at 0.8 mm with a diameter of roughly 0.005", corresponding to a radius of approximately 20 AU, which may represent a dense gas region within a future massive star. Additionally, we identified a compact dust continuum source at 0.8 mm with a diameter of approximately 0.02", or roughly 80 AU, located near the eastern edge of the filament; this object could be a protostellar envelope associated with a low-mass star. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the theory of massive star formation. These findings are accessible via the public data archive of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. (Abridged)

Primordial black holes (PBHs) are a promising dark matter candidate, requiring specific formation and evolution conditions to exist today. We introduce PopSyCLE PBH, a new code that models the formation and development of PBH populations by integrating the most recent astrophysical data. This tool simulates both the creation of PBHs during inflation and their growth through cosmic evolution, allowing researchers to predict current PBH populations and constrain them against observational data. The code accepts data from external sources, such as cosmological simulations, as input. To demonstrate its utility, we present two sample PopSyCLE output files representing extreme scenarios: one with no gas and another with high gas content. Additionally, we have released a Jupyter notebook on GitHub to facilitate the analysis of PopSyCLE results. This approach enables the simultaneous analysis of multiple population constraints and provides a clear method for identifying which constraints are most effective at limiting the PBH fraction. Our findings indicate that the most stringent limits are applied to the $\mu$ channel, followed by GW170817, Sgr A*, pulsar timing, and LIGO constraints. We have also updated the LIGO constraints, which now extend to approximately $10^{-8}M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, we have made the PopSyCLE PBH code and sample output files available on GitHub. This platform will foster collaboration between theorists and experimenters, allowing for the rapid generation of various PBH populations and facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of the field. We employed Monte Carlo simulations to investigate equilibrium systems featuring hard wedges, constructed from clusters of tangent spheres. Each wedge's geometry is defined by the number of spherical layers along its arms and the number of spheres in its base. The simulations cover various two-dimensional concentrations of these hard wedges, which preclude translational motion. The observed behaviors indicate a phase transition characterized by the emergence of splay nematic order. The count of wedge phases increases with concentration, and the simulated temperature range at a fixed concentration provides insight into their characteristics. At low temperatures, wedge molecules occupy specific sites within the available free space, leading to the formation of free-energy minima that correspond to noncrystalline, nonliquid states with local order. These states are identified as splay nematic states, where the orientation of wedges remains disordered within each of two- or three-membered rings. At high temperatures, the system behaves as a superposition of entropically favored states, with the number of accessible states increasing as wedge concentrations approach their maximum. The simulations demonstrate that the features of these splay nematic phases depend on the wedge's shape. Furthermore, we examined the nature of the phase transitions, finding that they are first-order at high concentrations and become second-order at the concentration where the two splay nematic phases merge. Additionally, we identified splay nematic states with local hexagonal order, and we theoretically derived the critical exponents and scaling laws for this splay nematic state. Finally, we theoretically determined the phase diagram for splay nematic states based on the number of spherical layers in a wedge's arms and the number of spheres in its base. In this diagram, the splay nematic phase is bounded by a second-order line separating it from the nematic phase and a first-order line separating it from the liquid phase. We also identified a splay nematic phase with local cubic order, which exists at high concentrations and temperatures. Overall, the simulation results align with theoretical predictions regarding the nematic phase, coexistence lines, and the critical exponent for the splay nematic phase. Furthermore, the splay nematic phase exhibits characteristics of both nematic and liquid phases, with its nematic nature arising from local hexagonal or cubic order. Theoretically, we demonstrated that the coexistence lines between the splay nematic nematic and splay nematic liquid phases are second-order. Parameter-efficient tuning focuses on adjusting a minimal subset of parameters when adapting pre-trained models for downstream applications. This paper introduces a highly efficient, scalable, and plug-and-play approach that modifies only the embeddings associated with special tokens. In contrast to prior methods, this technique is capable of handling long contexts. Empirical results demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning on tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, and natural language inference with long contexts, while simultaneously reducing computational costs and storage requirements. Furthermore, we show that integrating special tokens during parameter-efficient tuning yields substantial performance gains across various summarization tasks. Finally, the source code is accessible at https://github.com/Myra-Lab/Special-Token-Adaptation. This paper investigates the challenge of assessing element addition to a set, a critical task with significant applications in security, recommendation, and set management. We examine how prior elements in a set influence a user's preference for new additions. To investigate this, we created a new experimental platform, the Interactive Art Gallery, which features two distinct user studies. The first study involves an artist selecting elements for an existing artwork, while the second mirrors this by having a user choose items for a partially completed set. Our findings demonstrate that these two contexts are fundamentally different. Based on these results, we propose a context-aware model for preference ranking. Additionally, we evaluated a range of algorithms across both contexts and found that the optimal algorithms differ between them. Our proposed model, ESDA, surpasses all other algorithms in both contextual and non-contextual non-parametric settings. Finally, we offer insights and directions for future research based on our empirical evaluations.

This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the interconnections among key polymer fluid properties—specifically free volume, viscosity, and entanglement—through the lens of the Vrentas-Doolittle and Doolittle equations. We developed a novel theoretical framework by integrating these frameworks to formulate a new free volume theory. The resulting model successfully explains the thermally activated relationship between free volume and temperature, offering a unified description of free volume in both polymer and pure solvent systems. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrates strong predictive capabilities for free volume in polymer fluids. By combining the Doolittle viscosity model with the newly formulated free volume theory, we developed a free volume/viscosity/entanglement/traction model that simultaneously accounts for the influences of temperature, pressure, and molecular weight on free volume, viscosity, and entanglement. This framework offers a comprehensive description of the thermodynamic and thermodynamic–dynamic interrelations within polymer fluids. The model's predictive accuracy has been validated using polyethylene and poly(methyl methacrylate) as representative examples. Additionally, the thermodynamic–dynamic interrelations identified in this study may serve as a foundation for future research into the viscosity of other glass-forming materials. Finally, the study provides a detailed protocol for selecting the parameters necessary to construct the free volume/traction model. These findings collectively offer a robust framework for understanding the complex thermodynamic and dynamic behaviors of polymer fluids. Our findings contribute to the broader scientific community's understanding of the thermodynamic and thermodynamic–dynamic interrelations in polymer fluids. Recent research indicates that transformer-based language models (LMs) acquire a tacit understanding of negation, a complex linguistic construct. This study investigates whether such models can account for the intricate negation patterns observed in children's language development. We examine how these LM models represent the negation word "not" across various syntactic contexts, comparing their performance against performance-roughly-equivalent performance by non-human models. Transformer LMs display a nuanced grasp of negation development, differing from adult-like processing, where performance on negated sentences is generally poorer than on affirmative ones. This study offers a detailed analysis of how transformer LMs represent "not" within diverse syntactic structures. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive overview of a new, publicly accessible benchmark designed to assess negation capabilities in LM models and conclude by discussing the broader implications of these findings. Finally, we explore the potential applications of using LM models to study negation development and suggest how this approach can inform the design of educational materials and instructional resources. To facilitate reproducibility, we have made all code and data for this study available online. Specifically, we have released a code repository containing a publicly available benchmark for evaluating negation abilities in LM models. This repository includes a detailed tutorial on how to use the benchmark and a step-by-step guide for replicating our findings. These resources are intended to support researchers in the field of education and linguistics who are interested in using LM models to study negation development and in designing materials and resources that can be used to teach negation to children. Attention mechanisms have become a cornerstone of neural machine translation, yet they face challenges during decoding, including delayed alignment with future tokens and the lack of context for newly generated words. This paper introduces a novel attention approach that provides immediate access to future context to resolve these issues. We frame attention as a sequence of sets and propose a lookahead operator that incorporates future context by aligning with future set elements. This operator functions as a single-layer recurrent hidden state, enabling the model to anticipate context for the next word. Additionally, an early exit mechanism allows for the premature termination of recurrent propagation when sufficient context has converged. Experimental results on English-German and French Neural Machine Translation demonstrate that these models achieve performance comparable to or superior to strong baselines, while also reducing the average number of recurrent steps per sentence during decoding. An ablation study further confirms the efficacy of these components in enhancing both translation quality and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we present empirical evidence indicating that integrating this lookahead attention mechanism with Transformer models yields significant performance improvements. Finally, we highlight the mechanism's applicability to other sequence generation tasks, such as language modeling and text summarization. Our code is available at https://github.com/IBM/lookahead-attention. Project page: https://www.research.ibm.com/en-us/blog/lookahead-decoding-neural-machine-translation.

We present an explicit formula for the Kontsevich weights of graphs representing curvature and connection forms within the universal symplectic Chern–Weil form associated with a Poisson connection on a Poisson manifold. This expression is derived as the value of an integral along a specific path in the space of deformations of the symplectic form, with the path's velocity vectors corresponding to particular graph assignments. In certain cases, this formula adheres to distinct identities. Leveraging universal symplectic Chern–Weil forms, we demonstrate that the weights for these special graphs are either zero or can be expressed through the Poisson invariants of any constant rank symplectic manifold. Consequently, the proposed formula enables the calculation of Kontsevich weights for a broad category of graphs, significantly lowering the computational complexity of the standard formula. Additionally, we examine examples where the weights of the universal symplectic Chern–Weil form graphs are independent of the specific symplectic structure, thereby yielding formulas for the corresponding Kontsevich weights. Finally, we investigate extensions of these results to metric Chern–Weil forms. This work was partially supported by grant no. 19-01-00099a from the Russian Foundation for Basic Research. We investigate a class of large-$N$, strongly-coupled interacting conformal field theories (CFTs) that are derived from weakly-coupled CFTs at zero couplings. These theories are defined by the requirement that their free $SU(N)$ gauge theories at zero couplings, which include adjoint chiral multiplets, remain massless throughout the theory's history. We demonstrate that an emergent conformal symmetry emerges when the theory moves off the integrable curve, which is governed by an $R$-charge maximization principle. Utilizing this principle, we show that an $sl(2)$ subalgebra of the theory's symmetry can be constructed. Furthermore, we establish that the thermal entropy of these theories is bounded from below by their entanglement entropy at zero couplings, regardless of the $\lambda/N$ ratio. This finding suggests the existence of an $N$-dependent conformal window within the space of all possible couplings. Finally, we examine the implications of our results for theories involving an odd number of matter fields. Our analysis reveals that theories with $5$ and $7$ matter fields possess conformal fixed points, whereas those with $3$, $9$, $11$, and $13$ matter fields do not. Additionally, we note that the conformal window for $7$ matter fields closes at $l_{\rm max}=10.5N$, which exceeds the value of $l_{\rm max}=9N$ found in theories with $9$ matter fields. These distinctions between theories with $3$, $5$, and $7$ matter fields are attributed to the absence of a non-trivial weak-coupling phase in the latter cases. Cai and Kou (2012) proposed a framework for Asian option pricing within Markov models and applied it to CEV processes. However, this paper demonstrates that their results contain inconsistencies that lead to incorrect formulas and numerical inaccuracies. We provide a detailed explanation of these errors and present a corrected approach that yields more precise price estimates. Additionally, we extend these findings to general diffusion processes. Specifically, we detail a method to enhance the accuracy of their triangular spline approximation and outline a strategy to achieve any prescribed level of approximation error. Finally, we address a gap in their analysis by deriving a closed-form solution for Asian option pricing in a Merton jump-diffusion model. Throughout this work, we also derive exact formulas for the joint Laplace transform of Asian option payoffs and asset prices involving Brownian motion, Bessel processes, and gamma processes. These expressions are shown to satisfy specific partial differential equations that are solved using the separation of variables technique. To demonstrate the practical utility of our methodology, we present several further examples. Finally, our results yield exact formulas for the first passage time density of a CEV process with respect to a power function and for the occupation time density of a CEV process with respect to a power circuit. In each instance, the solution is expressed as a series expansion that converges rapidly. We provide numerical evidence confirming the validity of these findings. Our approach is also applicable to other one-dimensional Markov processes. Notably, the series expansions derived here exhibit the same asymptotic behavior as those for the first and second eigenfunctions of the Sturm-Liouville problem. We further show that the truncated series expansions for the first and second eigenfunctions, obtained via the separation of variables method, provide highly accurate approximations even with a very small number of terms. These results are consistent with those obtained using the asymptotic expansion method. Our findings also offer insight into the asymptotic behavior of the Gram determinant. To our knowledge, this represents the first time the root distribution of the Gram determinant has been analyzed in this manner. Our results also provide insight into the behavior of the first passage time density of a CEV process at the critical value $\nu=1/2$. Finally, we demonstrate that the series expansions for the first passage time density of a CEV process converge rapidly, in line with our earlier findings regarding the first and second eigenfunctions of the Sturm-Liouville problem. The origin of high-energy gamma rays in our universe remains a major unsolved mystery in astrophysics. Recent data from Fermi-LAT and MAGIC/HESS have prompted several investigations into whether extragalactic radio galaxies or clusters generate these rays. This study examines the gamma-ray flux from radio and non-radio clusters of galaxies (NGC) to determine if they can account for the observed diffuse gamma-ray background. Our analysis reveals that both radio and non-radio NGC emit gamma rays in the 100 MeV to 10 TeV range, with a flux density of $10^{-9}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ TeV$^{-1}$ at 100 MeV, peaking at 10 TeV, and declining to $10^{-11}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ TeV$^{-1}$ at 10 TeV. We conclude that NGC flux is primarily driven by jets in radio clusters and by the interaction of galaxy members' jets with the intracluster medium in non-radio clusters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NGC radiation can significantly contribute to the observed gamma-ray background. Future observations of NGC radiation are essential for a more comprehensive understanding of this enigmatic background. This research is based on the thesis by A. A. We demonstrate that the competition among electron-phonon, phonon-phonon, and Jahn-Teller interactions induces a strong attraction between long-lived charge and spin excitations at low energies in one-dimensional cuprates. This discovery offers a unified explanation for the diverse experimental observations regarding their excitation spectrum. The proposed mechanism is general and holds significant potential for unitary fermion-boson systems. Specifically, within one-dimensional high-temperature superconducting cuprates, these interactions lead to the formation of bound electron-hole pairs (phonon-polarons) and excitons at low energies. Consequently, superconductivity emerges via the pairing of these composite electrons, while an attractive phonon-mediated long-range force generates a Thomas-Fermi-like spin screening. These phenomena collectively account for the key phenomenological features of cuprates, including the universal $2\hbar\omega_{\rm LO}$ gap in photoemission spectra, the universal $T$-linear resistivity, the universal $I$-linear resistivity under high electric fields, and the universal current-voltage characteristics in field-emission microscopy. Furthermore, the universal $q^{-4}$ screening of the Coulomb interaction and the universal $q^{-2}$ screening of the exchange interaction represent two critical ingredients for the long-standing puzzle of the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates. Finally, the proposed mechanism may also explain the universal low-energy phonon spectral features observed in cuprates. This work introduces many-body physics beyond the conventional framework of simple phonon-mediated electron-phonon attraction. Specifically, it elucidates how the competition between electron-phonon and phonon-phonon-polaron interactions generates attractive long-range forces between fermionic and bosonic excitations. This leads to the formation of polarons and composite particles, thereby unifying various perspectives on phonon-mediated interactions in cuprates and advancing our understanding of their low-energy properties. Additionally, the proposed mechanism may also be applicable to other systems. For instance, it may explain the recent observation of a universal $2\Delta$ gap in phonon-polaron spectroscopy of two-dimensional cuprates and aid in interpreting recent findings on phonon-mediated interactions in doped two-dimensional and three-dimensional topological insulators. This discovery is expected to stimulate further research into low-energy properties of cuprates and advance the field of strong electron-phonon coupling. Finally, our theoretical predictions regarding universal low-energy phonon spectral features in cuprates can be tested through high-resolution inelastic neutron scattering

This paper offers a detailed examination of High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models, covering their primary assumptions and rationales, key theoretical results, and insights through elementary examples. A specific focus is placed on the significance of singular (or low-rank) factor models, which constitute the standard framework in current macroeconomic literature. Rather than providing an exhaustive historical survey, we prioritize an analysis of fundamental modeling and theoretical issues, with particular attention to inference in Singular DYNFAMs where both the time series dimension $p$ and sample size $T$ approach infinity. Additionally, we outline future research directions, emphasizing the need to relax restrictive assumptions regarding cross-sectional cross-dependence structures, as well as to resolve emerging challenges involving non-stationarity and time-varying rank. Our perspective integrates both micro-level microeconomic foundations and macro-level large-sample asymptotics.

Introduction Recently, the equilibrium problem has garnered significant attention within the mathematical community. First formulated by Blum and others, it has served as a unifying framework for various fundamental issues in mathematics, economics, and engineering. Originally introduced in 1994 by Blum and others [1], it has since become a foundational tool in game theory, optimization, and operations research. The framework involves n players, where each player's strategy is represented by an element from a nonempty set C. For any combination of strategies (x1, x2, ..., xn) ∈ C^n, the interactions among players are modeled by a function J : C^n → (-∞, ∞]. Specifically, for a player i, the function represents the cost incurred by i given the collective strategy profile (x1, ..., xn). An equilibrium point is a strategy configuration (x1, ..., xn) ∈ C^n such that no individual player can reduce their cost by unilaterally changing their strategy. This concept extends the traditional notion of a fixed point. In this work, we explore the relationship between equilibrium problems and the fixed points of nonlinear mappings. We establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the equilibrium problem under the condition that the underlying function J is both fixed-point-to-unique and nonexpansive. Additionally, we construct iterative processes to approximate these solutions and demonstrate their convergence. Our findings extend and complement earlier research by Xu [10], Takahashi and Takahashi [9], and Xu and Yao [11]. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly advanced reversible (lossless) steganography, yet current deep steganographic models often struggle with an overly optimistic estimation of their capacity. This leads to the inefficient allocation of bits for hiding data, resulting in suboptimal spatial bitrate allocation. To address this, we introduce a novel, lossless steganographic framework that integrates Bayesian neural networks with arithmetic coding. We investigate the three-dimensional (3D) dynamics of convective turbulence within a rotating, electrically conducting fluid using a truncated Fourier spectral direct numerical simulation global convective dynamo model. Our results reveal a rich spectrum of turbulent effects that are crucial for the global convective dynamo. Specifically, the dynamo operates only when the Rayleigh number is sufficiently high to trigger superadiabatic convection, generating significant kinetic energy and intense turbulent motions. These motions exhibit strong nonlocality in Fourier space and high nonlinearity in physical space, thereby amplifying smaller-scale magnetic field components across a broad range of scales. This leads to a magnetic field with a helical structure and significant small-scale contributions, characteristics typical of astrophysical objects. Consequently, we conclude that turbulent effects must be fully incorporated into global convective dynamo theories and simulations. Furthermore, our analysis of the critical Rayleigh number aligns with observations from numerical simulations and can be extended to astrophysical contexts by incorporating additional constraints, such as finite boundary layers and rotation rates. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings for dynamo simulations in Cartesian geometry, which are frequently employed in astrophysics as a preliminary test for dynamo action. In this configuration, we observe that locality in Fourier space is more pronounced, and turbulent effects are significantly weaker compared to simulations utilizing spherical geometry. This suggests that utilizing spherical geometry may be essential for accurately reproducing astrophysical phenomena. We present ALMA observations of a molecular outflow in the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 4945, utilizing a 1.5" x 1.5" field of view at a spatial resolution of 0.15". The data reveal a large-scale outflow extending at least 1.5 kpc from the galactic center, characterized by a molecular mass of 10^5 solar masses and a total momentum of 10^30 N s. The outflow exhibits a filamentary structure aligned with the galaxy's major axis, displaying a symmetric, butterfly-like morphology. This symmetry indicates that the outflow originates from a central region roughly 0.5 kpc across. The observed momentum aligns with the critical value of 10^30 N s derived from star formation models. We propose that a central starburst, driven by a supermassive black hole mass of 10^7 solar masses, is the source of this outflow. Our findings support the conclusion that the outflow is rooted in the central starburst region, which is comparable in size to the supermassive black hole's influence radius. Consequently, the outflow is likely driven by a combination of massive star clusters and the central supermassive black hole. This research is part of the NGC 4945 Key Project. This study introduces a family of variable stepsize semi-explicit singly-multiplicity symplectic methods (SDIMSIMs) for second-order ordinary differential equations. The approach is developed from a partitioned second-order difference scheme and adheres to the Discrete Lagrange's Theorem. Specifically, for any positive vector $(s_1, \dots, s_{m+1})$ where $m \geq 1$, we construct an $O(h^2)$ method. We establish the order conditions, demonstrate hyperbolic stability, and introduce a variant that achieves a higher order truncation error. This version corresponds to the difference of a higher-order partitioned scheme and, under certain conditions, satisfies extended order conditions. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical findings. The proposed methods are direct, straightforward to implement, and require no additional function evaluations. Furthermore, they exhibit superior performance compared to existing variable stepsize symplectic methods. Notably, unlike many current methods that rely on linear stepsize adjustments, our approach remains valid for arbitrary positive stepsize variations. Finally, the variable stepsize methods derived from difference schemes are shown to be variational, representing the Euler–Lagrange equations of a discrete variational problem. This contrasts with variational splitting methods, which are variational only up to an error term dependent on the stepsize. Consequently, difference schemes offer an alternative means to construct symplectic methods. Additionally, this work marks the first instance of applying difference schemes in the field of mechanics. Portfolio managers frequently evaluate their performance against a benchmark, typically defined as total return minus the benchmark return minus transaction costs. This relative return is closely tied to the hyperbolic growth function, which features an asymptotic growth rate. Because the hyperbolic growth function is merely a scaled and shifted version of the standard constant relative risk aversion (CRRA) power utility, it lacks the necessary mathematical properties to serve as a utility function within the stochastic maximum principle (SMP) framework developed by Fleming and Souganidis. To address this limitation, we introduce a new type of power utility termed "hyperbolic growth type utility." This novel utility incorporates both absolute and relative wealth, offering the necessary properties to be effectively utilized in the SMP framework for solving optimization problems. We apply this concept to establish verification theorems within the Fleming-Souganidis framework and demonstrate its application to portfolio optimization using the relative growth function. In this context, the optimal investment strategy is derived via the Fleming-Souganidis framework. Our methodology offers two primary advantages: first, it yields an explicit value function and investment strategy through the use of algebraic Riccati equations; second, it ensures the solution remains meaningful by utilizing the SMP approach, which imposes fewer constraints than traditional dynamic programming methods. Furthermore, we validate these theoretical findings through numerical examples. This approach offers the flexibility to define the relative growth function based on the portfolio manager's specific benchmark and to flexibly adjust the degree of relative risk aversion. Dwarf galaxies are the most abundant type of galaxy in the universe, yet our understanding of their interstellar medium (ISM) remains limited. This review examines the physical and chemical characteristics of the ISM in these dwarfs, with a specific focus on recent findings derived from high-resolution observations. We analyze the relationship between ISM properties and factors such as galactic mass, star formation history, and environmental context. Additionally, we explore the connection between a galaxy's ISM and its observable emission lines, while also addressing the challenges posed by ISM properties to the formation of cosmic structures. Finally, we outline current knowledge gaps and propose future research directions aimed at clarifying the role of ISM in galaxy evolution. This review is intended to highlight the significance of studying galactic environments with ISM properties that differ from those of the Sun's neighborhood. The instability of fermionic quasiparticles within Landau's Fermi-liquid framework is explored, specifically the scenario where quasiparticle-hole excitations condense. It is demonstrated that if the energy required to create quasiparticles and the energy for creating a quasiparticle-hole pair are both negative, these two distinct condensation modes can overlap, resulting in an even more exotic state. In this regime, quasiparticles themselves condense, leading to an unusual density matrix where the weight of the single-particle ground state exceeds one. The mechanism driving this phenomenon is a positive feedback loop, where the interaction between the system and local bosons, mediated by quasiparticles, is sufficiently strong. This process, termed the "rare collapse," draws a parallel to "spontaneous preamplification" observed in "stimulated emission depletion" (STED) microscopy. Furthermore, the characteristics of this collapse are linked to "borrowing" concepts from "enhanced emission" scenarios, where quasiparticle lifetimes appear to diverge. This synthesis of ideas generates a novel class of quantum phases, which are suggested to be accessible through STED-like quench dynamics. Finally, the article examines related issues concerning quasiparticle residues and the nature of the ground state when quasiparticle energy becomes negative. These themes connect to established paradoxes, such as the "zero gap problem" and "zero density of states" issues, which are linked to "quasiparticle resurrection" and "quasiparticle revival" phenomena, respectively. Additionally, the relationship between the rare collapse and "quarky matter" is analyzed, alongside the emergence of a new state known as "ghost matter," where ghost states dominate over zero-energy states in the density matrix. Finally, the article addresses the definition of the density matrix in interacting systems, proposing a resolution to the "nonlocality problem" via the concept of "quasi-orthogonality." These concepts collectively offer a fresh perspective on the density matrix within interacting quantum systems. (This research was conducted in collaboration with J. M. P. Breidbach, J. M. Peters, and J. Schmiedmayer.)

Golan and Nagnibeda recently introduced the braided-Thompson groups B_m, n as a broad extension of both Thompson's groups F and T, positioning them as natural candidates for such structures within braided monoidal categories. This paper investigates the divergence characteristics of these groups when viewed as action groups. Our primary finding is that B_m, n exhibits linear divergence, a result that complements the recently established divergence properties of the generalised Thompson groups V_m. Specifically, we demonstrate that the divergence of B_m, n is independent of the categorical generator d and relies solely on the product mn. Additionally, in an appendix, we provide an alternative proof of the known result stating that the divergence of V_m is V_m-linear. Finally, we outline conditions under which the divergence of B_m, n remains invariant under the braiding action. To facilitate these investigations, we also develop a novel normal form for elements of B_m, n. Furthermore, to address the problem of divergence, we construct an embedding of B_m, n into the shift space $\Sigma_{\mathbb{Z}}$. This construction offers an alternative proof of the fact that all elements of B_m, n possess finite braided-word length. These findings extend to a wider class of groups known as 'tangled braid groups,' which were recently formulated by the second author. Our results include the calculation of their divergence and the provision of explicit embeddings into $\Sigma_{\mathbb{Z}}$. This resolves an open question posed by Clark and Martelli regarding the existence of such embeddings for the tangled braid groups. Finally, our work contributes to the emerging field of braided geometric group theory by generating several new conjectures and directions for future research. Notably, we propose a novel application of the fundamental group of a braided category to the study of geometric divergence. This methodology offers a fresh perspective on established problems, such as the divergence of the braid group B_n, and suggests a natural extension to the divergences of the tangled braid groups T_m. We begin the experiment using an established public dataset, demonstrating how to efficiently adapt the full pipeline with just three lines of code. We evaluate the outcomes against an "all defaults" baseline, showing that fine-tuning the generation component alone offers no benefits over not fine-tuning at all. Subsequently, we explore the benefits of jointly fine-tuning both the retriever and the generator, which yields a 3.5-point enhancement in Recall@20 compared to the baseline. Finally, we examine the impact of varying fine-tuning configurations, data augmentations, metrics, and evaluation methods. Through this process, we validate the efficacy of jointly fine-tuning the retriever and generator while also addressing several challenges inherent in this approach. Our source code is accessible at: https://github.com/firstnorder/fine-tune-entire-rag-architecture. This work aims to encourage researchers to: 1) explore the potential of jointly fine-tuning retrievers and generators within a RAG framework, and 2) adopt a configuration where fine-tuning is applied to the entire architecture. Additionally, we provide a quick-start guide for replicating our experiment in under five minutes. Our analysis indicates that jointly fine-tuning the retriever and generator is particularly advantageous for small to medium-sized datasets. However, we also explore a configuration involving the pre-training of a large language model (LLM) from scratch using our data, which achieved notable improvements on our specific dataset. This paper determines the asymptotic behavior of recurrence coefficients for polynomials orthogonal against a logarithmic weight that has nonnegative moments. Our findings extend and complement a recent theorem by J. S. Kim and J. Shu, which was limited to specific cases. Furthermore, we illustrate how our derived formulas produce distinct asymptotic expressions. In addition to the primary result, we establish several supplementary theorems and provide various alternative proofs for existing literature results. These supplementary results and the other derivations can offer valuable insights and potentially assist in proving other related results. Specifically, Section 2 examines the case where the measures are symmetric and the support of the weights is independent of the index. In this scenario, we establish a complete solution for the asymptotics of the corresponding orthogonal polynomials. Section 3 is dedicated to the general case, where we analyze the asymptotic behavior of the recurrence coefficients. We identify conditions on the weights that ensure the limits of the recurrence coefficients exist and determine the resulting weights. Finally, Section 4 presents an application to a problem originally posed by J. Shu. Specifically, we demonstrate that the recurrence coefficients for the corresponding orthogonal polynomials exhibit a specific type of asymptotic behavior. In our proof, we utilize a criterion that identifies when a sequence of polynomials is orthogonal with respect to a logarithmic weight. This criterion relies on an inequality involving the norms of the polynomials, a concept that has been extensively studied. We believe this inequality will be useful in future research. Additionally, we provide a criterion for the asymptotic behavior of the recurrence coefficients that is less restrictive than the one currently available in the literature. This criterion is applied in the final section of the paper. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of such an application. Finally, the paper includes an appendix containing the statement and proof of an inequality that is distinct from the one currently found in the literature. This inequality is required to prove one of the theorems presented in this work. We also provide an alternative proof for this inequality, which offers a different perspective. We believe this alternative proof may be valuable for future research. This work is dedicated to the memory of our mentor, Professor Joseph Shu. We are deeply grateful for his unwavering support, guidance, and encouragement throughout our academic careers. His profound insights, dedication to research, and commitment to teaching have left an indelible mark on all of us. We are truly honored to have had the privilege of learning from him. His legacy will continue to inspire us for years to come.

This study evaluates the feasibility of recruiting high-quality annotators for human evaluation tasks on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a platform typically associated with lower quality. Our findings indicate that finding qualified annotators is extremely difficult and that their performance does not improve significantly with additional practice. We demonstrate that pre-screening applicants is essential to minimize waste on unqualified users, while post-screening is ineffective because their low performance persists even after multiple opportunities to retry. Furthermore, we show that requiring annotators to summarize a sample task before accepting other requests is the only effective strategy for gauging task performance. Finally, we provide a practical guide for researchers aiming to recruit high-quality workers for summarization tasks on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Code is available at https://github.com/salesforce/mturk-quality.

We establish that flavour-changing neutral currents (FCNCs) at the electroweak scale involving the top quark and any leptonic or quark flavour $f$ are naturally constrained by $\vert \lambda^{f}_{\rm EW}\vert\lesssim 10^{-3}$, where $\lambda^{f}_{\rm EW}$ represents the non-universal lepton flavour violation parameter in the electroweak sector. This finding is derived from the necessary and sufficient conditions for flavour within the fermion sector, which we have recently formulated as a set of Hermitian matrices. Furthermore, we explore the unique characteristics of top FCNCs and identify opportunities to investigate them through both current and upcoming high-energy colliders. Finally, we examine the connection between top FCNCs and dark matter. In this context, we derive that $\vert \lambda^{f}_{\rm EW}\vert\lesssim 10^{-3}$ arises from dark matter considerations when its mass is below the electroweak scale, owing to the flavour conservation inherent in the fermion sector. Conversely, for dark matter masses exceeding the electroweak scale, we observe that $\vert \lambda^{f}_{\rm EW}\vert\lesssim 1$ due to the flavour conservation in the dark matter sector. Consequently, we argue that top FCNCs are naturally suppressed in models that simultaneously address the dark matter problem and the flavour puzzle. In our conclusion, we argue that the mechanism responsible for electroweak symmetry breaking must be non-linear to ensure the natural suppression of top FCNCs. Finally, we outline the potential for new physics models to resolve both the dark matter and flavour issues simultaneously, while also detailing the requirements necessary to experimentally verify such a scenario. This study examines hybrid directed random networks formed by combining the preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms. The resulting models generate a scale-free degree distribution that decays as a power law, where the exponents can be calculated in closed form based on the ratios of attachment rates. Furthermore, the paper explores how these exponents are influenced by various network parameters, including initial network size, initial connectivity, and the proportions of in-links versus out-links. Finally, we analyze how these factors affect the scale-free characteristics of the networks. Additionally, we investigate whether hybrid networks remain scale-free when nodes are added sequentially, and we evaluate their robustness, mobility, and efficiency. Our findings indicate that while the scale-free property is preserved in these networks, both mobility and efficiency deteriorate as the ratio of in-degrees to out-degrees increases. We also introduce a specific model for comparing betweenness centrality scores of source and target nodes in individual links, demonstrating that this model remains effective regardless of the in-degree to out-degree ratio. Finally, we numerically verify our analytical results regarding the average path length of the network. These results hold true for networks constructed via both sequential and parallel growth processes. Overall, the paper concludes that the proposed hybrid network models are both realistic and effective. Finally, all code required to replicate the numerical results is made available in an open repository. In modern wireless environments, identifying co-channel interference is essential for ensuring robust and reliable communications. This study introduces a deep learning framework utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to classify interfering signals in wireless spectra. The proposed model is trained to generate interference maps across the spectrum, pinpointing the occupied frequency bands of each signal. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves high classification accuracy on both simulated and real-world data. Furthermore, the study confirms the model's ability to learn from training data with limited spectral dimensions and validates its effectiveness in classifying interfering signals on spectra with significantly higher dimensionalities. This research represents the first application of deep learning to wireless interference identification. The Python implementation of the proposed model is available at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/wireless-interference-deep-learning}. This study examines the corresponding Klein-Gordon equations for a scalar particle within the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime, which represents a generalization of the Godel universe incorporating a cosmological constant, a scalar field, and a spacelike screw-singularity characteristic of cosmic strings. The resulting equations are solved to determine the energy-vorticity and charge-vorticity correlations. The analysis demonstrates that the presence of a spacelike dislocation in the cosmic string metric influences these correlations, a factor that should be accounted for in cosmological research. These findings are closely related to the gravitational energy problem. Additionally, the paper investigates the geodesics of timelike particles in this spacetime, deriving the effective potential and identifying the conditions under which bound orbits can exist. It is concluded that both the vorticity and the cosmic string dislocation affect the stability of these bound orbits. Finally, the paper offers a novel contribution by presenting the first solution to the Klein-Gordon equation within a spacetime featuring a spacelike screw-singularity. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11405047). Keywords: Klein-Gordon equation; Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime; Geodesics; Dislocation; Cosmic string.

Countable locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair consisting of a Steinitz number and a real number that is at least 1. This result serves as an analogue to the theorems established by J. Dixmier and A. A. Baranov. Furthermore, the proof yields two additional theorems: one stating that an injective, locally standard Boolean $\sigma$-algebra over a complete, locally convex vector space admits a natural structure of a convex vector space, and another explaining that the space of measurable functions defined on a $\sigma$-algebra of a set is isomorphic to the collection of all convex combinations of functions selected from the algebra. Finally, the discussion examines various dimensions and densities associated with these measure algebras.

**Keywords:** dimension, density, Boole-$\sigma$ algebra, vector lattice, vector space, convex combination, convex closed subset, Steinitz number.

Generalized parton distributions (GPDs) characterize the interplay between a nucleon's quark momentum fractionations and transverse spatial localizations, offering a comprehensive view of its internal structure. Since extracting these GPDs requires separating the Dirac ($f_1$) and magnetic moment ($f_2$) GPDs, it is essential to measure the proton polarization flip term $f_2$. This study investigates the beam hand-shaking asymmetry in Deep Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS) as a novel observable sensitive to $f_2$. We demonstrate that, at HERA kinematics, this method is highly effective for distinguishing the $f_2$ contribution. Furthermore, we analyze the observables at the JLab 12 GeV electron accelerator, where we show that combining longitudinal and transverse (horizontal) beam asymmetries offers a significant advantage in separating $f_1$ and $f_2$. Finally, we examine the horizontal spin asymmetry at the Electron-Ion Collider, demonstrating its high sensitivity to the $f_2$ GPD. Our findings indicate that utilizing polarization flip in DVCS across various facilities provides a valuable tool for constraining the proton's magnetic moment GPD $f_2$. This work serves as a proof of principle, with future papers detailing the strategies necessary to observe these quantities. We conclude that incorporating polarization-flip DVCS observables into a global fit will substantially enhance the constraints on the magnetic moment components of the GPDs. Although Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have advanced significantly, they cannot yet address every challenge independently. Consequently, various hybrid models have emerged, integrating advanced algorithms with other technologies to enhance performance. This paper extends the concept of Augmented Learning to introduce a framework for Augmented AI (Augmented AI). This new framework is expected to foster further algorithmic development and enhance existing AI and ML capabilities. The Augmented AI framework comprises four components: Augmented Data, Augmented Algorithms, Augmented Problems, and Augmented Solutions. This work elaborates on each component and explores their interrelationships. To illustrate these concepts, specific examples are provided for Augmented Data, Augmented Algorithms, Augmented Problems, and Augmented Solutions. Ultimately, the goal is to explore how Augmented AI can improve current AI and ML systems and inspire novel augmented ideas. The paper is structured into two parts: the first details the conceptual framework, while the second examines practical applications and potential research directions. Additionally, the authors' blog offers a companion to this work, available at https://medium.com/@josephgong/a-i-augmented-conceptual-framework-101077770077. We examine the thermal properties of a Bose-Hubbard model incorporating Rashba spin-orbit coupling, beginning with a strong coupling mean-field (TFC) analysis. In the absence of correlations, we demonstrate that spin-orbit coupling causes a thermal transition from a uniform superfluid to a density-wave state within the Mott-insulator regime at low densities and low temperatures. This transition is driven by the competition between interaction energy and the zero-point energy of phonons. Furthermore, we show that this phenomenon can be accurately described by the Bose gas in the mean-field limit, as it occurs in the weakly correlated regime. Finally, we investigate the related features of the spin-orbit-coupled Bose gas situated in the Mott-insulator regime. In this context, correlation effects are significant, and we find that thermal transitions in the Mott regime are far more complex than in the weakly correlated Bose gas. Specifically, multiple transitions can occur, including a thermal transition from a Mott state to a density-wave state, which is closely linked to the spin-orbit coupling. Additionally, we observe that the width of the Mott plateau diminishes as spin-orbit coupling increases, leading to a thermal transition from a Mott state to a density-wave state in the spin-orbit-coupled system at specific temperatures and temperatures. These predictions regarding the complex thermal behavior of the spin-orbit-coupled Bose gas in the Mott regime can be readily validated through cold-atom experiments. Finally, we demonstrate that these predictions can be achieved by utilizing ultracold $^{87}$Rb atoms trapped in an optical lattice. By employing radio-frequency dressing techniques, the ground state of the $^{87}$Rb atom can be prepared in a superposition of two hyperfine states, thereby simulating spin-orbit coupling. This approach offers a promising avenue for exploring the complex thermal behavior of spin-orbit-coupled Bose gases in the Mott regime. Moreover, this research holds significant potential for advancing the field of quantum simulation. Specifically, it may pave the way for investigating the complex thermal behavior of spin-orbit-coupled Bose gases in the strongly correlated regime, a topic that has received limited attention in previous studies. This could provide valuable insights into the complex thermal behavior of spin-orbit-coupled Bose gases in the strongly correlated regime, thereby deepening our understanding of the Bose metal phase. Realizing graphs through finite abelian groups involves using group elements as vertices and defining a specific adjacency function, known a priori, within the group to establish edges. In 2018, Grolmusz demonstrated the existence of a non-planar group graph with a trivial generating set (comprising only short paths) that cannot be transformed into any other such graph via edge degenerations, thereby proving that the order of finite abelian groups realizing graphs is unbounded. This brief note aims to enhance Grolmusz's proof by clarifying its methodology, demonstrating its applicability to broader graphs (specifically Hamiltonian graphs), and providing a more comprehensive overview of the realization problem using groups. Furthermore, we present a more concise argument confirming that the order of groups is indeed unbounded. Finally, we illustrate that even when restricting generating sets to short paths, the order remains unbounded for certain classes of non-Hamiltonian graphs. Additionally, we establish that for any class of group graphs formed by generating sets comprising at most $k$ short paths, there exists a finite bound on the orders of the groups that can realize these graphs. Our findings also clarify the methodology behind recent computational results by various groups of authors. By leveraging the behavior of group realizations, we demonstrate the existence of non-planar group graphs with generating sets of seven short paths that, unlike those with four short generators, cannot realize any group of order less than $2^{15}$. This significantly enhances the effectiveness of using group realizations to investigate planar graphs. Overall, our results provide a more complete understanding of the realization problem's nature and the extent to which abelian groups can be utilized to address graph-theoretic questions. Finally, we offer a unified approach to understanding the methodology behind many recent computational results. By applying our techniques, we show that the methodology's effectiveness is inherently limited, as the specific graphs and groups involved do not yield any new insights. However, our results also confirm that these computational contributions are valuable, as they provide a deeper understanding of the realization problem and its nature. Specifically, our findings suggest that the choice of generating sets and the resulting group structures are crucial in determining whether a graph can be realized within a group. Furthermore, our results indicate that the computational complexity of realizing graphs within groups is significantly higher than previously thought, as the number of possible group structures and their corresponding properties play a critical role. In conclusion, our findings provide a more comprehensive understanding of the group-based realization problem and its potential applications in graph theory. Specifically

A wide range of kernel functions has been created to address the diverse needs of Gaussian Process (GP) models. However, selecting the most suitable kernel for a specific application can be difficult. To overcome this, we introduce a method to evolve Gaussian Process kernels derived from elementary mathematical expressions, enabling the creation of data-driven, interpretable kernels tailored to new tasks. This approach is grounded in Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence-based evolution, which tracks the transformation required to align one probability distribution with another. Our methodology involves sampling the space of possible kernels using an existing set and applying evolutionary operators to generate new kernels. A primary challenge in designing muon collider detectors is managing beam-induced background, which arises from off-beam interactions of beam muons with residual gas in the aperture space. These interactions generate secondary particles that reach the beam pipe and detector, potentially obscuring signals from beam-beau collisions. Since this background scales with the square of the residual gas density, mitigation strategies must focus on achieving ultra-high vacuum conditions, particularly in long beam-to-drift regions. This paper outlines various approaches to reduce beam-induced background through multiple methods, demonstrating that feasible solutions can be achieved by implementing high-temperature components and achieving high-impedance levels. Additionally, we present a background composition study to support detector simulations and provide a preliminary assessment of the detector's physics reach. Finally, we propose a detailed time schedule for the detector R&D phase. In summary, the development of a feasible detector is highly dependent on advances in cryogenic, vacuum, and other support technologies. Consequently, a parallel and integrated research and development effort is essential to achieve the first beam-beau collision. We recommend that a technology R&D task force be established to coordinate these activities and ensure that no time is lost during the path toward building the collider. This proposal aims to serve as a starting point for discussions regarding beam-induced background reduction and to initiate the necessary technology R&D work. We hope this approach will help avoid delays in collider construction and that these efforts will be included in the final proposal. A detailed discussion of these proposals can be found in our recent white paper, which is available in arXiv:2202.01936. We are available to discuss this topic further. Thank you.

We introduce Spartan, a framework for training sparse neural networks with a fixed sparsity target. Spartan integrates two differentiable sparsity techniques: the soft attention mask method and $q$-norm regularization. By applying optimal transport theory, we calculate the optimal coupling between these two approaches, enabling the optimal fusion of their gradients to create a hybrid method. We evaluate the Spartan framework across various $q$-norm values to demonstrate its versatility. Experimental results show that Spartan surpasses current state-of-the-art pre-trained sparse models. Additionally, we extend the framework to support a dynamic sparsity target, inspired by channel pruning methods. This capability streamlines sparsity training for channel pruning and facilitates a smooth transition from over-parameterized networks to sparse architectures. We provide comprehensive experiments covering both pre-training and fine-tuning scenarios. In both cases, Spartan achieves superior performance compared to existing sparsity techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Spartan significantly enhances fine-tuning sparsity, offering greater channel efficiency and superior feature extraction compared to other pruning methods. We also show that Spartan improves the robustness of model sparsity, ensuring a more stable transition from dense to sparse models. Finally, we illustrate that Spartan can be applied to various sparsity techniques, such as GradNorm, to achieve better results. The conventional understanding of Bose-Einstein condensation involves a macroscopic population of the ground state within a Bose gas of non-conserved particle number. In contrast, Bose condensation in a gas with conserved particle number arises when the population of low-momentum states becomes significant due to the quantization of the gas, causing these states to behave as if they possess an effective Pauli blocking. We demonstrate that even at temperatures far above the critical transition point, a weakly interacting Bose gas exhibits non-trivial modifications to its momentum distribution. This effect stems from a strong coupling between low and high momenta driven by strong fluctuations in the density field. Consequently, this phenomenon represents a novel form of emergent Pauli blocking in a Bose gas. Additionally, we show that within the framework of the Gross-Pitaevskii mean-field theory, this emergent Pauli blocking can be qualitatively reproduced. Furthermore, we provide a discussion of this effect in other weakly interacting quantum gases, including those with Fermi statistics. Finally, we explore applications of this discovery to recent experiments on Bose-molecular gases, offering a novel explanation for observations that were previously considered enigmatic. These findings underscore the critical role of weak interactions in shaping the momentum distribution of a Bose gas. While the established role of interactions is primarily in shifting and reshaping the broad component of the distribution, we demonstrate that they can also exert a profound influence on the narrow, quantum-dominated peak. This influence is mediated through a mechanism that is absent in the non-interacting case. Specifically, we show that weak interactions can enhance the broadening of low-momentum states, thereby increasing the effective Pauli blocking. This represents a new and profound insight into the behavior of weakly interacting Bose gases. Specifically, we show that weak interactions can significantly suppress thermal fluctuations at the lowest momenta, even though these effects are typically considered negligible. This finding is particularly relevant to recent experiments that have reported such phenomena. Our results provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the momentum distribution of weakly interacting Bose gases, with broad implications for a wide range of physical systems. By highlighting the existence of weakly interacting Bose gases with non-Gaussian momentum distributions, our findings open up new avenues for future research and technological applications. For instance, our results may have implications for the development of new atom interferometers and other quantum sensors that rely on the precise control of atomic momentum distributions. Furthermore, our findings may shed light on fundamental questions regarding the nature of quantum matter and the emergence of new phases of matter in weakly interacting Bose gases

Test code is frequently overlooked, leading to the gradual accumulation of test debt. This debt hinders tests from being utilized as a reliable guide for software evolution. This study investigates developers' perceptions regarding the severity of test smells, a factor that has previously been ignored in research. Through a survey of 104 developers, we found that test smells significantly impact test quality. Furthermore, the severity of these smells varies based on whether they are detected in tests for well-maintained or poorly maintained code. Based on these findings, we offer recommendations for future research. The survey data and our conclusions are available for review.

Keywords: Test Smells, Quality of Software Testing, Severity, Developers' Perception, Empirical Study.

This paper investigates and discusses a novel integro-differential sweeping process featuring a nonconvex moving set. Furthermore, we apply our findings to a control problem involving nonconvex moving target constraints and demonstrate that the resulting Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation aligns with an existing $\phi$-variational inequality involving the $\delta$-subdifferential. Finally, we provide an application to a two-phase flow model that incorporates a novel type of viscosity regularization.
