We introduce {\tt KKMCee} 6.0, a Monte Carlo event generator designed for electron-positron annihilation into lepton and quark pairs, incorporating the effects of external magnetic fields. Building upon the analytical framework of our prior publication [arXiv:1906.00272], this updated version features a comprehensive implementation of initial and final state radiation, as well as vacuum polarization. The radiation emission calculations rely on the FFNLO approach, which allows for the inclusion of structured targets such as atoms, ions, and nuclei. To facilitate various physics analyses, we provide an extensive suite of observables, including cross sections, angular distributions, energy and momentum spectra, polarization, and the magnetic dipole moment of the final state. Additionally, the tool supports the study of the radiative cross section as a function of the photon virtuality. We outline several application scenarios, including new physics searches at colliders like ILC, CLIC, and FCC-ee, alongside investigations into QED in strong fields, molecular formation, and high-energy astrophysics. The source code is released under the GNU General Public License, and an interface is available for web-based usage. Detecting heartbeats is a fundamental task in biomedical engineering, with applications extending beyond heart rate monitoring to the identification of cardiac arrhythmias and fetal cardiac activity. This study introduces the Tiramisu model, which leverages the inherent temporal structure of heartbeat data by representing beats as a sequence of point clouds derived from Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). Each heartbeat is modeled as a point cloud that resides on a shared, low-dimensional nonlinear manifold, capturing the consistent structural patterns across all beats. We demonstrate that this approach yields superior inter-beat interval estimation compared to state-of-the-art methods, while also offering enhanced resistance to noise and outliers. Furthermore, the model effectively reduces dependency on the hyperparameter governing the number of nearest neighbors. By integrating multiple heartbeat representations into the Tiramisu framework, we achieve exceptional performance in estimating inter-beat intervals. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python implementation of the model, facilitating its application to various heartbeat time-series problems. We introduce a randomized singular value decomposition (R-SVD) algorithm designed to compute an initial estimate of the SVD for a tensor of order $d$ and dimension $n$ with error passing through $k$ iterations. This method extends the Subspace SVD (S-SVD) algorithm, which completes a single pass over the input data by identifying low-rank factors. Compared to S-SVD, our R-SVD offers superior computational efficiency for a fixed error level, particularly when $k$ is small. The core approach involves selecting random matrices to generate "sketches" of the $d$ modes of the tensor. By applying S-SVD to these sketches, we derive estimates for the tensor modes, which are iteratively refined over $k$ passes of the data. The final approximations of the factors are projected back onto the tensor. We establish a bound on the expected relative error of the computed singular values and demonstrate that the probability of this error exceeding a threshold $\epsilon$ diminishes exponentially as $\epsilon$ increases. Furthermore, we prove the algorithm's capability to execute exactly one pass over the data ($k=1$) while ensuring a specified error bound is met with a defined probability. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that our R-SVD is more efficient than S-SVD for solving SVD problems with a fixed error tolerance. The presented theoretical analysis and error bounds are substantially tighter than those of the Power SVD algorithm, which requires $O(n^2)$ passes to achieve a single pass while maintaining the same error bound. Additionally, we provide a practical implementation of the refined error bound for $k=1$. This implementation incorporates a stopping criterion to terminate the R-SVD algorithm once the theoretical error bound reaches a specified threshold. The proposed implementation of the refined error bound is significantly faster than directly computing the bound. The experiments indicate that this error bound serves as an effective tool for completing a single pass over the data. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/rajkumarvivek/R-SVD. Embedding static graphs has been extensively investigated and has emerged as a vital area of machine learning, serving as a powerful method to translate complex relational data into low-dimensional vector representations. These vectors effectively capture intrinsic structural and semantic properties, facilitating the application of diverse machine learning techniques. However, this survey concentrates on a less explored aspect: embedding dynamic graphs. As their name implies, these graphs are not static; both their structure and attributes evolve over time. This characteristic is crucial for numerous real-world scenarios, including online social networks, evolving relationships, and temporal events. Furthermore, dynamic graph embedding holds significant potential for downstream applications by enabling the analysis of temporal properties and facilitating the prediction of future states. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of dynamic graph embedding, covering the spectrum from foundational concepts and basic models to advanced techniques and specific use cases. It begins by defining dynamic graphs and embedding them within the broader context of graph embedding. Subsequently, it categorizes existing research based on graph characteristics, temporal properties, and intended applications. The survey then details various approaches and techniques, followed by an analysis of challenges within the field and proposed future research directions. Finally, the report examines case studies to illustrate how dynamic graph embedding can be applied in practice. By offering a thorough examination of the field, this survey aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners engaged with dynamic graph embedding. Additionally, it seeks to inspire further exploration of temporal properties in graph embedding and their application across diverse domains. Finally, the report underscores the potential of dynamic graph embedding to serve as a foundational tool for advanced applications, such as predicting future graph states. Overall, this survey provides a thorough reference for anyone interested in dynamic graph embedding. Keywords: Dynamic graph embedding, Temporal graph neural networks, Temporal link prediction, Time series on graphs. 1. Introduction Embedding nodes within a graph involves mapping them into a lower-dimensional space. This mapping preserves essential structural information, allowing nodes to be represented as vectors. These vectors facilitate the application of various machine learning techniques, such as link prediction and node classification. Dynamic graphs, characterized by changing structures over time, present additional challenges. They must account for temporal properties, such as how edge connections evolve. This survey focuses on dynamic graph embedding, which represents graphs in a time-aware manner. This field has gained considerable attention in recent years. Dynamic graph embedding is a specialized subfield of graph embedding, which has itself become a critical area of research over the past decade. Dynamic graphs extend beyond simple temporal time series on graphs, as they consist of interconnected nodes.

This study investigates the properties of the $^7$H nucleus by modeling it as a four-neutron resonance attached to a $^3$H core. The $^7$H$\to$ $^4$H+3n reaction is analyzed using a coupled-channel framework that incorporates $^3$H$\to$ $^2$H+n resonances within an optical potential model. This work provides the first calculation of the photodisintegration cross section for the $^7$H$\to$ $^4$H+3n process. Additionally, the binding energy, virtuality, width, and radius of $^7$H are determined, with the latter derived using the $^7$H$\to$ $^4$H+3n cross section. Results for the width align with findings from an alternative microscopic cluster model. Furthermore, the calculated bond energy, virtuality, and width are compared with those of other one-neutron halos. The study also examines the $^7$H$\to$ $^3$H+2n decay channels, predicting the branching ratios for $^3$H+$3n$, $^3$H+$4n$, $^2$H+$3n$, and $^2$H+$4n. Finally, the ground state of $^7$H is characterized as a four-neutron resonance bound to a $^3$H core. This characterization is supported by the system's large radius, low binding energy, and significant decay width. These predictions are compared with other theoretical approaches and existing experimental data. Finally, the potential observability of these reactions at the Facility for Intense Neutron Beams and Reactions (FIBRE) is discussed. For instance, in the image retrieval sector, an embedding function $f$ maps images from a source domain into a low-dimensional target domain such that the distribution $p_q$ of image labels in the encoded space aligns closely with the original label distribution $p_d$. Current approaches primarily rely on either (i) divergences or (ii) optimal transport to achieve these deep optimal embeddings. This paper introduces a novel framework that integrates both optimal transport and divergence measures. We propose a new generative model that characterizes both input and output label distributions using a family of distributions derived via the Sinkhorn divergences of these two distributions. This model is learned via a variational approach that approximates the intractable log-likelihood likelihood using neural networks. This methodology enables a more precise alignment of label distributions in the encoded space compared to existing techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in retrieval and clustering tasks. Furthermore, we validate the practicality of the approach by highlighting its ability to function without requiring a large dataset. We also present an ablation study comparing our approach against other deep optimal embedding methods, revealing that our framework outperforms all of them. Finally, we explore how this framework can be applied to semi-supervised clustering using USPS and CIFAR-10 datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results. The cluster's galactocentric distance is $R_{GC} = 8.02 \pm 0.01$ kpc, and its galactic latitude is $\varphi = 10.25 \pm 0.01$ degrees. We establish bounds on the average Betti numbers for a Gaussian random field, conditioned on the field being sparse with a prescribed probability. These estimates are valid within a regime characterized by a positive lower curvature. Our primary finding indicates that, within this regime, the average 1-dim Betti number exhibits at most linear growth relative to the field's complexity, measured by the integral of the Hessian's determinant. This result refines the previously established exponential upper bound. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this linear estimation is optimal within certain sub-regimes. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of these findings to more general settings. The proof relies heavily on techniques from topological data analysis, with a significant emphasis on persistent homology. Additionally, we present relevant background on topological persistence and provide an overview of recent advancements in this area. Through computational experiments, we illustrate the behavior of Betti numbers in various regimes. These examples not only validate our theoretical findings but also highlight the potential for future research applications. Notably, our results offer a framework for estimating the average Betti numbers of point clouds derived from sparse observations of Gaussian fields. This could enable the construction of a statistical model that characterizes the intrinsic geometry of such point clouds. The latter contribution represents a future direction for investigation. Our approach builds upon recent work in geometric statistics, which has utilized statistical properties of point clouds to infer the geometry of their underlying support manifolds. Our results suggest that this line of inquiry can be broadened to include geometric properties of point clouds generated by random fields defined over manifolds of positive curvature. Eye-in-hand camera calibration is a critical process for integrating robots into vision systems, enabling applications such as vision-based pick-and-place operations. While numerous self-calibration methods exist, they predominantly depend on rigorous requirements, including precise knowledge of the robot's joint configuration and multi-image datasets captured from various poses. Our approach significantly lowers the data demands by utilizing just a single image. Although this method currently supports only eye-to-hand setups, we demonstrate that it can be readily extended to the eye-in-hand configuration with minimal modifications. Furthermore, we adapt a learning-based self-calibration technique designed for single 2D images of planar objects to our use case. This adaptation involves learning a 3D-to-2D projection for each possible joint configuration, followed by aggregating these projections into a learning dataset. Our method exhibits minimal sensitivity to environmental factors like lighting and background, and our current implementation does not necessitate the calibration pattern commonly used in traditional approaches. We validate our approach across three real-world scenarios: a planar object on a table, a robotic arm grasping a coffee cup, and a robot arm manipulating a tool on a workbench. Additionally, we show that our single-image learning method performs comparably to existing methods relying on extensive pose data. Finally, we provide open-source code and pre-trained models to facilitate the deployment of our method. By streamlining the integration of robots into vision systems, our method has the potential to significantly enhance the accessibility and efficiency of robot-assisted tasks. Drawing inspiration from reinforcement learning, this work formulates a novel inverse constrained reinforcement learning problem. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a prominent method for integrating prior physical knowledge into machine learning models. Despite their widespread use, error estimation techniques capable of validating PINN solutions have been largely absent. This study introduces a novel a posteriori error estimation framework for PINNs that provides rigorous, guaranteed error bounds. The proposed method accommodates a diverse range of PINN architectures, ranging from basic implementations to those featuring automatic differentiation, refined mesh adaptation, and residual reconstruction. By applying this technique to a canonical PINN designed for solving the 2D Stokes equations, we demonstrate that the error estimator produces reliable, tight bounds and supports adaptive mesh refinement strategies. Furthermore, our findings indicate that adaptively concentrating the computational mesh in regions of high error results in more efficient error bounds and superior solution accuracy compared to adaptive approaches targeting the underlying physical model. Finally, we outline several directions for future research to expand the applicability and efficiency of this error estimation methodology. This approach incorporates Ohmic dissipation effects, which are crucial for interpreting experimental data, into the tunneling Hamiltonian. The resulting tunneling current distributions are characterized by two electrodes' resistances, known as backscattering resistances. A statistical analysis of these distributions is conducted under two scenarios: (i) when the pseudozero-mode's real part vanishes, and (ii) when its imaginary part is negligible. Our findings indicate that the tunneling current distributions for these zero pseudo-modes diverge significantly from those of Majorana modes. Furthermore, the tunneling current distributions for Majorana modes are shown to be independent of the tunneling voltage but remain dependent on the two backscattering resistances. Additionally, the degree of asymmetry in the tunneling current distributions between source and drain is governed by the ratio of the two backscattering resistances. We establish a theoretical framework for linear bandits featuring a extensive action space, comprising $K$ choices selected from $L$ "atoms." This setup models scenarios where limited linear combinations of basic components yield viable final options, applicable to both online learning and inference problems. Our framework accommodates two distinct regimes: the "sparse" regime, where optimal actions are combinations of a small number of atoms ($K \ll \max\{L, 1/L\}$), and the "dense" regime, where $K$ is approximately $L/\log(L)$. Unlike prior work primarily focused on the dense case, we derive new bounds for the sparse environment that match existing tight bounds for the two-atom scenario, thereby unifying and clarifying the understanding of these previously separate regimes. Furthermore, we introduce a novel perspective on the dense setting by demonstrating that our bounds hold even when atoms are nearly collinear, a condition that renders standard dense-bandit algorithms ineffective. Finally, we extend our analysis to inference tasks, proving that the same exploration strategies required for regret minimization in bandits are essential for achieving optimal error rates in parameter estimation. Specifically, we show that inference bounds for linear bandits are identical regardless of whether atoms are sparse or dense. Additionally, we identify a critical distinction between the two settings: while error rates in average reward prediction require the same sample complexity for both sparse and dense cases, inferring the true parameter vector necessitates significantly more data in the dense setting. This necessitates a new exploration strategy that prioritizes actions maximizing the variance of the parameter vector rather than the reward. We prove that this approach yields optimal error rates in the dense setting, whereas the bandit regret bound remains unaffected by this shift in exploration objective. To our knowledge, this represents the first exploration strategy designed specifically for inference that simultaneously achieves optimal error rates for both sparse and dense parameters. Empirical results confirm that this new approach substantially outperforms current state-of-the-art bandit algorithms in both regimes. Gapped graphene has been suggested as a promising platform for observing the valley Hall effect in experimental settings. This proposal relies on specific conditions where valley and spin are not separate quantum numbers, enabling backscattering that depends on spin. Although valley Hall currents have been detected in charge transport experiments, this work demonstrates that such currents are ineffective for spin transport because they cancel each other out. To overcome this limitation, we propose two alternative approaches for spin current injection as seen in spin Hall geometry: applying a Zeeman field or breaking time-reversal symmetry through magnetic dopants. The first method is shown to be superior for spin current injection. Furthermore, by examining the spin dependence of the valley Hall effect, we have derived a new term known as the orbital Hall effect, which is expected to be more robust in experimental realizations. Finally, we demonstrate that the orbital Hall effect can be directly measured using the Kerr effect in optical Hall geometry. Additionally, we illustrate that the Kerr effect in graphene can be interpreted as a combination of valley, spin, and orbital Hall effects. These findings suggest that the orbital Hall effect will play a crucial role in future spintronics research. Notably, the orbital Hall effect is a property inherent to any band structure, making it a fundamental concept in this field. Consequently, gapped graphene serves as an ideal system for investigating orbital Hall phenomena. We emphasize that the orbital Hall effect can be observed in a variety of geometries, including charge, spin, and optical configurations. Specifically, we show that both charge and spin Hall effects in graphene can be viewed as manifestations of the orbital Hall effect. This discovery may pave the way for the discovery of new topological materials. Overall, this study may stimulate a new era in the research of orbital physics. To achieve this, we have developed a theoretical framework that can be applied to any material. This approach enables the prediction of orbital Hall phenomena in any band structure and establishes a systematic method for identifying suitable materials for experimental observation. We anticipate that this theoretical approach will significantly advance the field of orbital physics. Additionally, it may help address the long-standing challenge of experimentally detecting the orbital magnetic moment in graphene. To this end, we have also proposed a scheme for measuring this moment. Finally, we demonstrate that the orbital Hall effect can be observed in any two-dimensional topological insulator, including graphene. This finding may help resolve the persistent issue of experimentally determining the orbital magnetization of graphene. Adversarial Machine Learning represents a dynamic and evolving domain where attackers strive to compromise models, while defenders work to maintain their integrity. This paper introduces a method for data poisoning attacks targeting semi-supervised node classification graphs, aiming to degrade graph-based neural network performance on unlabeled nodes using as few labeled seeds as possible. We develop three Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches to determine how few labeled seeds are needed to corrupt a specific target node class. These RL frameworks learn a policy that selects seeds based on the current state to maximize a defined reward function. Our results demonstrate that these RL-based attackers outperform both graph-based and machine-learned poisoning methods, achieving a 10% improvement in attack success rates while using 50% fewer labeled labeled seeds. Furthermore, experiments across three different graph datasets confirm that the proposed RL frameworks transfer effectively to unseen graph induction layer architectures. Catalogue matching serves as a critical method for assigning identifiers to sources across multiple surveys, thereby enabling cross-survey analysis. This process involves comparing source characteristics from different catalogs to determine if they represent the same object. We illustrate the effectiveness of our external catalogue matching algorithm through a real-world example: merging the Gaia DR2 catalogue with the Hubble Space Telescope Catalogue (HSTCAT) to generate a combined catalogue that includes both parallax and UVIC photometry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that sources in the HSTCAT were likely missed during the initial matching phase with Gaia DR2 due to measurement uncertainties in the UVIC photometry. This paper identifies the infinite hypergraphs whose finite vertex covers achieve the minimum possible cardinality. A hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ possesses the minimum cover property (MCP) if, for any other hypergraph $\mathcal{G}$ with the same union of vertex sets and where every edge is a subset of an edge in $\mathcal{H}$, the covering numbers satisfy $\operatorname{cov}(\mathcal{H}) \le \operatorname{cov}(\mathcal{G})$. The study demonstrates that, for finite hypergraphs, the MCP is equivalent to the inclusion-exclusion minimum cover property (ICMCP), a concept linked to the inclusion-exclusion principle. The inclusion-exclusion inclusion-exclusion property (ICIE) of a hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ is defined by the natural number equation:
$$\left|\bigcup_{v \in X} v\right| = \sum_{k=1}^{|X|} (-1)^{k-1} \sum_{X' \subseteq X} \operatorname{cov}(X'),$$
which must hold for every subset $X$ of the vertex set. The relationship between ICIE and ICMCP for infinite hypergraphs is more nuanced. The paper proves that if $\mathcal{H}$ has ICIE and its covering number is strictly less than the cardinality of its vertex set, then $\mathcal{H}$ also exhibits ICMCP. Furthermore, specific MCP hypergraphs are identified that do not satisfy ICIE, and an infinite family of such hypergraphs is constructed. Additionally, the relationship between the inclusion-exclusion property (IEP) and the minimum union property (UP)—where any subset of vertices intersects every edge—was previously established; this work confirms that two distinct UP MCP hypergraphs exist that possess the IEP. Finally, the minimum transversal property (MTRP) of $\mathcal{H}$, characterized by any subset of vertices intersecting every edge implying the existence of a minimum set intersecting all edges, is also examined. It is noted that an MTRP hypergraph may fail to satisfy ICIE, and the previous findings are utilized to construct an MCP hypergraph that does not satisfy ICMCP. The paper concludes by determining the conditions under which an MCP hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ ensures that any subset of its edges contains a minimum transversal. Ontologies serve as formal models for conceptualizing and structuring knowledge, enabling various ontology-based applications to utilize this structured data. Visualizing ontologies allows users to explore the knowledge they encode. However, current visualization techniques struggle to effectively represent large ontologies due to their high node and edge counts. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization method that employs node aggregation to organize concepts within large ontologies. By utilizing a hierarchical structure defined by a selected root concept, OntoPlot arranges the visualization in layers based on their distance from that root. We outline the design and implementation of OntoPlot and evaluate its performance on three ontologies containing 10,000 to 20,000 concepts. The visualizations produced are intuitive and easy to interpret. Furthermore, user studies indicate that OntoPlot is perceived as a valuable approach for visualizing large ontologies. Finally, we demonstrate how OntoPlot can facilitate knowledge discovery by enabling users to navigate the ontology's structure. We introduce a new approach that leverages CycleGAN to enhance semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (SEEG) models. This technique utilizes an unpaired domain conversion model to generate synthetic data from unlabeled data, thereby enriching the model's exposure to data-like information without relying on data augmentation. Additionally, we propose a straightforward yet effective strategy to simultaneously exploit unpaired unbalanced data for both data augmentation and supervised training. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to derive the two most crucial metrics for evaluating the quality of synthetic data—synthetic-data-like information and diversity—directly from the model's latent space. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves a 16.7% relative word error rate reduction compared to data augmentation methods and a 10.4% relative improvement over pre-trained OpenSpace models. Additionally, our method significantly outperforms previous synthetic data generation techniques in automated evaluations. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach is easily generalizable to other datasets and tasks. This paper is a long version of our ICASSP 2022 submission [1]. Active inference serves as the theoretical framework explaining how biological agents perceive and interact with their environment, driving the development of the free energy principle and related computational models of brain function. This study utilizes a deep active inference (DAI) agent to solve multi-robot path planning problems, a task that mirrors key biological behaviors such as social interaction and food foraging. These scenarios are represented as Markov decision processes (MDPs) derived from 2D laser scans of real-world indoor spaces. The research investigates how DAI agents address these MDPs and examines the impact of specific biological-inspired mechanisms on their performance. Specifically, we analyze the effects of introducing a dynamic prior over an agent's location within a multi-agent system, modeling a self-referential capacity common in primate cognition, and explore how this prior influences the agent's ability to track the location of a moving object. Using non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, we examined the Soret effect in binary mixtures of dimers and monomers, specifically isolating the contribution of internal degrees of freedom in flexible molecules to the phenomenon. Our results demonstrate that both the isothermal thermal diffusion ratio and the temperature-induced rotation in the flexible system are positive. Notably, we observed that rotating molecules possess a higher temperature-dependent mobility than rigid ones, leading to upward thermal diffusion for these soft molecules. We attribute this behavior to an enhanced translational diffusion coefficient in the rotating molecules, which stems from a reduced effective collision cross section. Furthermore, we determined that among all contributing factors, the shift in translational diffusion coefficients between heavy and light species is the primary driver of the Soret effect in these mixtures. These findings are corroborated by the Brokaw theory, which is subsequently extended to accommodate internal degrees of freedom. Finally, we compared our Soret coefficients with experimental data for a diphenyl ether and water mixture, achieving qualitative agreement. This supports the conclusion that the Soret effect in diphenyl ether is primarily determined by its larger translational diffusion coefficient relative to that of water. Additionally, we successfully estimated the cross correlation time between translational and rotational velocities, a parameter that could not be derived from the Soret coefficient alone. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive numerical analysis of how internal degrees of freedom influence the Soret effect in binary mixtures. These insights are valuable for interpreting experimental data, particularly regarding upfield Soret effects in flexible organic molecules, and may aid in the design of organic molecules for specific applications, such as the separation of organic compounds from water via thermal fractionation. Finally, our methodology is applicable to various molecular mixtures, including those involving alcohols, ketones, and carbohydrates. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to calculate the Soret coefficient for any binary mixture, regardless of whether upfield or downfield thermal diffusion occurs. This capability is particularly significant for investigating the upfield Soret effect in proteins and other large molecules, a topic that has been the subject of conflicting experimental and theoretical views. Our analysis indicates that the positive upfield Soret coefficient in these large molecules is largely driven by their enhanced temperature-dependent mobility. Automated Essay Scoring (AES) has been a primary driver for introducing pre-trained transformer language models to the natural language processing field. This paper explores using these models to address the high cost of human grading, which remains a major challenge in large-scale language assessment. To do this, we adapt a variety of state-of-the-art AES systems by integrating both single-model and multi-model approaches that leverage a collection of pre-trained and fine-tuned hidden state-of-the-art language models. Through an in-depth analysis of these models' performance on the automatic grading of human-written essays, we provide practical guidance on efficiently customizing them for specific AES tasks. Our experiments, which involve both fine-tuning and zero-shot settings, were conducted on two datasets: the Oxford University exam dataset and the GMAT writing dataset. While our multi-model approach yields significant improvements with full fine-tuning, we demonstrate that combining models can achieve notable gains even without fine-tuning. This confirms that a diverse ensemble of pre-trained models can effectively tackle the unique challenges of automated essay grading. Consequently, our work offers a scalable solution for automatically evaluating student writing at scale. In fine-tuned scenarios, this enables human graders to focus on scoring only a subset of essays, while our zero-shot capability allows for real-time, on-the-fly grading. We anticipate these findings to provide valuable insights for both researchers and practitioners in the field of automated essay scoring. False positives remain a significant challenge in domain adaptive pedestrian detection, where pre-trained models often generate numerous spurious detections in test images, hindering practical deployment. To address this, we introduce Box Re-Ranking, a method designed to suppress these false positives through an unsupervised process. Our approach leverages the observation that while multiple boxes may map to the same person, their aspect ratios are typically similar. We propose a box re-ranking algorithm that simultaneously adjusts both the ranking of boxes and the available aspect ratio features, followed by a simple filtering step to eliminate false positives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, without any additional training, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on real-world domain adaptation tasks. Low-quality music recordings, often captured by consumer devices like smartphones, frequently suffer from distortions such as background noise, reverberation, and microphone-induced artifacts. This study investigates a deep learning approach to music enhancement by framing music enhancement (ME) as a mapping from low-quality to high-quality music in the frequency domain. We introduce a novel method that employs a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to translate low-quality spectrograms and phase components into their high-quality equivalents. To support training, we developed a synthetic dataset of spectrograms by combining real audio signals with artificially generated noise and reverberation. This approach enables the model to learn a non-linear mapping between frequency domains of varying quality levels. Additionally, the vocoder is trained specifically to reconstruct mel-spectrograms into the original audio waveforms. Our results demonstrate that this method effectively removes noise and reverberation, significantly outperforming other state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, human evaluations confirm a substantial improvement in perceived audio quality. Finally, this method is versatile and can be applied to various scenarios, including multi-condition ME tasks such as divergence, inversion, and colorization. Although the method was developed and assessed using multi-conditional evaluation, its underlying architecture is capable of handling other ME tasks like speech separation and speech enhancement. Consequently, this technique holds the potential to enhance user-generated content on social media platforms. This paper introduces three Motional Dectors, which are novel network architectures designed to extract semantic vector representations from human motion sequences. These vectors encode critical information such as the execution of a throwing action, the object held, and the point of release. We demonstrate that these vector representations facilitate various applications within a framework that manipulates template-driven animated sequences by altering the throwing motion, the object, and the point of release. Furthermore, quantitative and qualitative evaluations indicate that the network can simultaneously and robustly learn these three concepts. The study also reveals that errors in the point of release are the most difficult to detect, and we explore the impact of such errors on the overall sequence. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first research to explicitly address and analyze the effects of an incorrect point of release in throwing animations. Our code and videos are accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/MotionalDecator. Additionally, we have released a dataset of 3D mocap throwing sequences to facilitate learning and evaluation, which can be downloaded from https://github.com/ashishkumar123/MotionalDecator/tree/master/data. We anticipate this dataset will be valuable for animating and manipulating human throwing motions. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the background and related work; Section 3 details the proposed Motional Decator and its applications; and Section 4 presents the experimental results. The binding energy (BE) of molecules on icy grains is a critical parameter for modeling astrochemical reactions. This value significantly influences adsorbed species' mobility and reactivity, the efficiency of radical formation, and the kinetics of molecular dissociation. This study introduces the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP), a database containing 1,050 computed BEs derived from 111 publications. These values pertain to ice-phase systems involving water, ammonia, and ammonia hydrate matrices. The dataset encompasses 100 atomic and diatomic species, as well as hydrides and hydrates of heavy atoms. All calculations were performed using the Gaussian 16 software suite. This work details the methodology employed to generate the database and assesses its utility. The findings indicate that BEEP offers a valuable resource for astrochemists and computational chemists by providing a wide range of BEs derived from diverse theoretical methods. This variety enables researchers to calibrate their own computational approaches. Furthermore, the study compares two BE calculation methods, revealing that the cluster-fragment correction method yields more accurate results. Finally, the paper analyzes the relationship between gas-phase and ice-phase chemical properties. This analysis confirms that, with few exceptions, a molecule's BE increases as it adheres to an ice grain. Additionally, the data suggests that a molecule's BE is intrinsically linked to its bond energy. These insights are essential for chemists seeking to predict molecular behavior in icy grain environments. The BEEP platform is freely available at https://bEEP.chemistry. (Accessed 2021-07-12). The source code can be found at https://github.com/Ankit-1234/BEEP, and the dataset itself is accessible via https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4822508. (Accessed 2021-07-12). This resource is intended to facilitate the design of future computational methods for calculating binding energies. Additionally, it will aid astrochemists in calibrating computational methods to predict ice-phase properties and assist experimentalists in interpreting their experimental data. We present a new approach for estimating expectations of Pauli operators that involves only a minimal increase in Pauli depth relative to circuits computing the expectation directly. Our method involves executing the original circuit a small number of times with randomly chosen low-depth virtual Pauli depth layers inserted between gates, followed by estimating the average expectation across these variations. Under assumptions regarding higher-order moment bounds, we demonstrate an expectation estimate with the same sample complexity as direct measurement, accompanied by an additive overhead of $O(d^2)$, where $d$ represents the target depth. This technique is particularly advantageous when applied to quantum states prepared via randomized quantum compilation, as their average Pauli depth is substantially lower than the maximum possible depth. Consequently, our technique can achieve significant runtime reductions in this context with merely a small depth increase. We also provide a variant of our method that maintains a constant number of additional measurements rather than depth, though it may require more runtime to converge. Furthermore, we illustrate how our findings can be merged with a recent strategy combining shadow tomography and variational algorithms to propose a new scheme that estimates a large collection of expectation values with minimal overhead in either depth or measurement count. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments on state families with varying average depths to assess the performance of our proposed methods. These experiments indicate that our approach outperforms existing techniques in both sample efficiency and circuit depth. Additionally, we examine the efficacy of our methods on states from the IQP problem, which are known to pose difficulties for shadow tomography. Our results show that while our methods do not guarantee an improvement over direct measurement for these specific states, they still achieve notable gains in runtime. Overall, our findings suggest that shallow shadows can serve as a valuable supplementary tool to shadow tomography, potentially enabling the practical application of shadow protocols to larger quantum systems. Spectral graph transformation has served as a robust and effective alternative to conventional image transformations like cropping and color adjustments. These techniques have enhanced model robustness against adversarial attacks and improved generalization, particularly within deep learning frameworks. We propose extending these methods to natural language by introducing sibylgraph transformations, a novel approach that generates Sibyl Graphs through a new model capable of capturing semantic relationships between words, phrases, and sentences. This SibylGraph model unifies existing linear and nonlinear transformation methods, yielding superior performance. Furthermore, sibylgraph transformations produce meaningful, interpretable, and diverse textual representations that reinforce their ability to improve model robustness. Our empirical findings demonstrate that sibyl transformations effectively increase a model's resilience to adversarial examples, maintain high accuracy on unseen data, and achieve strong results on standard text classification benchmarks. Additionally, we show that sibyl transformations outperform SibylNet, a recently developed popular graph convolutional network (GCN) model. To support research, we have made our code and model publicly available at https://github.com/abhishekgupta101/SibylGraph. Meta-learning has recently demonstrated significant potential for learning efficient representations. However, current methods lack theoretical guarantees regarding their generalization performance. This work derives generalization bounds that apply to the meta-learning of linear representations using linear chain rule descent. We demonstrate that non-negative datasets, such as word-frequency data, possess intrinsic low-dimensional structures. Furthermore, we prove that when meta-learning is applied to recover these low-rank structures from non-negative data, the process is provably stable and converges to the true representations. Finally, we provide empirical evidence indicating that these theoretical findings hold for non-convex meta-learning algorithms. By offering the first generalization bounds for meta-learning linear representations, this study establishes a foundation for developing more robust and efficient meta-learning techniques. The real numbers are partitioned into three distinct categories: rationals, irrationals, and transcendental numbers. We examine the implications of treating an object as rational, irrational, or transcendental within the frameworks of object-oriented programming and set theory. Furthermore, we present a Lagrangian density for a single hypergraph that is irrational in a specific variable and discuss the consequences of this classification. In this paper, we aim to foster interest in the properties of rational and irrational numbers, foster collaboration between mathematicians and computer scientists, and demonstrate that in set theory, classifying an object as rational can introduce unwarranted constraints into computational approaches. We contend that regardless of whether numbers are rational or irrational, they possess significant properties and hold value. Our focus is on promoting collaboration and generating novel ideas, given that the rational treatment of numbers often limits their potential. We conclude that the collaboration initiated in this work represents an original and valuable contribution. This is the third article in a series dedicated to collaborative efforts between these two disciplines. In the first paper, we derived a transcendental density for a two-dimensional plane containing points with transcendental coordinates, utilizing a fermionic and a quark-like particle. This model incorporates a Lagrangian density featuring an infinite series and employs a specific gamma matrix representation. We demonstrated that this density yields finite results for momentum and energy. In the second paper, we derived the equations of motion from that Lagrangian density, which describe a single particle capable of jumping between lattice sites in both spatial and temporal dimensions. We established that the particle's trajectory is a single fractal curve, specifically a Cantor set, and that its function is irrational. This work further illustrates that collaborative endeavors can produce novel ideas, such as the construction of a finite plane with fractional coordinates and the discovery of a finite set of points with transcendental coordinates. Additionally, the particle's position is described by a fractal set, and its trajectory forms a Cantor set. These findings open avenues for further research, including the investigation of other collaborative possibilities and the development of novel methodologies. The present study extends these collaborative results by formulating an irrational Lagrangian density for a single hypergraph. This density is derived from an infinite series and utilizes a well-known set of gamma matrices. The resulting particle is fermionic, and its trajectory constitutes a fractal set. We demonstrate that this model generates novel fractal sets, thereby advancing our understanding of collaborative research outcomes. Furthermore, this work extends the concept of a finite plane with fractional coordinates to a finite-dimensional space

Deep learning-based segmentation algorithms have demonstrated superior performance in identifying lung regions within chest X-rays (CXRs) for the subsequent task of pneumonia detection. However, the need for large amounts of labeled data to train these models remains a significant challenge. To address this, we propose a novel method that reduces data requirements by training segmentation models on unlabelled CXRs using class labels derived from an image classifier. Specifically, we evaluate various image augmentations to generate diverse training sets from a single image, thereby enhancing segmentation algorithm performance. Our approach is tested with a fully convolutional network (FCN) on the open-source LUNA16 dataset. Experimental results indicate that the model performed best when trained on a single original CXR image from LUNA16, alongside the use of the ResNet50 image classifier and five carefully selected augmentations. These algorithms were optimized to minimize the degradation of segmentation performance. The proposed method achieves an IoU score of 0.702 on LUNA16, marking an improvement of 2.8% over the baseline FCN trained on labelled CXRs. This paper introduces "Prompt Controllable Captioning," an advanced framework for generating image captions that permits users to specify desired styles or topics. While existing unstructured datasets hold potential for providing diverse and varied captions, they cannot support granular control. To address this, the study constructs a dataset comprising images paired with captions drawn from multiple classes. A novel non-GAN framework is proposed to train a model capable of producing images annotated with multiple class names. A new loss function, termed "prompting class-naming loss," is developed to enhance the diversity and quality of the generated captions. Furthermore, a non-adversarial approach to disambiguating class names is introduced to improve accuracy. Additionally, a weight-based mechanism allows users to adjust the balance between the diversity and accuracy of the generated captions. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method effectively facilitates controllable caption generation and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both generating additional labels and allowing for the management of output diversity. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has offered such control over caption generation. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/Controllable-Image-Captioning. We introduce a novel, principled, and causal framework for analyzing harm, termed the Formalism of Causal Harm (FCH). Within this framework, harm is regarded as a causal property inherent to events, which enables the application of established causal tools to evaluate phenomena like transitivity, comparability, and identity regarding various instances of harm. To ensure this analysis remains tractable, we employ a straightforward yet sufficiently expressive temporal causal model to characterize harmful events. A core assumption of our approach is that all causes of harm possess the potential, either wholly or partially, to activate an underlying "harmfulness" mechanism. By characterizing harmful events through their etiology, we provide a unified explanation for diverse empirical observations concerning human judgments of harm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework can be extended to incorporate comparisons of harm across different domains, thereby facilitating a comprehensive formalization of causal harm that supports causal inference, harm comparison, and decision-making processes. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the inaugural formal attempt to characterize harm as a causal phenomenon. This paper introduces MMLSpark, a new open-source library that unifies the advantages of PyTorch and Spark. Built on the foundation of ZFSSpark, which offers a scalable alternative to TensorFlow, MMLSpark provides an intuitive, high-level API that enables seamless integration with existing PyTorch workflows. Applications written in PyTorch can execute on a Spark cluster with minimal code adjustments, leveraging built-in data transformations and optimization techniques. Additionally, the library supports in-memory caching for training sets and predictions, which accelerates iterative models. Currently, the implementation focuses on Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) and neural networks. Future versions are expected to expand support to a broader spectrum of PyTorch components, facilitating training on larger datasets and more complex models. The paper also explores how MMLSpark can be utilized for ensemble learning and inference. This work serves as a foundation for the ongoing open-source project at http://mmlspark.org. Keywords: Deep Learning, Spark, PyTorch, Scalability, Ensembles.

We introduce a novel formulation and extension of classical heat conduction equations, encompassing cases with or without fading memory, subject to dynamic boundary conditions on bounded domains. This framework encompasses the theory of phase-field models featuring nonlocal terms and can be viewed as a Coleman-Gurtin type generalization of standard heat and stress-diffusion equations. We establish the well-posedness of this system by employing a variational approach alongside a suitable application of Banach's fixed point theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, under specific choices of internal variables and nonlocal terms, this extended model reduces to a variational system previously analyzed in our work. Finally, utilizing an appropriate energy estimate, we prove the global asymptotic stability of the equilibrium solution for a suitable variational system. These findings hold significant implications for the development of effective mathematical models in materials science. Additionally, numerical simulations are provided to illustrate the behavior of these equations. The study relies heavily on recent advancements in the analysis of nonlocal problems featuring memory-dependent interactions. Specifically, we utilize novel estimates concerning the decay of decay-type problems and the regularity of fractional Laplacians, which are derived from recent research. These results are essential for the comprehensive analysis presented herein. The introduction of this work provides a detailed exposition of these novel results and their associated proofs. Accurate short-term energy consumption forecasting is essential for managing energy systems, particularly when addressing the impact of renewable energy sources on the grid. This study focuses on predicting the electricity load of a single building, analyzing the effects of data preprocessing and improving forecast accuracy through the integration of multiple models via optimal weighted averaging. Additionally, the forecast error is evaluated using a peak-based metric designed to capture daily demand peaks. This approach is demonstrated using one year of smart meter data from a residential building equipped with a photovoltaic system. The results show that accuracy can be enhanced by utilizing multiple forecasting models and combining them using an optimal weighting scheme. However, despite these improvements, the analysis also reveals that data preprocessing can have an unexpected detrimental effect on prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the paper investigates the influence of solar irradiance on the building's load and explores the potential of blending horizontal and vertical model combinations to achieve even greater improvements. Finally, it is observed that while load models effectively capture the impact of solar irradiance, they struggle to accurately predict the building's daily peak demand. To address this, a simple yet effective solution is proposed: combining a load model with a model that forecasts peak demand occurrence. This combined model successfully predicts that the maximum consumption occurs during the morning, accounting for variability in solar irradiance. The benefits of this approach are highlighted by the network's ability to reduce morning peak demand through the activation of controllable loads. The study concludes that this proposed solution can be easily adapted to other networks by providing an estimate of the probability distribution of peak demand. The entire analysis was conducted using the Julia programming language, with all code available online. Additionally, a new extension to the OpenFBS.jl package has been developed to facilitate forecast accuracy analysis using a peak-based metric. This paper provides a detailed examination of this metric and its implementation. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that modeling peak demand is a complex challenge that requires further investigation. The methods and tools developed here can be readily extended to other networks, and the Julia package is available to support such future research. Numerous machine learning algorithms have emerged recently to boost model performance across various artificial intelligence domains. However, challenges remain stemming from insufficient data and resources. To some extent, embedding knowledge into machine learning models can mitigate these issues, although this process is intricate and demands specialized expertise. This article presents a roadmap for integrating knowledge into machine learning algorithms. It begins by defining key concepts and outlining a framework for knowledge integration. Subsequently, it reviews existing approaches for knowledge integration and induction, followed by a summary of four primary applications where such integration is fundamental. Finally, the text addresses open questions and highlights future research directions. We anticipate that this overview will assist practitioners in grasping the landscape of knowledge integration within machine learning and guide them in selecting the most appropriate algorithm for their specific tasks. Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are essential for numerous clinical tasks involving spine analysis, yet they remain challenging due to the dense packing of vertebrae in the spine and significant variations in spine orientation across different patients. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework that combines an aesthetically motivated cost function with an anatomically-based optimization strategy. This approach achieves robust localization of the entire spine in arbitrary orientations while simultaneously assigning correct labels to individual vertebrae. Specifically, we employ an aesthetically-inspired cost function that models the smooth curves of vertebrae using B-splines and localizes the spine by minimizing the total variation of these curves. For identification, we utilize a generative model that incorporates anatomical constraints, such as the normal aging process of vertebrae, to estimate the probability distribution of vertebrae types and perform labeling. We validate our method's performance and robustness through in vivo experiments across a diverse dataset of 100 CT images from various patients with spines in different orientations. The results demonstrate that our framework achieves a localization accuracy exceeding 99% and a labeling accuracy exceeding 98%. Furthermore, our framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and robustness. By integrating a simple yet effective cost function with an anatomically-motivated strategy, our framework facilitates accurate and robust localization and identification of vertebrae in CT images. Additionally, our framework supports automatic spine localization and offers a solid foundation for subsequent vertebral analysis. Although spring-based actuators have enhanced the dynamic capabilities of legged robots, they introduce complex dynamics that are difficult for standard controllers to harness. This study investigates the potential of "learning by breaking" control policies by employing an elastic actuator that is designed to deform under high torques during dynamic tasks. The controller relies on electrical measurements of the actuator's deformation to make informed decisions. Through reinforcement learning, the resulting policies effectively utilize this deformation to boost task performance. Experimental results demonstrate that compared to systems without electrical deformation sensors and corresponding controllers, the proposed approach yields an order-of-magnitude increase in running speed on a full-scale quadruped robot. Furthermore, we observe that this mechanism allows for the efficient execution of highly energetic gaits that a quasi-rigid actuator cannot support. Our findings indicate that learning control policies capable of exploiting actuator elasticity is a highly effective technique for locomotion planning and control on legged robots. We introduce the variational separability distance, a new quantum variational problem that extends the use of variational methods in quantum computing to the separability challenge. This approach is promising because it can be solved on near-term hardware and offers a straightforward interpretation of the quantum state entanglement distance. Drawing inspiration from the distance maximization techniques used in the variational quantum eigensolver, we formulate this problem as a cost minimization task. We demonstrate that minimizing the quantum cost is equivalent to maximizing the entanglement distance between pure product states and a target pure state, as well as between mixed states and a target pure state. Additionally, we investigate whether specific ansatz states are separable, examining the cost function landscape for both pure and mixed states. Finally, we explore applications of the variational separability distance within variational quantum algorithms. This study offers a novel perspective on the separability problem and provides a foundation for developing quantum algorithms that leverage variational principles. This study examines the linear physics of small-scale tearing modes in the current sheet separating two field-aligned plasma beams under slab-plasma conditions. While small-scale tearing modes are well-established in normal collisional plasmas, their characteristics in collisionless slabs differ significantly. Through an analytical dispersion relation, we demonstrate that these modes remain present in weakly collisional slabs but transition into damped Alfv\'en waves at very small scales. Unlike normal collisional plasmas where growth rates are independent of scale, here they exhibit strong scale dependence. Furthermore, we identify additional physics unique to small scales, such as the impact of finite beam width and the formation of current sheets between opposing beam directions. At very small scales, these modes become sensitive to the initial sheet's width and the relative density of the beams, with these factors directly determining the growth rate. These insights regarding small-scale tearing modes in current sheets separating field-aligned beams may have broader applications to other scenarios involving current sheets separating distinct plasma conditions. Finally, a global model of these small-scale tearing modes is established, and their potential role in the formation of magnetic islands within the magnetosheath is explored. This is particularly relevant given recent observations of unusually large magnetic islands in that region. We propose that a chain of moderately growing small-scale tearing modes could provide a viable explanation for the observed slow growth rates of these islands. Additionally, we suggest that the initial width of the background current sheet and the relative densities of the beams are likely contributors to variations in island growth rates seen in both observations and simulations. These mechanisms could also explain the slow growth rates of large islands within the low-speed boundary of Earth's bow shock. Finally, we propose that the interaction between small-scale and large-scale tearing modes in these systems may be more complex than previously assumed. These findings could offer a new perspective on the physics governing small-scale tearing modes and magnetic island growth. Finally, we outline future work to investigate the stability of these small-scale tearing modes in finite slabs and their potential influence on current sheets separating other distinct plasma conditions. This could provide a general framework for studying small-scale tearing modes in various plasma environments. This paper addresses the challenge of Fashion Image Search (FIS) within a Semi-supervised Feature-Level Attribute Manipulation (SFLAM) environment. FIS involves searching for a target garment using a single query image, whereas SFLAM refers to the capability of generating new image variants by modifying specific attributes. To date, no research has integrated these two paradigms. Our primary contribution lies in explicitly combining image retrieval with attribute manipulation, thereby simultaneously advancing both fields. We introduce a novel framework that employs a GAN-based generator to learn attribute representations and a specific search network to handle attribute queries. Our approach utilizes training data from the public Shopify fashion dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving a mean average precision of 0.6102. The accompanying video provides a comprehensive overview of our framework and its performance in both image search and attribute manipulation tasks. Furthermore, we have released a web-based tool that allows users to explore attribute search capabilities using open-source images. This tool supports a broad spectrum of attributes, including clothing items, accessories, and attributes such as "thin" and "thick." The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ahmed-ayoub/SEMISUPER-IMAGE-SEARCH-ATTRIB-MANIPULATION. Our framework holds significant potential for real-world applications, such as online fashion search engines and virtual try-on systems. By enabling users to modify attributes like "thin" or "thick," our system could facilitate more precise and satisfying shopping experiences. Additionally, our approach could enhance virtual try-on experiences by allowing users to adjust attributes like "thin" or "thick" before simulating garment fits. Ultimately, our work represents a significant step toward a more intelligent and user-centric fashion image search system. We hope this research will inspire further advancements in the field of fashion image search and attribute manipulation. This work addresses finding the $\R$-minimizing solution to the ill-posed equation $Ax=y$ within a Banach space, where $X$ carries the $\R$-norm and $Y$ a norm. The operator $A:\X\to\Y$ is assumed to be linear and bounded, potentially unbounded, and $Y$ need not be reflexive. A dual gradient flow on $Y$ is defined to locate the Bregman stable weak solution, utilizing the dual norm's modulus of smoothness to ensure dual Bregman stability. Convergence proofs are provided for both noisy and exact data scenarios, alongside an order of convergence result for exact data under a source condition, which extends the classical Fockhaus condition for Hilbert spaces. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the dual gradient flow approximates $X$-minimization under source conditions similar to those in Banach space problems, thereby extending the equivalence between Bregman stability and source conditions known in Banach spaces to the dual Banach space setting. Finally, numerical examples illustrate the method's performance on both Hilbert and non-Hilbert spaces. Notably, the method is applied to a non-Hilbert space problem with exponentially decaying data, yielding results superior to those obtained via standard $\r$-regularization. Additionally, the proposed approach serves as a new tool for solving Banach space problems, offering dual insights not achievable through standard $\R$-regularization. Finally, the paper provides an explicit convergence rate under a source condition for the reflexive case, $L^2$ spaces, and compact operators. Key concepts include Bregman stability, Banach spaces, ill-posed problems, and order of convergence.

This study addresses light field (LF) depth estimation, which is crucial for applications such as virtual reality, augmented reality, and head-mounted displays (HMDs). Unlike traditional methods, we utilize 4D light field data captured by an LF camera integrated into the device. To achieve this, we employ a convolutional neural network (CNN) featuring a U-Net architecture. A key innovation is our novel cost constructor, which generates a differentiable occlusion cost function. This function is built by analyzing epipolar slices across multiple views, allowing the network to compute a per-pixel occlusion cost that guides the depth estimation process. Experimental results on public benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach yields promising outcomes, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/oc4lf. LF images can be requested via email at olivier.bourdeaut@univ-tours.fr. We hope our contributions will enable researchers to evaluate their own depth estimation solutions. We invite you to visit our website to explore sample results. \newline

Non-Riemannian gravitational frameworks offer new avenues for analyzing gravitational phenomena within a restricted spacetime context. This approach is particularly relevant for investigating high-energy physics near singularities and space regions with limited access, such as those influenced by stringy effects, black hole horizons, and membrane surfaces. The present study examines how non-Riemannian double field theory (dft)—an extension of standard dft that incorporates corrections via nonlinearities in a small parameter $\alpha$—can yield actions for various non-Riemannian geometries. Specifically, we analyze the $\tau$-deformed D3 geometry, which exhibits membrane non-metricity, demonstrating how its associated action evolves as $\alpha$ increases. Our findings indicate that when $\alpha$ reaches the order of the string scale, the action transforms into one resembling an AdS$_5$ structure. Furthermore, we verify that these actions remain invariant under non-Riemannian gauge transformations, including local translations, $O(d,d)$ rotations, and T-duality. These results suggest that dft, even when extended with higher-order $\alpha$ corrections, maintains its capacity to unify stringy geometry, membrane non-metricity, and stringy symmetry within a unified framework. Consequently, this opens a pathway for elucidating how stringy symmetry and membrane non-metricity evolve near the membrane. A key advantage of this methodology is its reliance on a unified stringy symmetry, which facilitates the analysis of membrane non-metricity through a global $O(d,d)$ transformation. This stands in contrast to the Rosen scenario, where membrane non-metricity arises from Lorentz symmetry breaking. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that the AdS$_5$ action derived from non-Riemannian geometry is equivalent to that of Rosen. Finally, the derived actions can be viewed as an extension of the Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) action, which is essential for describing membrane dynamics. In this context, the membrane is modeled as a probe within a non-Riemannian background, with its action formulated using global $O(d,d)$ symmetry. This provides a comprehensive description of the membrane's dynamics. Overall, these findings underscore the significant role of membrane dynamics in understanding stringy geometry and non-Riemannian gravity. Additionally, they offer a means to investigate how stringy symmetry and membrane non-metricity interact, a topic of fundamental importance in string theory. To enhance performance in the next-generation home WiFi network, we introduce a channel load-aware AP/Extender selection mechanism leveraging IEEE 802.11k/v key features. This protocol allows User Stations (STAs) to identify an Access Point (AP) operating on a less congested channel and to accelerate the association process through pre-authentication. The proposed framework was implemented in the Open Source 802.11k/v Testbed (OSKVT) to validate its efficacy. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this framework boosts ST throughput by up to 10% regarding average throughput, while reducing average association time by up to 40% compared to the IEEE 802.11 standard. Furthermore, STs utilizing this mechanism achieve a 30% reduction in average frame loss probability relative to conventional 802.11 pre-authentication. Additionally, we present a channel load-aware Extender selection approach that enables STs to connect to the AP/Extendant operating on the least loaded channel. Extensive evaluations confirm that this proposed mechanism significantly improves the average uplink throughput of the STs. Extendsets that are capable Extenders show an average throughput improvement of approximately 10% compared to standard 802.11 pre-authentication. In contrast, uplink throughput for STs associated with in-efficient Extenders remains comparable to that of 802.11 pre-authentication. Our analysis indicates that STs associated with in-efficient Extenders experience a 20% increase in average frame loss probability compared to those using efficient Extenders. However, the Extender capability evaluation method is applicable to existing 802.11k/v pre-authentication schemes as well. Overall, our proposed channel load-aware AP/Extender selection scheme offers substantial improvements in uplink throughput, surpassing the results achieved by standard 802.11 pre-authentication. Additionally, the framework exhibits low computational complexity, making it suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Finally, we assess the impact of various traffic types on uplink throughput and recommend adopting a channel load-aware ST/Extender selection strategy for networks handling both voice and video traffic. This approach results in a 20% improvement in average end-to-end throughput for uplink voice traffic and a 10% improvement for uplink video traffic compared to standard 802.11 pre-authentication schemes.
